uni-ba-hist-ancient-india.title: Ancient India (Prehistory to c. 650 CE)
uni-ba-hist-ancient-india.description: Sources, prehistory, Harappan civilisation, Vedic age, Mahajanapadas, Mauryas, post-Mauryan polities, Sangam age, Guptas and Harsha. Study companion; topics commonly taught in Indian BA History programmes.

courses.title: Unit 1 · Sources and Prehistory
curricula: UGC CBCS / NEP 2020 (History of India I)
courses.summary: How historians reconstruct early India from literary, epigraphic, numismatic and archaeological sources, and the Palaeolithic, Mesolithic, Neolithic and Chalcolithic phases.
outcomes: Classify sources for ancient India and state their limits
Explain how Brahmi was deciphered and why inscriptions matter
Distinguish Palaeolithic, Mesolithic and Neolithic cultures by tools and economy
Name key prehistoric sites with their evidence
Describe Chalcolithic village cultures

scenes.text: A palm-leaf manuscript of a Buddhist text is copied for the tenth time, centuries after the events it describes.
The historian asks: who wrote it, when, for whom, and what did they want readers to believe?

steps.title: Religious literature
steps.body: Brahmanical texts include the four Vedas, Brahmanas, Aranyakas, Upanishads, the epics (Ramayana, Mahabharata), Dharmasutras/Dharmashastras and Puranas. Buddhist texts include the Pali Tipitaka and Jatakas; Jain texts include the Agamas. They reveal belief, social norms and some political memory, but were composed and redacted over long periods.

steps.title: Secular literature
steps.body: Kautilya's Arthashastra (statecraft; compiled over centuries), Panini's Ashtadhyayi (grammar, c. 5th–4th c. BCE), Kalidasa's plays, Banabhatta's Harshacharita, and Kalhana's Rajatarangini (12th c., history of Kashmir) are key. Sangam poems describe Tamil society.

steps.title: Foreign accounts
steps.body: Megasthenes' Indica survives only in quotations (Strabo, Arrian). Faxian visited in the Gupta period (early 5th c.) and Xuanzang in Harsha's time (7th c.). The Periplus of the Erythraean Sea (1st c. CE) describes Indian Ocean trade.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Do not treat normative texts (what 'should' happen, e.g. Manusmriti) as descriptions of actual practice, and do not assume foreign visitors understood local languages or society fully.

quiz.q: Kalhana's Rajatarangini is a history of:
quiz.why: Kalhana wrote the Rajatarangini in the 12th century as a chronicle of the kings of Kashmir.

options: Only in quotations by later writers
quiz.why: The original is lost, so it is known only through fragments quoted by Strabo, Arrian and others.

quiz.q: Xuanzang visited India during the reign of:
quiz.why: Xuanzang travelled in India in the 7th century and described Harsha's court and Nalanda.

scenes.text: In 1837–38 James Prinsep compares short donor inscriptions at Sanchi and cracks Brahmi.
Suddenly a king called 'Devanampiya Piyadasi' speaks across many edicts.

steps.title: Epigraphy
steps.body: Inscriptions on rock, pillars, copper plates and temple walls are contemporary and often datable. Ashokan edicts are mostly in Prakrit in Brahmi script; in the north-west Kharosthi was used, and Greek and Aramaic in Afghanistan. Land-grant copper plates become common from the Gupta period.

steps.title: Numismatics
steps.body: Punch-marked silver coins appear around the 6th–5th c. BCE. Indo-Greek coins carry royal portraits and bilingual legends; Kushanas issued large gold coinages; Gupta gold dinaras show kings performing horse sacrifice or playing the veena. Coin hoards show trade and economic health.

steps.title: Archaeology
steps.body: Excavation (vertical and horizontal), stratigraphy (lower layers usually older), pottery sequences such as Painted Grey Ware and Northern Black Polished Ware, and radiocarbon dating give material evidence independent of texts.

steps.title: Worked example: a radiocarbon estimate
steps.body: Carbon-14 has a half-life of about 5,730 years. A charcoal sample retaining 25% of its original C-14 has passed two half-lives: 2 × 5,730 = 11,460 years. Retaining 50% means about 5,730 years.

activity.prompt: A sample retains 12.5% of its original carbon-14 (half-life ≈ 5,730 years). How many years old is it?

quiz.q: Ashokan edicts were deciphered first by:
quiz.why: James Prinsep deciphered Brahmi in 1837–38, making Ashoka's edicts readable.

quiz.q: In stratigraphy, an undisturbed lower layer is usually:
quiz.why: Layers accumulate over time, so deeper undisturbed deposits are generally older.

quiz.q: Punch-marked coins were mostly made of:
quiz.why: The earliest punch-marked coins of the subcontinent were mainly silver, with some copper.

scenes.text: In Madhya Pradesh, painted rock shelters show hunting, dancing and animals.
These people lived by hunting and gathering, using stone tools that changed over thousands of years.

steps.title: Palaeolithic phases
steps.body: Lower Palaeolithic: hand-axes and cleavers (Acheulian), e.g. Attirampakkam (Tamil Nadu), Hunsgi (Karnataka), Sohan valley (chopper-chopping tools). Middle: flake tools such as scrapers and points (Nevasa). Upper: blades and burins, linked with modern humans.

steps.title: Mesolithic
steps.body: Microliths (tiny geometric stone tools hafted into arrows and sickles), more intensive foraging, early animal domestication at some sites. Sites: Bagor (Rajasthan), Adamgarh (MP), Langhnaj (Gujarat), Sarai Nahar Rai and Mahadaha (Ganga plains, with burials).

steps.title: Rock art
steps.body: Bhimbetka (a UNESCO World Heritage Site) has paintings spanning from the Upper Palaeolithic/Mesolithic to historic periods.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: 'Mesolithic' is a cultural stage, not a fixed date range across India; dates vary by region. Microliths are not 'small hand-axes'—they are composite tool parts.

quiz.why: Microliths, tiny hafted stone blades, are the hallmark tool type of the Mesolithic.
Acheulian industries of the Lower Palaeolithic are defined by bifacial hand-axes and cleavers.
The Bhimbetka rock shelters lie near Bhopal in Madhya Pradesh.

scenes.text: At Mehrgarh (Balochistan), from about 7000 BCE, people grew barley and wheat and kept cattle, sheep and goats.
Mud-brick houses and granaries mark a shift to settled life.

steps.title: Neolithic features
steps.body: Ground and polished stone tools, agriculture, animal domestication, pottery and settled villages. Regional sites: Mehrgarh; Burzahom and Gufkral (Kashmir, pit dwellings); Chirand (Bihar); Koldihwa (Belan valley, early rice claims); Utnur, Piklihal and Budihal (south India, ash mounds linked to cattle pens).

steps.title: Chalcolithic
steps.body: Copper and stone used together. Ahar–Banas (Rajasthan), Kayatha and Malwa (MP), Jorwe (Maharashtra; Inamgaon, Daimabad). Painted black-on-red pottery, village farming, some fortified settlements.

steps.title: Worked comparison
steps.body: Burzahom: pit dwellings, bone tools, dog buried with humans. Inamgaon (Jorwe): large village with houses, granaries, a possible chief's house, and burials of children in urns beneath floors.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Chalcolithic cultures of the Deccan are largely later than the Mature Harappan; do not call all of them 'pre-Harappan'.

quiz.q: Pit dwellings are a feature of:
quiz.why: Neolithic Burzahom in Kashmir is known for pit dwellings dug into the ground.
Chalcolithic combines Greek chalcos (copper) and lithos (stone).

quiz.q: Ash mounds of south India are linked with:
quiz.why: Ash mounds at Utnur and Budihal are interpreted as burnt cattle-dung accumulations at Neolithic pens.

questions.q: Which source is contemporary and often precisely datable?
questions.why: Inscriptions were made at the time of the event they record and frequently carry dates or regnal years.
Faxian travelled in the early 5th century, during Chandragupta II's reign.

questions.q: Kharosthi script was used mainly in the:
questions.why: Kharosthi, written right to left, was used in Gandhara and the north-west.
Gupta gold coins are known from inscriptions as dinaras.

questions.q: A sample retaining 50% of its C-14 is about how old?
questions.why: One half-life of carbon-14 is about 5,730 years.
Mehrgarh lies on the Kachi plain of Balochistan, Pakistan.
Jorwe is a Chalcolithic culture of Maharashtra, with Inamgaon and Daimabad among its sites.

questions.q: Northern Black Polished Ware is associated with:
questions.why: NBPW is a deluxe pottery of the early historic, roughly 6th–2nd century BCE, Ganga plains.
The Manusmriti prescribes ideal social conduct rather than recording what actually happened.
The Middle Palaeolithic is marked by flake tools such as scrapers and points.

questions.q: Ashoka's edicts in Afghanistan include inscriptions in:
questions.why: The Kandahar edicts are in Greek and Aramaic, the languages of that region's administration.

questions.q: Sarai Nahar Rai is significant for:
options: Mesolithic burials in the Ganga plain
questions.why: Sarai Nahar Rai in Pratapgarh (UP) yielded Mesolithic human burials and microliths.

courses.title: Unit 2 · The Harappan Civilisation
curricula: UGC CBCS / NEP 2020 (History of India I)
courses.summary: Origins, phases, town planning, economy, crafts, trade, religion, script and the debates on decline of the Harappan (Indus–Sarasvati) civilisation.
outcomes: Date the Early, Mature and Late Harappan phases
Describe Harappan town planning with examples
Explain the agrarian, craft and trade economy
Evaluate theories of decline
Assess the problem of the undeciphered script

scenes.text: In the 1850s railway builders used ancient bricks from Harappa as ballast.
In 1924 John Marshall announced a new civilisation after excavations by Daya Ram Sahni (Harappa, 1921) and R.D. Banerji (Mohenjodaro, 1922).

steps.title: Phases
steps.body: Early Harappan c. 3200–2600 BCE (regional cultures such as Kot Diji, Amri, Sothi-Siswal); Mature Harappan c. 2600–1900 BCE; Late Harappan c. 1900–1300 BCE (de-urbanised regional cultures).

steps.title: Extent
steps.body: From Shortughai (northern Afghanistan) to Daimabad (Maharashtra), and from Sutkagen-dor (Makran coast) to Alamgirpur (western UP). Major cities: Harappa, Mohenjodaro, Ganweriwala, Rakhigarhi, Dholavira.

steps.title: Rakhigarhi
steps.body: Rakhigarhi in Haryana is among the largest Harappan sites; ancient-DNA work on a skeleton there (published 2019) drew wide debate.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Do not call Harappa an 'Aryan' civilisation or merge it with the Vedic period; the Mature Harappan precedes the Rigveda by several centuries on mainstream chronology.

quiz.q: Mature Harappan phase is dated to about:
quiz.why: The urban, Mature Harappan phase is generally dated c. 2600–1900 BCE.
R.D. Banerji began work at Mohenjodaro in 1922.

quiz.q: The easternmost major Harappan site often cited is:
quiz.why: Alamgirpur near Meerut marks the eastern limit of Harappan settlement.

scenes.text: You enter the Lower Town: straight streets, houses opening into lanes, covered drains.
On the raised Citadel lies the Great Bath, waterproofed with bitumen.

steps.title: Planning
steps.body: Settlements often divided into a raised Citadel and a Lower Town; roads in a rough grid; standardised bricks in the ratio 1:2:4 (thickness:width:length); covered drains with inspection holes; wells in many houses.

steps.title: Key structures
steps.body: Great Bath (Mohenjodaro), the so-called Granary (Harappa and Mohenjodaro; function debated), dockyard-like basin at Lothal (debated), reservoirs and a tripartite plan at Dholavira, fire altars at Kalibangan.

steps.title: Worked example: brick ratio
steps.body: A brick 7 cm thick in the 1:2:4 ratio is 14 cm wide and 28 cm long. If a brick is 10 cm thick, it is 20 × 40 cm.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Dholavira is divided into three parts (citadel, middle town, lower town), not two. 'Granary' is a label given by excavators; many scholars doubt it.

activity.prompt: A Harappan brick in the 1:2:4 ratio is 32 cm long. What is its thickness in cm?

quiz.q: Harappan bricks typically follow the ratio:
quiz.why: Thickness, width and length of standard bricks were in the proportion 1:2:4.

quiz.q: Which site had a three-part layout and large reservoirs?
quiz.why: Dholavira in Kachchh had a citadel, middle town and lower town plus elaborate water reservoirs.
Kalibangan in Rajasthan yielded rows of fire altars along with a ploughed field.

lessons.title: Economy, crafts, trade, religion and script

scenes.text: A square steatite seal with a unicorn and signs is pressed onto a bundle of goods.
Mesopotamian texts mention ships from 'Meluhha', probably the Indus region.

steps.title: Agriculture
steps.body: Wheat, barley, lentils, sesame, cotton (Mehrgarh and later sites give early evidence), some rice; ploughed field at Kalibangan; cattle, sheep, goats, buffalo.

steps.title: Crafts and trade
steps.body: Bead-making (Chanhudaro, Lothal), shell work (Nageshwar, Balakot), copper-bronze, standardised chert weights (binary then decimal multiples). Lapis lazuli from Shortughai/Badakhshan, copper from Khetri and Oman. Harappan seals found in Mesopotamia.

steps.title: Religion and script
steps.body: Terracotta female figurines (fertility, interpretations vary), the 'proto-Shiva/Pashupati' seal (Marshall's label, debated), sacred trees and animals. The script has about 400 signs, is generally read right to left, and remains undeciphered.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Claims that the script has been 'deciphered' are not accepted by mainstream scholarship; avoid stating any reading as fact.

quiz.q: 'Meluhha' in Mesopotamian texts likely refers to:
quiz.why: Most scholars identify Meluhha with the Harappan region trading with Mesopotamia.
No proposed decipherment has been widely accepted, partly because inscriptions are very short.

quiz.q: Lapis lazuli was probably obtained via:
quiz.why: Badakhshan in Afghanistan was the main ancient lapis source, and Shortughai sat near it.

scenes.text: By around 1900 BCE, big cities shrink; seals, weights and script fade.
People move east and south into smaller villages.

steps.title: Theories
steps.body: Aryan invasion (Wheeler; now largely rejected—the 'massacre' skeletons of Mohenjodaro come from different levels), floods (Sindh), shifting/drying of the Ghaggar-Hakra, climate change and weaker monsoons, ecological stress, decline of Mesopotamian trade.

steps.title: Multi-causal view
steps.body: Most historians now see a gradual transformation from urban to rural cultures with regional variation, caused by several interacting factors rather than one catastrophe.

steps.title: Model answer outline
steps.body: Q: 'Was the end of the Harappan civilisation a sudden collapse?' Intro (phases); evidence of de-urbanisation; review each theory with evidence for/against; conclude with regional continuity (Late Harappan, Cemetery H, Jhukar).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Do not quote Wheeler's 'Indra stands accused' as an accepted conclusion; cite it as a discredited hypothesis.

statements.s: Wheeler's invasion theory is the accepted explanation today.
statements.why: Later analysis showed the skeletons did not belong to a single massacre level.

statements.s: Shifts in the Ghaggar-Hakra river system are cited as a factor.
statements.why: River shifts would have damaged agriculture in that basin.

statements.s: Late Harappan cultures show continuity in some crafts.
statements.why: Pottery and farming continued in regional forms after the cities declined.

statements.s: All Harappan sites were abandoned in a single year.
statements.why: Decline was gradual and varied by region over centuries.

quiz.q: Who proposed the Aryan invasion explanation for decline?
quiz.why: Mortimer Wheeler argued that invaders destroyed the cities, a view now largely rejected.

quiz.q: The current mainstream view of decline is:
quiz.why: Scholars stress several interacting ecological and economic causes acting over time.

quiz.q: Cemetery H culture is associated with:
quiz.why: Cemetery H at Harappa is a Late Harappan regional culture.

questions.why: Daya Ram Sahni began excavations at Harappa in 1921.
The Great Bath stands on the citadel mound of Mohenjodaro.

questions.q: A ploughed field was found at:
questions.why: Kalibangan preserved furrow marks of an Early Harappan ploughed field.

questions.q: Harappan weights were made mostly of:
questions.why: Standardised cubical weights were usually made of chert.

questions.q: A brick 9 cm thick in the 1:2:4 ratio is how long?
questions.why: Length is four times thickness, so 4 × 9 = 36 cm.

questions.q: Early Harappan phase is dated about:
questions.why: Regional Early Harappan cultures flourished c. 3200–2600 BCE.
Chanhudaro has bead-making workshops with drills and unfinished beads.
The Khetri copper belt in Rajasthan is a likely source of Harappan copper.

questions.q: The Harappan script is usually read:
questions.why: Sign spacing and overlaps suggest it was written mostly right to left.

questions.q: Which statement on the 'Pashupati' seal is best?
questions.why: Marshall called it proto-Shiva, but many scholars find the identification uncertain.

questions.q: Which factor is NOT usually cited for decline?
questions.why: Iron was not in use in that region c. 1900 BCE, so iron-armed invaders do not fit the evidence.
A large inscription of ten signs, the so-called signboard, was found at Dholavira's gateway.

courses.title: Unit 3 · Vedic Age, Mahajanapadas and New Religions
curricula: UGC CBCS / NEP 2020 (History of India I)
courses.summary: Early and Later Vedic society, polity and economy; second urbanisation and the sixteen mahajanapadas; rise of Magadha; Buddhism and Jainism.
outcomes: Contrast Early and Later Vedic economy, polity and society
Explain the evolution of varna
List the mahajanapadas and explain Magadha's rise
Summarise the teachings of the Buddha and Mahavira
Explain why heterodox sects spread

scenes.text: A Rigvedic hymn praises Indra for helping the tribe win cattle in battle (gavishti).
The rajan consults the sabha and samiti.

steps.title: Geography and date
steps.body: Rigveda composed c. 1500–1000 BCE in the Sapta Sindhu region (Punjab and neighbourhood). Ten books (mandalas); books 2–7 are the oldest 'family books'.

steps.title: Polity and economy
steps.body: Tribal (jana) polity under a rajan; assemblies sabha, samiti, vidatha; gifts (bali) rather than regular taxes. Pastoral economy with cattle as wealth; some farming of barley (yava). Battle of Ten Kings (dasarajna) on the Parushni (Ravi).

steps.title: Society and religion
steps.body: Kinship-based; the term 'shudra' appears only in the late Purusha Sukta (Book 10). Women attended assemblies; deities Indra, Agni, Varuna, Soma; sacrifice (yajna) central.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Rigvedic society did not have a rigid four-varna caste system; the Purusha Sukta is a late addition.

pairs: Hymn on origin of four varnas

quiz.q: The Purusha Sukta is in Rigveda book:
quiz.why: The Purusha Sukta is in Mandala 10, among the latest parts of the Rigveda.

quiz.q: The main form of wealth in Rigvedic times was:
quiz.why: Rigvedic hymns repeatedly pray for cattle, which were the chief measure of wealth.

quiz.q: The Battle of Ten Kings was fought on the river:
quiz.why: The dasarajna battle was fought on the Parushni, identified with the Ravi.

scenes.text: Settlers move into the Ganga–Yamuna doab; Painted Grey Ware pots appear.
A king performs the ashvamedha to proclaim his power.

steps.title: Economy
steps.body: c. 1000–600 BCE. Agriculture becomes primary; rice (vrihi) appears; iron (shyama ayas, 'black metal') known; PGW sites like Hastinapura and Atranjikhera.

steps.title: Polity
steps.body: Janapadas (territorial units); larger kingdoms like Kuru-Panchala; grand sacrifices rajasuya, vajapeya, ashvamedha; sabha and samiti lose power; ratnins assist the king.

steps.title: Society and religion
steps.body: Varna hardens; four ashramas take shape in later texts; gotra exogamy; women's status declines. Prajapati and ritualism rise; Upanishads question ritual and focus on atman and brahman.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Do not claim iron caused all expansion by itself; historians debate how much iron tools drove forest clearance.

quiz.why: Painted Grey Ware sites such as Hastinapura correspond broadly to the Later Vedic doab.
Upanishadic thought explores the identity of the self (atman) with ultimate reality (brahman).

options: High functionaries in the king's court
quiz.why: Later Vedic texts list ratnins as officials and dignitaries connected with the royal consecration.

lessons.title: Mahajanapadas and the rise of Magadha

scenes.text: The Anguttara Nikaya lists sixteen mahajanapadas, from Gandhara to Assaka.
Magadha, with iron, elephants and fertile land, swallows its rivals.

steps.title: The sixteen
steps.body: Anga, Magadha, Kashi, Kosala, Vajji, Malla, Chedi, Vatsa, Kuru, Panchala, Matsya, Surasena, Assaka, Avanti, Gandhara, Kamboja. Most were monarchies; Vajji and Malla were ganas/sanghas (oligarchic).

steps.title: Dynasties of Magadha
steps.body: Haryanka: Bimbisara, Ajatashatru (capital Rajagriha; Pataliputra founded by Udayin). Shishunaga. Nanda: Mahapadma Nanda, enormous wealth. Then Maurya (c. 321 BCE).

steps.title: Why Magadha rose
steps.body: Iron ores of south Bihar, fertile alluvium, rivers for transport and defence (Ganga, Son), forests supplying elephants, ambitious rulers, strategic capitals (Rajagriha ringed by hills, Pataliputra at river confluence).

steps.title: Second urbanisation
steps.body: Cities (Rajagriha, Shravasti, Kaushambi, Ujjayini), NBPW pottery, punch-marked coins and guilds appear c. 6th–4th c. BCE.

activity.text: The list of sixteen mahajanapadas is found in the Buddhist text ___. Magadha's first capital was ___, and its later capital was ___.

quiz.why: Vajji was a confederacy governed by an assembly of clan leaders rather than one king.
Tradition credits Udayin, Ajatashatru's successor, with establishing Pataliputra as capital.
Nearby iron ores allowed better tools and weapons, strengthening Magadha.

scenes.text: At Bodh Gaya, Siddhartha Gautama attains enlightenment.
At Sarnath he preaches the first sermon, 'turning the wheel of dhamma'.

steps.title: Buddha's teaching
steps.body: Four Noble Truths (suffering, its cause in craving, its cessation, the path) and the Eightfold Path (right view, intention, speech, action, livelihood, effort, mindfulness, concentration). Middle Way; rejection of Vedic ritual authority; sangha open to all castes and, later, women.

steps.title: Jainism
steps.body: Vardhamana Mahavira, the 24th tirthankara (Parshvanatha the 23rd). Triratna: right faith, right knowledge, right conduct. Five vows: ahimsa, satya, asteya, aparigraha, brahmacharya (added by Mahavira). Later split into Digambara and Shvetambara.

steps.title: Councils
steps.body: Buddhist councils: Rajagriha (under Ajatashatru), Vaishali, Pataliputra (under Ashoka), and Kashmir (under Kanishka), where Mahayana ideas gained ground.

steps.title: Why they spread
steps.body: Use of Prakrit/Pali, patronage by kings and merchants, appeal to new urban classes, and opposition to costly animal sacrifice that hurt farmers.

quiz.q: The fifth vow brahmacharya was added by:
quiz.why: Jain tradition says Mahavira added celibacy to Parshvanatha's four vows.

quiz.q: The Fourth Buddhist Council was held under:
quiz.why: The Fourth Council in Kashmir was held under the Kushana king Kanishka.

quiz.q: The Buddha's first sermon was at:
quiz.why: He gave the first sermon in the deer park at Sarnath near Varanasi.

questions.q: The Rigveda has how many mandalas?
questions.why: The Rigveda is arranged in ten books called mandalas.

questions.q: Vrihi in Later Vedic texts means:
questions.why: Vrihi denotes rice, which appears in Later Vedic texts as farming expands east.
Mahavira is counted as the 24th and last tirthankara of the present age.
Ujjayini was the capital of northern Avanti.
Bimbisara was a Haryanka king of Magadha.
Later Vedic texts call iron 'black metal', shyama or krishna ayas.

questions.q: Which is NOT in the Eightfold Path?
questions.why: Sacrifice is not part of the Eightfold Path, which rejects ritual as the route to liberation.
Sabha and samiti were tribal assemblies in the Rigveda.
Digambara means sky-clad, and its monks renounce clothing.
NBPW pottery and punch-marked coins accompany the rise of early historic cities.
The Buddhist Anguttara Nikaya gives the standard list of sixteen.

questions.q: Best explanation for the spread of Buddhism among merchants:
options: It valued ethics over birth and costly ritual
questions.why: Its emphasis on conduct rather than birth and ritual suited the new urban commercial groups.

courses.title: Unit 4 · Mauryas, Post-Mauryan India and the Sangam Age
curricula: UGC CBCS / NEP 2020 (History of India I/II)
courses.summary: Mauryan state and administration, Ashoka's dhamma, decline; Shungas, Indo-Greeks, Shakas, Kushanas and Satavahanas; Sangam Tamilakam and Indo-Roman trade.
outcomes: Describe Mauryan administration from the Arthashastra, Indica and edicts
Explain Ashoka's dhamma and its purpose
Evaluate causes of Mauryan decline
Compare major post-Mauryan polities
Describe Sangam society and Indo-Roman trade

scenes.text: Around 321 BCE Chandragupta Maurya, advised by tradition's Kautilya, overthrows the Nandas.
He later defeats Seleucus Nicator, who sends Megasthenes as envoy to Pataliputra.

steps.title: Rulers
steps.body: Chandragupta (c. 321–297 BCE), Bindusara (Amitraghata), Ashoka (c. 268–232 BCE). Chandragupta is said in Jain tradition to have retired to Shravanabelagola.

steps.title: Administration
steps.body: King aided by a council (mantriparishad); provinces under princes (kumaras) at Taxila, Ujjayini, Tosali, Suvarnagiri; officials such as samaharta (revenue collector) and sannidhata (treasurer) in the Arthashastra; Megasthenes describes a six-board committee for Pataliputra.

steps.title: Economy
steps.body: Land revenue (bhaga, typically one-sixth in texts), state farms (sita), control of mines and trade, standing army and spy network.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: The Arthashastra's final form is later than Chandragupta; use it as a guide to ideals of statecraft, not a literal Mauryan record. Some scholars (e.g. Gerard Fussman) argue the empire was less centralised than once thought.

quiz.why: After their treaty, Seleucus sent Megasthenes to Chandragupta's court.
Both served as seats of Mauryan provincial governors, often princes.
Amitraghata, from Greek Amitrochates, means destroyer of enemies.

scenes.text: Rock Edict XIII records that about 1,50,000 people were deported and 1,00,000 killed in the Kalinga war.
Ashoka expresses remorse and turns to conquest by dhamma.

steps.title: Edicts
steps.body: 14 Major Rock Edicts, Minor Rock Edicts (Maski and Gujarra name 'Ashoka'), Pillar Edicts (seven; Delhi-Topra has all seven), Kalinga Separate Edicts. Most in Prakrit, Brahmi script.

steps.title: Dhamma
steps.body: An ethical code: respect for elders, kindness to slaves and servants, tolerance of all sects (Rock Edict XII), restraint in speech, non-violence towards animals. Dhamma-mahamattas appointed (Rock Edict V). It was not identical with Buddhism, though Ashoka was a Buddhist lay follower.

steps.title: Outreach
steps.body: Missions to Sri Lanka (Mahinda and Sanghamitra, per tradition) and Hellenistic kings named in Rock Edict XIII (Antiochus, Ptolemy, Antigonus, Magas, Alexander).

steps.title: Model answer: was dhamma political?
steps.body: Argue both: (1) personal ethic after Kalinga; (2) unifying ideology for a diverse empire, run through officials. Conclude it blended conviction and statecraft (Romila Thapar's view).

statements.s: Rock Edict XIII describes the Kalinga war.
statements.why: It records the casualties and Ashoka's remorse.

statements.s: Dhamma required all subjects to become Buddhist.
statements.why: It was a general moral code urging tolerance of all sects.

statements.s: The Maski edict names Ashoka.
statements.why: Maski is one of the minor rock edicts that uses the name Ashoka.

statements.s: Ashokan edicts are mostly in Sanskrit.
statements.why: Most are in Prakrit dialects.

quiz.why: Rock Edict V announces officers to promote dhamma among all groups.

quiz.q: Which edict calls for tolerance of all sects?
quiz.why: Rock Edict XII urges respect for the sects of others and restraint in speech.

quiz.q: Ashoka's Kalinga war is in present-day:
quiz.why: Kalinga lay in coastal Odisha.

scenes.text: About 185 BCE the general Pushyamitra Shunga kills Brihadratha, the last Maurya.
In the north-west, Indo-Greek kings mint coins with portraits and Greek-Prakrit legends.

steps.title: Decline debate
steps.body: H.C. Raychaudhuri blamed Ashoka's pacifism; H.P. Shastri a brahmanical reaction; Romila Thapar stresses over-centralisation and weak successors; D.D. Kosambi points to economic strain (e.g. debased coins). Present a balanced, multi-causal answer.

steps.title: North India
steps.body: Shungas (Pushyamitra; Bharhut stupa railings), Kanvas; Indo-Greeks (Menander/Milinda, dialogue Milindapanho with Nagasena); Shakas (Rudradaman's Junagadh inscription, 150 CE, early long Sanskrit inscription); Kushanas (Kanishka, era of 78 CE, Gandhara and Mathura art).

steps.title: Deccan
steps.body: Satavahanas: Gautamiputra Satakarni (Nasik inscription of his mother Gautami Balashri); metronymics; land grants to Buddhist monks; ports linked to Roman trade.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Kanishka's era (78 CE) is the basis of the Shaka era used in the Indian national calendar; don't confuse it with the Vikrama era (58/57 BCE).

events.text: Start of Shaka era (linked to Kanishka by many scholars)

quiz.q: Milindapanho records dialogue between Menander and:
quiz.why: The Milindapanho is a dialogue between King Milinda (Menander) and the monk Nagasena.
Rudradaman's Junagadh record of 150 CE describes repairing the Sudarshana lake.
Gandhara sculpture blends Buddhist themes with Hellenistic and Roman techniques.

scenes.text: Sangam poems describe Yavana ships bringing gold and taking pepper from Muciri (Muziris).
At Arikamedu near Puducherry, Roman amphorae and Arretine ware are excavated.

steps.title: Sangam literature
steps.body: Tamil poems c. 3rd c. BCE–3rd c. CE (dating debated): Ettuthogai and Pattupattu; Tolkappiyam (grammar). Poems are akam (love) and puram (war, heroism). Five tinai landscapes: kurinji, mullai, marutam, neytal, palai.

steps.title: Polities
steps.body: Three crowned kings (muvendar): Cheras, Cholas (Karikala), Pandyas; and chieftains (velir). Hero stones (nadukal) for fallen warriors.

steps.title: Trade
steps.body: Pepper, pearls, beryl, textiles exported; Roman gold and silver coins found in large hoards in south India; Periplus lists ports. Pliny complained of the drain of Roman gold to India.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: 'Sangam' refers to a later tradition of poets' academies at Madurai; treat the three-sangam legend as tradition, not documented fact.

quiz.why: Excavations at Arikamedu revealed Roman amphorae and Arretine ware, proof of Indo-Roman trade.
Akam, meaning interior, covers love and private emotion, while puram covers public life.
Muvendar are the Chera, Chola and Pandya crowned kings of Sangam texts.

questions.q: Ashoka's Kalinga war is described in:
questions.why: Rock Edict XIII narrates the war and Ashoka's remorse.
Brihadratha was killed by Pushyamitra Shunga c. 185 BCE.

questions.q: Which Satavahana ruler is praised in the Nasik inscription?
questions.why: Gautami Balashri's Nasik inscription praises her son Gautamiputra Satakarni.
The Shaka era starts in 78 CE.

questions.q: Delhi-Topra pillar is notable because it has:
questions.why: Delhi-Topra is the only pillar carrying all seven pillar edicts.
He reports six boards of five members each managing the city.

questions.q: Who blamed Brahmanical reaction for Mauryan decline?
questions.why: H.P. Shastri argued Ashoka's policies provoked a brahmanical reaction.

questions.q: Bharhut stupa railings are associated with the:
questions.why: Bharhut's carved railings date to the Shunga period.
Muziris was on the Kerala coast, near Pattanam.

questions.q: Hero stones in Tamil are called:
questions.why: Nadukal are memorial stones raised for warriors who died in battle.

questions.q: Which is the best description of Ashoka's dhamma?
options: A broad ethical code also serving unity
questions.why: Dhamma combined personal ethics with an ideology that helped hold a diverse empire together.

options: Drain of Roman gold to India
questions.why: Pliny lamented Rome spent large sums on Eastern luxuries, including Indian goods.

courses.title: Unit 5 · Guptas, Harsha and Revision
curricula: UGC CBCS / NEP 2020 (History of India II)
courses.summary: Gupta political history, administration, economy and culture; the 'Golden Age' debate; Harsha and the Pallava–Chalukya south; a revision lesson with exam-style answer practice.
outcomes: Outline Gupta political history from inscriptions
Explain land grants and agrarian change
Evaluate the 'Golden Age' label
Describe Harsha's reign from Bana and Xuanzang
Write structured long answers on ancient India

story.title: A poet's praise on an old pillar

scenes.text: Harishena's Prayaga Prashasti is carved on the same Allahabad pillar that carries Ashoka's edicts.
It praises Samudragupta as conqueror, poet and musician.

steps.title: Rulers
steps.body: Chandragupta I (Gupta era from 319–20 CE; marriage to Licchavi princess Kumaradevi), Samudragupta (Prayaga Prashasti; southern campaign of capture-and-release), Chandragupta II Vikramaditya (defeat of the Western Kshatrapas; Mehrauli iron pillar; Faxian's visit), Kumaragupta I (Nalanda's foundation traditionally credited), Skandagupta (resisted the Hunas).

steps.title: Administration
steps.body: Grand titles (maharajadhiraja); provinces (bhukti) under uparikas, districts (vishaya) under vishayapatis; local bodies of merchants and artisans at Kotivarsha (Damodarpur plates).

steps.title: Economy
steps.body: Brahmadeya land grants to brahmanas and religious bodies, often with fiscal and administrative rights; gold dinaras; scholars debate decline of long-distance trade and of towns.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Samudragupta did not annex the southern kingdoms; he defeated and reinstated them (grahana-moksha-anugraha).

events.text: Gupta era begins with Chandragupta I

quiz.q: The Prayaga Prashasti was composed by:
quiz.why: Harishena, Samudragupta's court poet, composed the Allahabad pillar prashasti.

quiz.q: Chandragupta I married a princess of the:
quiz.why: His marriage to the Licchavi Kumaradevi is celebrated on Gupta coins.

quiz.q: Which Gupta ruler fought the Hunas?
quiz.why: Skandagupta's Bhitari inscription records his victory over the Hunas.

scenes.text: Nationalist historians praised Kalidasa, Aryabhata and Ajanta as a golden age.
Others asked: golden for whom—what of shudras, untouchables and women?

steps.title: Achievements
steps.body: Kalidasa (Abhijnanashakuntalam, Meghaduta), Aryabhata (Aryabhatiya, 499 CE; rotation of the earth), Varahamihira; Puranas in their present form; early structural temples (Deogarh Dashavatara, Sanchi Temple 17); Sarnath Buddha; Ajanta murals (under the Vakatakas).

steps.title: The critique
steps.body: R.S. Sharma and others link land grants to growing peasant subjection and the rise of 'Indian feudalism'; Faxian notes chandalas living outside towns; decline of urban centres in some regions.

steps.title: Structuring a 15-mark answer
steps.body: Intro: define the label and its nationalist origin. Body 1: political unity and culture. Body 2: economy and land grants. Body 3: social hierarchy and gender. Conclusion: 'golden' for elites in culture; uneven for society.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Ajanta paintings of the 5th century are largely Vakataka-patronised, not 'Gupta paintings'.

activity.prompt: Supports or questions the 'Golden Age' label?

items.text: Chandalas forced to live outside towns
Land grants with rights over peasants

quiz.why: Aryabhata states he wrote it at age 23 in 499 CE.
The Gupta-period Dashavatara temple stands at Deogarh in Uttar Pradesh.
R.S. Sharma argued land grants created a feudal order from the Gupta period onward.

lessons.title: Harsha and the south (Pallavas and Chalukyas)

scenes.text: Harsha of Kanauj marches south; Pulakeshin II of Badami stops him on the Narmada.
Ravikirti's Aihole inscription (634 CE) records the victory.

steps.title: Harsha (606–647 CE)
steps.body: Pushyabhuti dynasty of Thanesar; moved capital to Kanauj. Sources: Bana's Harshacharita, Xuanzang. Held assemblies at Kanauj and Prayaga; patron of Nalanda; wrote plays Ratnavali, Priyadarshika, Nagananda.

steps.title: Pallavas and Chalukyas
steps.body: Chalukyas of Badami (Pulakeshin II; temples at Aihole, Badami, Pattadakal). Pallavas of Kanchi (Mahendravarman I, Narasimhavarman I 'Mamalla' who took Badami c. 642; Mamallapuram rathas and shore temple, the latter under Rajasimha).

steps.title: Nalanda
steps.body: Xuanzang studied at Nalanda under Shilabhadra; it was a major Buddhist mahavihara with many monks.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: The Shore Temple is later (Rajasimha, c. 700) than the Pancha Rathas (Narasimhavarman I).

quiz.why: Pulakeshin II stopped Harsha's southern advance, as the Aihole inscription records.
Narasimhavarman I took Badami and gained the title Vatapikonda.
Harsha ruled from Kanauj after uniting the Pushyabhuti and Maukhari realms.

lessons.title: Revision: key points and exam answer writing

scenes.text: You have 3 hours for 5 long answers. A one-page key-point sheet saves you.
Each answer: intro, 3–4 themed paragraphs with evidence, a historiographical point, conclusion.

steps.title: Key dates sheet
steps.body: c. 7000 BCE Mehrgarh farming; c. 2600–1900 BCE Mature Harappan; c. 1500–1000 BCE Rigveda; c. 1000–600 BCE Later Vedic; 6th c. BCE mahajanapadas; c. 321 BCE Mauryas; c. 261 BCE Kalinga; c. 185 BCE Shungas; 78 CE Shaka era; 150 CE Junagadh; 319–20 CE Gupta era; 499 CE Aryabhatiya; 606 CE Harsha; 634 CE Aihole inscription.

steps.title: Evidence words
steps.body: Name the source type with every claim: 'the Nasik inscription shows…', 'Faxian reports…', 'excavations at Lothal reveal…'. Examiners reward specific evidence.

steps.title: Sample question styles (original)
steps.body: 1. 'Assess the role of iron in Later Vedic expansion.' 2. 'Discuss Ashoka's dhamma as statecraft.' 3. 'Was the Gupta age a golden age?' 4. 'Examine sources for Sangam society.' 5. 'Explain the rise of Magadha.'

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Narrating dynasties without argument; quoting one historian as final truth; mixing up BCE and CE ordering (counting down before 0).

activity.prompt: Order the steps of writing a long answer
items: Read the directive word (discuss, assess, examine)
Plan 3–4 themes with evidence for each
Write a short introduction stating your argument
Develop each theme with named sources
Conclude by answering the question directly

quiz.why: The Kalinga war (c. 261 BCE) precedes 78 CE, 150 CE and 499 CE.

options: Weigh arguments and reach a judgement
quiz.why: Assess means evaluating strengths and weaknesses before giving a reasoned verdict.

quiz.q: How many years between 185 BCE and 78 CE?
quiz.why: There is no year zero, so from 185 BCE to 78 CE is 185 + 78 − 1 = 262 years.

questions.why: The Gupta era is reckoned from 319–20 CE.

questions.q: Faxian visited during the reign of:
questions.why: Faxian was in India c. 399–412, under Chandragupta II.

questions.q: Mehrauli iron pillar is linked with:
questions.why: Its 'Chandra' is generally identified with Chandragupta II.

questions.q: Bhukti in Gupta administration was a:
questions.why: Bhuktis were provinces under uparikas.
Kalidasa wrote the lyric poem Meghaduta.

questions.q: Ajanta's 5th-century caves were largely patronised under the:
questions.why: Vakataka ruler Harishena's era saw most later Ajanta caves.
Harsha is credited with Nagananda, Ratnavali and Priyadarshika.
Pattadakal is a Chalukyan temple complex in Karnataka.

questions.q: Samudragupta's southern policy is described as:
questions.why: The prashasti says he captured southern kings and then released and reinstated them.
With no year zero, 261 + 150 − 1 = 410 years.

options: Local merchant/artisan representation in district administration
questions.why: They name the chief merchant, guild head and scribe as members of the district administration at Kotivarsha.

questions.q: A strong critique of the 'Golden Age' idea rests on:
questions.why: Critics point to growing caste hierarchy and peasant dependence created through land grants.

uni-ba-hist-historiography.title: Historiography & Historical Methods
uni-ba-hist-historiography.description: What history is, sources and criticism, major schools (Rankean, Marxist, Annales, Subaltern), Indian historiography, and research methods. Study companion; topics commonly taught in Indian BA History programmes.

courses.title: Unit 1 · Meaning, Nature and Scope of History
courses.summary: What history is, facts and interpretation (E.H. Carr), objectivity and bias, causation, and history's relation to other disciplines.
outcomes: Define history and distinguish past from history
Explain Carr's view of facts and the historian
Discuss objectivity, bias and relativism
Analyse causation and contingency
Relate history to social sciences and literature

scenes.text: Millions crossed the Rubicon stream; only Caesar's crossing became a historical fact.
E.H. Carr compares facts to fish the historian chooses to catch.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body: 'History' means both the past and the study/writing of it. Greek historia = inquiry (Herodotus). Carr (What is History?, 1961): 'an unending dialogue between the present and the past'.

steps.title: Facts and interpretation
steps.body: Ranke's ideal: show the past 'wie es eigentlich gewesen' (as it actually was). Carr: facts become historical only when selected by historians; study the historian before the facts. R.G. Collingwood (The Idea of History, 1946): history is re-enactment of past thought.

steps.title: Scope
steps.body: Political, economic, social, cultural, environmental, gender, global history, history from below; micro-history (Carlo Ginzburg's The Cheese and the Worms).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Do not equate 'past' and 'history'; the past is gone, history is our reconstruction of it from evidence.

pairs: Unending dialogue between present and past

quiz.q: What is History? was written by:
quiz.why: E.H. Carr delivered these Trevelyan lectures in 1961.
He argued historians rethink the thoughts behind past actions.

quiz.q: The Cheese and the Worms is an example of:
quiz.why: Ginzburg reconstructs the world of one miller, Menocchio.

scenes.text: One textbook calls 1857 a mutiny; another calls it a war of independence.
Is one simply wrong, or do both select facts differently?

steps.title: Objectivity
steps.body: Positivists sought scientific objectivity. Critics note selection, language and perspective shape all accounts. Peter Novick's That Noble Dream (1988) traced debates among American historians.

steps.title: Bias types
steps.body: National, religious, class, gender, confirmation bias, presentism (judging the past by present values), anachronism.

steps.title: Controls
steps.body: Multiple sources, transparency (footnotes), peer review, stating assumptions, considering counter-evidence.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Relativism does not mean 'anything goes'; claims must still be tested against evidence.

items.text: Using only sources that support your thesis
Condemning medieval people for not knowing germ theory
Ignoring evidence that contradicts your argument

options: Judging the past by today's values
quiz.why: Presentism imposes present-day values on past actors.
Novick traced the objectivity question in American historiography.
Citing and cross-checking let readers test the argument.

scenes.text: Pascal joked that if Cleopatra's nose had been shorter, history would have changed.
Carr calls such accidents real but not useful for general explanation.

steps.title: Kinds of causes
steps.body: Long-term (structural), short-term (precipitating), triggers; necessary vs sufficient causes; multi-causality.

steps.title: Chance and determinism
steps.body: Determinism (e.g. crude economic determinism) vs contingency; Carr: rational causes can be generalised, accidental ones cannot. Counterfactuals used carefully (Niall Ferguson's Virtual History).

steps.title: Example: WWI
steps.body: Long-term: alliances and militarism. Short-term: July Crisis. Trigger: Sarajevo assassination. Contingency: wrong turn by the Archduke's driver.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Listing causes without weighing them; confusing trigger with cause.

options: The immediate event that sets off change
quiz.why: A trigger is the precipitating event, not the underlying cause.
He accepted chance occurs but said it cannot yield general lessons.
Counterfactuals imagine alternative outcomes to test causal claims.

story.title: An archaeologist, an economist and a poet

scenes.text: An archaeologist dates a village by pottery.
An economist reads its grain prices; a poet's songs reveal its feelings. The historian needs all three.

steps.title: Social sciences
steps.body: Economics (price series, cliometrics—Fogel and Engerman's Time on the Cross, 1974, debated), sociology (class, caste), anthropology (ritual, kinship), geography (environment—Braudel), political science.

steps.title: Humanities
steps.body: Literature (texts as evidence, narrative form—Hayden White's Metahistory, 1973), philosophy, art history.

steps.title: Sciences
steps.body: Archaeology, radiocarbon and dendrochronology, ancient DNA, climate proxies.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Borrowing models uncritically; history attends to change over time and specific context.

quiz.why: Hayden White published Metahistory in 1973.
It applies economic theory and statistics to history.
It counts and matches annual tree-ring patterns.

questions.why: Historia means inquiry or investigation.

questions.q: 'Wie es eigentlich gewesen' is linked to:
questions.why: Ranke used the phrase in 1824.
It was published posthumously in 1946.
It applies a modern institution to an ancient context.

options: Without it the event could not happen
questions.why: A necessary condition must be present for the outcome.

questions.q: Time on the Cross is an example of:
questions.why: Fogel and Engerman applied quantitative methods to slavery.

questions.q: Carr's advice before studying the history:
questions.why: Carr said to understand the historian's position first.

options: Perspective shapes accounts, but evidence still matters
questions.why: Moderate relativism accepts perspective while requiring evidential testing.

options: Small units to illuminate larger patterns
questions.why: It studies a person, village or event in depth.
It stresses accidental influences on events.

questions.q: Which is a structural cause of 1857?
questions.why: Annexations and revenue burdens built discontent over time.

options: Evidence-based interpretation of change over time
questions.why: Historians interpret evidence to explain change and continuity.

courses.title: Unit 2 · Sources and Source Criticism
courses.summary: Primary and secondary sources, external and internal criticism, archives, oral history and memory, visual and digital sources.
outcomes: Classify primary, secondary and tertiary sources
Apply external criticism (authenticity) and internal criticism (credibility)
Use archives and catalogues
Conduct and evaluate oral history
Analyse visual and digital sources

story.title: A letter, a textbook, an encyclopedia

scenes.text: A 1942 letter from a Quit India activist sits in an archive.
A 2005 monograph uses it; an encyclopedia summarises the monograph.

steps.title: Primary
steps.body: Created at or close to the time by participants or witnesses: inscriptions, coins, official records, letters, diaries, newspapers, photographs, oral testimonies, artefacts.

steps.title: Secondary and tertiary
steps.body: Secondary: later analyses based on primary sources (monographs, journal articles). Tertiary: compilations (encyclopedias, textbooks).

steps.title: Non-textual
steps.body: Material culture, landscapes, buildings, maps, songs, films. Whether a source is primary depends on the question asked: a 1909 book on 1857 is secondary for 1857 but primary for 1909 nationalist thought.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: 'Primary' does not mean 'reliable'; every source needs criticism.

activity.prompt: For a study of the 1930 Salt March, classify

quiz.q: A diary written during the Partition is a:
quiz.why: It was created by a participant at the time.

quiz.q: Savarkar's 1909 book is primary for studying:
quiz.why: It reveals early 20th-century nationalist interpretation.
Primary sources can be biased, mistaken or forged.

scenes.text: A copper-plate grant claims to be from the 6th century but uses letter forms of the 11th.
Palaeography exposes it as a later forgery.

steps.title: External criticism (authenticity)
steps.body: Is it genuine? Check material, script (palaeography), language, seals, dating formulas, provenance (chain of custody). Example: Valla's linguistic proof that the Donation of Constantine was forged; the 'Hitler Diaries' hoax (1983) exposed by paper and ink analysis.

steps.title: Internal criticism (credibility)
steps.body: Is its content trustworthy? Who wrote it, when, for whom, why; was the author in a position to know; internal consistency; corroboration by independent sources.

steps.title: Worked example: Barani
steps.body: Barani praises Alauddin's market control. Internal criticism: Barani wrote decades later, held aristocratic views, and wished to give advice to rulers—so treat his precise prices cautiously but accept the existence of controls (corroborated by other sources).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: An authentic document can still be untrue; authenticity and credibility are separate tests.

activity.prompt: Order the steps to evaluate a document
items: Record provenance and where it was found
Check material, script and language for authenticity

quiz.why: Palaeography dates and authenticates texts by their script.
Internal criticism asks whether what the source says can be trusted.

options: Forensic analysis of paper and ink
quiz.why: Materials post-dating the war proved them forged.

story.title: Reading the record against the grain

scenes.text: At the National Archives of India, police files describe 'rioters'.
A historian reads them for what the peasants themselves wanted.

steps.title: Archives
steps.body: National Archives of India (New Delhi), state archives, British Library India Office Records (London), private papers, Nehru Memorial Museum & Library. Use catalogues, finding aids, file numbers; note proceedings series (e.g. Home Political).

steps.title: Silences
steps.body: Archives reflect power: they record what states wanted to know. Michel-Rolph Trouillot (Silencing the Past, 1995) on how silences enter at creation, assembly, retrieval and narration. Guha's 'prose of counter-insurgency'.

steps.title: Note-taking
steps.body: Record full reference (archive, series, file no., year, folio) with every note; separate quotation from paraphrase from your own comment.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Assuming that because something is not in the archive, it did not happen.

activity.prompt: Before leaving an archive, check that you have
items: Exact quotations marked in quotation marks
Photographs logged with file numbers (where permitted)
Notes on gaps or missing files
Your own interpretive comments kept separate

quiz.q: Silencing the Past was written by:
quiz.why: Michel-Rolph Trouillot published it in 1995.

quiz.q: India Office Records are held at:
quiz.why: They are in the British Library's Asian and African collections.

options: Using records for purposes their creators did not intend
quiz.why: It extracts the voices of those the records were designed to control.

scenes.text: An 85-year-old recalls leaving Lahore in 1947.
A student records it with consent, noting what she says and how she says it.

steps.title: Oral history
steps.body: Interviews with participants; reveals experience of ordinary people. Issues: memory changes over time, later narratives, interviewer influence. Ethics: informed consent, right to withdraw, anonymity where needed. 1947 Partition Archive collects such testimony.

steps.title: Visual sources
steps.body: Paintings, photographs, cartoons, films: ask who made them, for whom, what is framed or excluded. Company paintings in colonial India were made for European patrons.

steps.title: Digital
steps.body: Digitised archives, databases; evaluate provenance, metadata, possible manipulation; cite URLs and access dates.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Treating memories as direct windows to the past, or dismissing them as worthless; both are errors.

a.text: You arrive to interview a Partition survivor. What first?

choices.label: Explain the project and get informed consent

b.text: How do you ask about violence?

choices.label: Open, gentle questions; allow silence; let them decline
Press for graphic details
choices.feedback: This can harm the narrator and distort testimony.

c.text: Afterwards, how will you use the testimony?

choices.label: Corroborate with other sources and discuss memory's role

d.text: You have conducted an ethical, critical oral-history interview.

quiz.why: Narrators must understand and agree to the project.

options: Memory can be reshaped over time
quiz.why: Later events and narratives can influence how people remember.

quiz.q: When citing a digital source you should include:
quiz.why: Online content changes, so readers need the address and date.

questions.why: They were issued in Ashoka's time.
Provenance traces where a document came from.
External criticism establishes authenticity.
Independent agreement strengthens credibility.
Textbooks synthesise secondary scholarship.
He identified four moments where silences arise.

questions.q: Company paintings were made largely for:
questions.why: Indian artists painted them for East India Company officials.
Authenticity differs from truthfulness.

options: With attention to his date and views
questions.why: His later writing and aristocratic bias shape his account.

questions.q: Guha's phrase for colonial records of revolt:
questions.why: He named the official discourse 'the prose of counter-insurgency'.

questions.q: Which is NOT a test of internal criticism?
questions.why: Ink analysis belongs to external criticism.

options: Critically, with corroboration and attention to memory
questions.why: Oral testimony is valuable when analysed critically.

courses.title: Unit 3 · Traditions of Historical Writing in the World
courses.summary: Greco-Roman, Chinese and Islamic historiography; Enlightenment and Rankean history; Marxist history; the Annales school; postmodernism and gender history.
outcomes: Compare Herodotus and Thucydides
Describe Sima Qian and Ibn Khaldun's contributions
Explain Ranke's methods
Explain Marxist historical materialism
Describe the Annales school and postmodern challenges

scenes.text: Herodotus collects stories of the Persian Wars from many peoples.
Thucydides, an Athenian general, analyses the Peloponnesian War with strict attention to evidence.

steps.title: Greece and Rome
steps.body: Herodotus (Histories; 'father of history'; wide inquiry, includes hearsay), Thucydides (History of the Peloponnesian War; critical, political, speeches reconstructed), Polybius (pragmatic history), Livy and Tacitus.

steps.title: China
steps.body: Sima Qian's Shiji (Records of the Grand Historian, c. 100 BCE), model for official dynastic histories.

steps.title: Islamic
steps.body: Al-Tabari (isnad chains of transmission), Ibn Khaldun's Muqaddimah (1377): asabiyya (group solidarity), cyclical rise and fall of dynasties, critique of uncritical reports.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Medieval Christian chronicles (e.g. Augustine's providential view) treated history as divine plan—a different aim from Thucydides' secular analysis.

quiz.why: Ibn Khaldun completed it in 1377.
He insisted on careful verification of accounts.
Ibn Khaldun saw social cohesion as driving dynastic rise.

scenes.text: Leopold von Ranke trains students to read archival documents critically in his seminar.
Footnotes become the professional historian's badge.

steps.title: Enlightenment
steps.body: Voltaire (history of civilisation and manners), Gibbon (Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire, 1776–89), Vico (New Science, cyclical ages), Hegel (history as unfolding of spirit).

steps.title: Ranke (1795–1886)
steps.body: Archive-based, critical study of primary sources, seminar method, focus on states and diplomacy; 'every epoch is immediate to God' (each age to be understood on its own terms).

steps.title: Positivism
steps.body: Auguste Comte; belief in laws of society; in history, emphasis on facts; Buckle's History of Civilization in England.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Ranke was not a naive fact-collector; he had a religious and statist outlook that shaped his choice of subjects.

statements.s: Ranke promoted the seminar and archival method.
statements.why: He trained students at Berlin in critical source study.

statements.s: Gibbon wrote the Muqaddimah.
statements.why: Gibbon wrote Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire.

statements.s: Comte is associated with positivism.
statements.why: He founded positivist philosophy.

statements.s: Ranke focused mainly on peasants and everyday life.
statements.why: He focused on states, politics and diplomacy.

quiz.q: Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire is by:
quiz.why: Edward Gibbon published it between 1776 and 1789.
He grounded history in critical study of documents.
Vico described recurring ages of gods, heroes and men.

lessons.title: Marxist history and history from below

scenes.text: Marx argues that the economic base shapes law, politics and ideas.
British Marxist historians turn to the lives of workers and peasants.

steps.title: Historical materialism
steps.body: Modes of production (forces + relations of production), class struggle as motor of history, stages (primitive communism, slave, feudal, capitalist); base–superstructure. Preface to A Contribution to the Critique of Political Economy (1859).

steps.title: British Marxists
steps.body: Communist Party Historians' Group: E.P. Thompson (class as experience; 'enormous condescension of posterity'), Eric Hobsbawm (Age of Revolution… trilogy), Christopher Hill, Rodney Hilton. Journal Past and Present (1952).

steps.title: In India
steps.body: D.D. Kosambi (An Introduction to the Study of Indian History, 1956), R.S. Sharma, Irfan Habib, Bipan Chandra (nationalist–Marxist).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Thompson rejected crude economic determinism; he stressed human agency and culture in class formation.

pairs: Making of the English Working Class
Introduction to the Study of Indian History

quiz.q: The 'motor of history' for Marx is:
quiz.why: Marx saw conflict between classes as driving historical change.

quiz.q: Who said history should rescue workers from 'the enormous condescension of posterity'?
quiz.why: Thompson wrote this in the preface to The Making of the English Working Class.
Kosambi applied Marxist analysis to ancient Indian history.

scenes.text: In Braudel's The Mediterranean (1949), the sea and mountains matter more than Philip II.
Later, postmodern critics ask whether history is a kind of narrative.

steps.title: Annales school
steps.body: Founded with the journal Annales (1929) by Marc Bloch and Lucien Febvre. Total history, interdisciplinarity, mentalités. Bloch: Feudal Society, The Historian's Craft. Braudel's three times: longue durée (geography), conjoncture (economic cycles), événements (events). Le Roy Ladurie's Montaillou.

steps.title: Postmodernism
steps.body: Lyotard's incredulity towards metanarratives; Foucault on power/knowledge and discourse; Hayden White on emplotment; Keith Jenkins. Critics: Richard Evans, In Defence of History (1997).

steps.title: Gender history
steps.body: Joan Scott: 'Gender: A Useful Category of Historical Analysis' (1986). Women's history and history of masculinities.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Braudel did not ignore events; he placed them within slower structures.

items.text: Mountains and climate of the Mediterranean

quiz.why: Marc Bloch and Lucien Febvre launched the journal in Strasbourg.
It denotes very slow geographic and structural change.

quiz.q: In Defence of History is by:
quiz.why: Richard Evans defended historical knowledge against postmodern scepticism in 1997.

questions.why: Cicero called Herodotus the father of history.
Sima Qian compiled it around 100 BCE.
Ibn Khaldun finished the first draft in 1377.
Bloch wrote it before his execution in 1944.
Le Roy Ladurie studied a 14th-century French village.
It examines the mental worlds of past societies.

questions.q: Gender as a category of analysis was argued by:
questions.why: Joan Scott's 1986 article is foundational.
Ranke wrote political and diplomatic history.
Lyotard defined postmodernism thus in 1979.

questions.q: Which belongs to British Marxist historians?
questions.why: Hill was a member of the Historians' Group.
Événements are the surface events of political history.

questions.q: A fair critique of postmodern history is that it:
options: Can underplay the constraint of evidence on interpretation
questions.why: Critics like Evans argue evidence limits which narratives are valid.

courses.title: Unit 4 · Indian Historiography
courses.summary: Itihasa-purana and early Indian historical consciousness, Indo-Persian chronicles, colonial (Orientalist, Utilitarian), nationalist, Marxist, Cambridge and Subaltern schools.
outcomes: Evaluate the claim that early India lacked historical sense
Describe Indo-Persian historical writing
Explain colonial historiography and its legacy
Compare nationalist and Marxist schools
Explain the Cambridge and Subaltern approaches

scenes.text: Colonial scholars claimed India had no historians before Kalhana.
Romila Thapar replies: historical consciousness took different forms—genealogies, prashastis, chronicles.

steps.title: Itihasa-purana
steps.body: Epics and Puranas preserve genealogies (vamshanucharita) of dynasties; Buddhist chronicles of Sri Lanka (Dipavamsa, Mahavamsa); Jain prabandhas.

steps.title: Prashastis and charitas
steps.body: Court eulogies in inscriptions (Prayaga Prashasti, Aihole), biographies (Bana's Harshacharita, Bilhana's Vikramankadevacharita).

steps.title: Kalhana
steps.body: Rajatarangini (1148–49 CE): uses earlier chronicles, inscriptions and coins; critical outlook; often called the closest to modern history-writing in early India.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Saying 'India had no sense of history' repeats a colonial stereotype; the forms differed from European chronicles.

quiz.why: Kalhana completed it in 1148–49.
Bilhana wrote it on the Chalukya king Vikramaditya VI.
She identified embedded and externalised historical traditions.

scenes.text: Abul Fazl compiles the Akbarnama from official records, interviews and memoirs.
Badauni secretly writes a critical counter-history.

steps.title: Sultanate
steps.body: Minhaj-us-Siraj (Tabaqat-i-Nasiri), Barani (Tarikh-i-Firuz Shahi; history as moral guide for kings), Amir Khusrau, Isami (Futuh-us-Salatin), Afif.

steps.title: Mughal
steps.body: Babur's memoir, Gulbadan Begum's Humayun-nama (by a woman), Abul Fazl (Akbarnama, Ain-i-Akbari with statistical data), Badauni, Nizamuddin Ahmad (Tabaqat-i-Akbari), Khafi Khan.

steps.title: Features
steps.body: Court-centred, didactic, Persian literary style, use of documents; also regional histories and Rajput khyats, Maratha bakhars.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Persian chronicles were not uniformly 'Muslim views'; authors held diverse, often contrary positions.

quiz.why: Babur's daughter Gulbadan wrote it at Akbar's request.
Bakhars are Marathi prose chronicles.
He wrote to instruct kings in good government.

scenes.text: James Mill divides Indian history into 'Hindu', 'Muslim' and 'British' periods (1817).
Nationalist historians respond by celebrating ancient glories and resistance.

steps.title: Colonial
steps.body: Orientalists (Jones, Prinsep) valued ancient texts; Utilitarians (Mill) condemned Indian society; administrator-historians (Elphinstone, V.A. Smith—Early History of India, 1904); Elliot and Dowson's translated Persian chronicles (with communal framing). Theme of 'Oriental despotism' and changeless village.

steps.title: Nationalist
steps.body: R.G. Bhandarkar, K.P. Jayaswal (Hindu Polity, 1924: ancient republics), R.C. Majumdar, H.C. Raychaudhuri, Jadunath Sarkar (Mughal history, critical of Aurangzeb), R.C. Dutt and Naoroji (economic critique).

steps.title: Problems
steps.body: Both colonial and some nationalist works used religious periodisation and glorification; communal historiography grew from this.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Economic nationalism (Dutt, Naoroji) differs from cultural revivalist nationalism; do not merge them.

quiz.why: Jayaswal argued ancient India had republican institutions.

quiz.q: Early History of India (1904) is by:
quiz.why: Vincent Smith's survey became a standard colonial textbook.
Mill used religious labels for periods, an influential distortion.

scenes.text: In 1982 Ranajit Guha launches Subaltern Studies, criticising both colonialist and nationalist 'elitism'.
Gayatri Spivak asks whether subaltern voices can be recovered from elite records at all.

steps.title: Marxist
steps.body: Kosambi, R.S. Sharma (Indian Feudalism), Irfan Habib (Agrarian System), Romila Thapar (social history), Bipan Chandra, Sumit Sarkar; focus on modes of production, class, agrarian relations.

steps.title: Cambridge school
steps.body: Anil Seal (Emergence of Indian Nationalism, 1968), John Gallagher, Gordon Johnson, C.A. Bayly: nationalism as competition among elites for patronage and locality-province-nation linkages. Criticised for 'animal politics' (Tapan Raychaudhuri's phrase).

steps.title: Subaltern Studies
steps.body: Ranajit Guha, Shahid Amin (Gandhi as Mahatma, Gorakhpur 1921–22), Gyanendra Pandey, Partha Chatterjee, Dipesh Chakrabarty (Provincializing Europe). Later 'cultural turn'; Spivak's essay 'Can the Subaltern Speak?' (1988).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Subaltern Studies is not simply Marxist; it drew on Gramsci and later on postcolonial theory.

quiz.q: Subaltern Studies first volume appeared in:
quiz.why: Guha edited the first volume in 1982.
Guha borrowed it from Gramsci's prison writings.

quiz.q: The Cambridge school viewed nationalism largely as:
options: Elite competition for power and patronage
quiz.why: Seal and others traced nationalism to rival elite interests.

questions.why: Kalhana wrote the Rajatarangini.
It forms the third volume of the Akbarnama.
Chakrabarty published it in 2000.
Colonial writers portrayed Asian rule as arbitrary despotism.
Their History of India as Told by Its Own Historians translated Persian texts.
Anil Seal wrote it.
Spivak published the essay in 1988.
Khyats are Rajasthani chronicles.
Sharma's book applies Marxist analysis.

options: Peasant perceptions of Gandhi in Gorakhpur
questions.why: Amin examined rumours and peasant images of Gandhi in 1921–22.
It is a Pali chronicle of Sri Lankan kings.

questions.q: Common critique of the Cambridge school:
options: It reduces nationalism to self-interest, ignoring ideals and mass mobilisation
questions.why: Critics argued it neglected ideology and popular participation.

courses.title: Unit 5 · Research Methods, Writing and Revision
curricula: UGC CBCS / NEP 2020 (Historical Method / Research project)
courses.summary: Choosing a research question, literature review, note-taking, citation and plagiarism, structuring a dissertation, and revision for the historiography paper.
outcomes: Frame a focused, researchable historical question
Write a literature review
Cite sources correctly (Chicago notes-bibliography)
Avoid plagiarism
Structure a project and revise the paper

story.title: Too big, too small, just right

scenes.text: 'History of Indian women' is far too big for a BA project.
'How did Marathi periodicals discuss widow remarriage, 1870–1890?' is focused and answerable.

steps.title: Good questions
steps.body: Specific (place, time, theme), answerable with available sources, arguable (not just descriptive), significant. Use 'how' and 'why' rather than 'what'.

steps.title: Literature review
steps.body: Survey existing scholarship: group works by approach, identify debates and gaps, position your question. Use JSTOR, Shodhganga (Indian theses), university libraries.

steps.title: Hypothesis and sources
steps.body: State a working hypothesis; list primary sources you can actually access (archives, digitised newspapers, oral interviews).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Choosing a topic before checking sources exist; writing a summary of books rather than a review of debates.

items.text: Why did the Pabna tenants form an agrarian league in 1873?
How did Kolkata newspapers report the 1943 famine?
How did the Mahad satyagraha use public space to claim rights?

quiz.why: Focus and arguability let you build an evidence-based answer.
Shodhganga is the INFLIBNET repository of Indian theses.
It positions your question within existing scholarship.

scenes.text: A student copies a paragraph from a website without quotation marks.
Plagiarism software flags it; the project is returned.

steps.title: Chicago notes-bibliography
steps.body: Book note: 1. Romila Thapar, Early India: From the Origins to AD 1300 (London: Allen Lane, 2002), 45. Bibliography: Thapar, Romila. Early India: From the Origins to AD 1300. London: Allen Lane, 2002. Article: author, "title," journal volume, no. (year): pages.

steps.title: Plagiarism
steps.body: Using others' words or ideas without acknowledgement, including close paraphrase and self-plagiarism. UGC (Promotion of Academic Integrity and Prevention of Plagiarism) Regulations 2018 set similarity-level penalties for research work.

steps.title: Paraphrasing well
steps.body: Read, close the source, write in your own structure and words, then check and cite. Quote only distinctive phrases.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Citing only in the bibliography but not at the point of use; changing a few words of a sentence (patchwriting).

activity.text: 1. Ranajit Guha, Elementary Aspects of Peasant Insurgency in Colonial India (Delhi: Oxford University Press, ___), 12.

options: Changing a few words of copied text
quiz.why: Light rewording without quotation marks still counts as plagiarism.

quiz.q: In Chicago notes-bibliography, the bibliography lists the author as:
quiz.why: Bibliography entries invert the first author's name for alphabetising.

options: Use someone's idea even in your own words
quiz.why: Ideas, not just words, must be credited.

scenes.text: Your note cards are sorted into three themes.
Each theme becomes a chapter with an argument.

steps.title: Structure
steps.body: Title; abstract (150–250 words); introduction (question, historiography, sources, method, chapter plan); 2–4 thematic chapters; conclusion; bibliography (primary then secondary); appendices.

steps.title: Paragraphs
steps.body: Topic sentence → evidence (with citation) → analysis → link back to the argument (PEEL).

steps.title: Word budget example
steps.body: For an 8,000-word project: introduction 1,000 (12.5%), three chapters of 2,000 each (6,000; 75%), conclusion 1,000 (12.5%).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Chronological narration without argument; conclusions introducing new evidence.

activity.prompt: A 10,000-word dissertation gives 15% to the introduction and 10% to the conclusion; the rest is split equally among 3 chapters. How many words per chapter?

quiz.why: PEEL structures an analytical paragraph.
Separation shows the evidence base clearly.
It frames the project for the reader.

scenes.text: Examiners reward linking historians to concepts and examples.
A table of schools, thinkers, key works and critiques is your best revision tool.

steps.title: Key sheet
steps.body: Herodotus/Thucydides (inquiry/critical); Sima Qian (Shiji); Ibn Khaldun (asabiyya); Ranke (archives, seminar); Marx (modes of production); Annales (Bloch, Febvre, Braudel: longue durée); British Marxists (Thompson, Hobsbawm); Carr (dialogue); Collingwood (re-enactment); postmodern (Foucault, White, Lyotard); India: Kalhana, Barani, Abul Fazl, Mill, Smith, Jayaswal, Kosambi, Sharma, Habib, Seal, Guha.

steps.title: Original practice questions
steps.body: 1. 'Are historical facts objective?' 2. 'Assess the Annales contribution.' 3. 'Compare colonial and nationalist historiography of ancient India.' 4. 'What did Subaltern Studies add?' 5. 'Explain internal and external criticism with Indian examples.'

steps.title: Using examples
steps.body: Pair every theoretical point with a concrete example from Indian or world history, e.g. internal criticism → Barani's prices; longue durée → monsoon agriculture.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Listing names without explaining ideas; mixing up Bloch and Braudel; attributing the 'Hindu–Muslim–British' periodisation to nationalists.

quiz.why: Marc Bloch published Feudal Society in 1939–40.

quiz.q: A theory point should be paired with:
quiz.why: Examples show you can apply concepts.
Mill introduced it in his History of British India (1817).

questions.why: Historians widely use Chicago notes-bibliography.
Abstracts briefly summarise question, method and findings.
Unacknowledged use of ideas is plagiarism.
The UGC issued them in 2018.

questions.q: 12,000 words with 10% intro and 10% conclusion leaves for 4 chapters each:
questions.why: 80% of 12,000 is 9,600, divided by 4 gives 2,400.

options: How did the Bombay press report the 1918 influenza?
questions.why: It specifies place, time, source and theme.
It shows how your work contributes.

options: Answer the question and not add new evidence
Repeat the introduction word for word
questions.why: They synthesise the argument.
Amin was a core Subaltern Studies member.
Monsoon agriculture is a slow structural pattern.

questions.q: Reading archives against the grain helps to:
questions.why: It finds subaltern perspectives in elite records.

questions.q: Best answer approach for 'Are facts objective?':
options: Discuss Ranke, Carr, postmodern critique and evidence-based middle ground
questions.why: A strong answer weighs positions and reaches a reasoned judgement.

uni-ba-hist-medieval-india.title: Early Medieval & Medieval India (c. 650–1707)
uni-ba-hist-medieval-india.description: Early medieval polities and feudalism debate, Cholas, Delhi Sultanate, Vijayanagara and Bahmanis, Bhakti and Sufi movements, and the Mughal empire. Study companion; topics commonly taught in Indian BA History programmes.

courses.title: Unit 1 · Early Medieval India (c. 650–1200)
curricula: UGC CBCS / NEP 2020 (History of India III)
courses.summary: Tripartite struggle for Kanauj, Rajput origins, the feudalism debate, Chola state and society, and the early Turkish invasions.
outcomes: Explain the tripartite struggle among Palas, Pratiharas and Rashtrakutas
Evaluate theories of Rajput origins
Compare the feudalism and segmentary/integrative models
Describe Chola administration and village assemblies
Assess Mahmud of Ghazni and Muhammad Ghuri

scenes.text: After Harsha, Kanauj becomes the prize of north India.
Palas of Bengal, Gurjara-Pratiharas of western India and Rashtrakutas of the Deccan fight for it for about two centuries.

steps.title: The three powers
steps.body: Palas: Gopala (elected, per tradition), Dharmapala (founded Vikramashila), Devapala. Pratiharas: Nagabhata II, Mihira Bhoja (praised by the Arab traveller Sulaiman). Rashtrakutas: Dantidurga, Krishna I (Kailasa temple at Ellora), Amoghavarsha I.

steps.title: Outcome
steps.body: No power won lasting control; all were weakened, contributing to the fragmentation that later Turkish armies met.

steps.title: Kailasa temple
steps.body: The Kailasanatha temple (Cave 16, Ellora) was cut from a single rock under Krishna I in the 8th century.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Do not call this 'the dark age'; the period saw temple-building, agrarian expansion and new regional languages.

quiz.q: The object of the tripartite struggle was:
quiz.why: Control of Kanauj symbolised imperial status in post-Harsha north India.
The Pala king Dharmapala founded the Vikramashila mahavihara.

quiz.q: Kailasa temple at Ellora was built under:
quiz.why: The Rashtrakuta king Krishna I had the Kailasanatha temple carved in the 8th century.

scenes.text: A legend says four Rajput clans rose from a sacrificial fire at Mount Abu (agnikula).
Historians instead trace social processes of state formation and legitimation.

steps.title: Rajput origins
steps.body: Theories: foreign origin (Tod, linking to Shakas/Hunas), indigenous kshatriya descent, and the process view (B.D. Chattopadhyaya): local lineages rose through land control and gained kshatriya status via genealogies written by brahmanas.

steps.title: Indian feudalism (R.S. Sharma)
steps.body: Land grants transferred revenue and administrative rights, leading to decline of trade, towns and coinage, peasant subjection and a hierarchy of intermediaries (samantas).

steps.title: Alternatives
steps.body: Burton Stein's segmentary state (Cholas: ritual sovereignty, local power); B.D. Chattopadhyaya's integrative polity: expansion of agrarian settlements and state society. Critics question evidence for urban decline (e.g. coins and trade persisting).

steps.title: Answer frame
steps.body: Q: 'Was early medieval India feudal?' Present Sharma's model and evidence; Mukhia's 'Was there feudalism in Indian history?' (1981) critique; Stein and Chattopadhyaya; conclude with regional variation.

quiz.q: The 'segmentary state' was proposed for the:
quiz.why: Burton Stein applied the segmentary model to the Chola state.
Samantas were subordinate rulers owing tribute and service to an overlord.

quiz.q: Agnikula legend traces Rajput origin to:
quiz.why: The legend, found in later texts like the Prithviraj Raso, places it at Mount Abu.

scenes.text: The Uttaramerur inscriptions (Parantaka I, 10th c.) describe choosing sabha committees by kudavolai—names drawn from a pot.
In Thanjavur, Rajaraja I builds the Brihadishvara temple (c. 1010).

steps.title: Rulers
steps.body: Vijayalaya (c. 850) refounds Chola power; Rajaraja I (985–1014) conquers north Sri Lanka and the Maldives; Rajendra I (1014–44) campaigns to the Ganga (Gangaikondacholapuram) and sends a naval expedition to Srivijaya (c. 1025).

steps.title: Administration
steps.body: Mandalam (province), valanadu, nadu, and villages. Assemblies: ur (non-brahmana villages), sabha (brahmadeya villages), nagaram (merchants). Revenue surveys under Rajaraja I.

steps.title: Temples
steps.body: Temples were economic centres: land, employment, lending. Dravida style with vimana; bronze casting (Nataraja).
