steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Uttaramerur sabha rules applied to a brahmadeya, not to all villages; avoid calling it 'democracy' without qualification.

items.text: Merchant body in a market town

quiz.q: Brihadishvara temple at Thanjavur was built by:
quiz.why: Rajaraja I completed the Brihadishvara temple about 1010 CE.
About 1025 he raided ports of Srivijaya in Southeast Asia.
Kudavolai was the pot-and-ticket method used to pick committee members.

scenes.text: Mahmud of Ghazni raids the Somnath temple in Gujarat.
Over a century later, Muhammad of Ghur fights Prithviraj Chauhan at Tarain.

steps.title: Mahmud of Ghazni (998–1030)
steps.body: About 17 raids (traditional count) for wealth and prestige; annexed Punjab. Al-Biruni accompanied him and wrote Kitab-ul-Hind on Indian sciences and society.

steps.title: Muhammad of Ghur
steps.body: First Battle of Tarain 1191 (Prithviraj won); Second Battle 1192 (Ghuri won). Chandawar 1194 defeat of Jaichand of Kanauj. Qutbuddin Aibak left in charge.

steps.title: Why the Turks succeeded
steps.body: Mobile cavalry and mounted archery, unified command, political fragmentation of Indian states, and central Asian military recruitment.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Mahmud raided but did not establish rule in the Ganga valley; Ghuri's conquests laid the base of the Delhi Sultanate.

quiz.why: Al-Biruni wrote Kitab-ul-Hind after studying Sanskrit and Indian learning.

quiz.q: The Second Battle of Tarain was in:
quiz.why: Muhammad of Ghur defeated Prithviraj Chauhan at Tarain in 1192.

quiz.q: Who won the First Battle of Tarain?
quiz.why: Prithviraj Chauhan defeated Ghuri in 1191 before losing the next year.

questions.why: The 9th-century Arab merchant Sulaiman described the Pratihara king's strong cavalry.
Rajendra I founded it to commemorate his campaign to the Ganga.
They date to Parantaka I's reign in the 10th century.
Sharma linked land grants to declining towns and growing control over peasants.

questions.q: Mahmud of Ghazni's capital was in present-day:
questions.why: Ghazni is in eastern Afghanistan.
The sabha governed villages granted to brahmanas.
It was excavated top-down from a single basalt rock.

questions.q: Which historian wrote on Rajput state formation as a process?
questions.why: Chattopadhyaya explained Rajputs as emerging lineages legitimised through land and genealogy.
Ghuri defeated Jaichand of Kanauj at Chandawar.
Fast mounted archers gave Turkish armies mobility and firepower.
Nagaram was the merchants' assembly in Chola towns.

options: Ritual sovereignty with local segments holding real power
questions.why: Stein argued Chola kings held ritual supremacy while local nadus held effective control.

courses.title: Unit 2 · The Delhi Sultanate (1206–1526)
curricula: UGC CBCS / NEP 2020 (History of India IV)
courses.summary: Dynasties of the Sultanate, consolidation under Iltutmish and Balban, Khalji market reforms, Tughluq experiments, iqta system, and the Lodis.
outcomes: List Sultanate dynasties with dates
Explain the iqta system and its changes
Analyse Alauddin Khalji's market and revenue reforms
Evaluate Muhammad bin Tughluq's experiments
Explain the decline of the Sultanate

lessons.title: Early Turks: Aibak, Iltutmish, Razia, Balban

scenes.text: Iltutmish, once a slave, receives a robe of investiture from the Abbasid caliph in 1229.
Later Balban proclaims the sultan the 'shadow of God' (zil-i-ilahi).

steps.title: Dynasties
steps.body: Mamluk/early Turkish (1206–90), Khalji (1290–1320), Tughluq (1320–1414), Sayyid (1414–51), Lodi (1451–1526).

steps.title: Iltutmish (1211–36)
steps.body: Consolidated the Sultanate, introduced silver tanka and copper jital, organised the iqta system, formed the Turkan-i-Chahalgani ('the Forty'). Completed the Qutb Minar.

steps.title: Razia and Balban
steps.body: Razia (1236–40), first woman ruler of Delhi, opposed by Turkish nobles. Balban (1266–87) broke the Forty, introduced sijda and paibos, set up a spy system (barids) and the military department (diwan-i-arz).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Qutbuddin Aibak began the Qutb Minar; Iltutmish completed the upper storeys.

quiz.why: Iltutmish created the group of forty Turkish nobles.

quiz.q: Sijda and paibos were introduced by:
quiz.why: Balban made prostration and kissing the feet part of court ritual to raise royal prestige.
Iltutmish standardised the silver tanka and copper jital.

scenes.text: Barani reports that grain prices in Delhi stayed fixed even in drought.
Alauddin needed a large army against Mongol attacks at a cost the treasury could bear.

steps.title: Market control
steps.body: Separate markets for grain (mandi), cloth and costly goods (sarai-i-adl), horses, cattle and slaves; officials shahna-i-mandi; strict punishment for short weighing; grain stored in royal granaries.

steps.title: Revenue
steps.body: Land measured (masahat); demand raised to half the produce (in the doab); taxes on houses (ghari) and grazing (charai); curbs on rural intermediaries (khuts, muqaddams).

steps.title: Military
steps.body: Branding of horses (dagh) and descriptive rolls of soldiers (huliya/chehra); cash salaries to soldiers.

steps.title: Worked example: share of produce
steps.body: A peasant's field yields 60 maunds. At Alauddin's demand of 1/2, the state takes 30 maunds. Under a one-third demand (Sher Shah's later norm), it would take 20 maunds—10 fewer.

activity.prompt: A field yields 84 maunds. Under Alauddin's 50% demand, how many maunds does the peasant keep?

quiz.q: Main purpose of the market reforms (per Barani):
quiz.why: Barani links low fixed prices to paying a large army modest salaries against the Mongols.
Dagh was branding horses to stop soldiers presenting substandard mounts at musters.

quiz.q: Alauddin's land revenue demand in the doab:
quiz.why: Barani states the demand was raised to half of the produce.

lessons.title: Muhammad bin Tughluq and Firuz Shah

scenes.text: Muhammad bin Tughluq issues bronze/copper token coins to pass at the value of silver.
Forgers mint them at home; the experiment is withdrawn.

steps.title: Experiments (1325–51)
steps.body: Transfer of capital to Daulatabad (Devagiri) c. 1327; token currency c. 1329–30; tax increase in the doab during famine; Khurasan and Qarachil expeditions; agricultural department (diwan-i-amir-i-kohi) with loans (taqavi).

steps.title: Assessment
steps.body: Ideas were bold but executed poorly; rebellions followed and Vijayanagara and the Bahmani kingdom emerged (1336, 1347). Ibn Battuta served him as qazi of Delhi.

steps.title: Firuz Shah (1351–88)
steps.body: Canals, new towns (Hisar, Firozabad), hereditary iqtas, imposed jizya on brahmanas, department of slaves; wrote Futuhat-i-Firuz Shahi; moved Ashokan pillars to Delhi.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Timur's invasion (1398) came after Firuz's death; it sacked Delhi under the weak later Tughluqs.

quiz.why: Ibn Battuta was a Moroccan traveller who served as qazi under Muhammad bin Tughluq.
Timur sacked Delhi in 1398.

quiz.q: The token currency failed mainly because:
quiz.why: Without state monopoly on minting, mass forgery flooded the market.

scenes.text: A noble is assigned revenue of a territory (iqta) instead of salary.
In return he keeps troops and sends surplus to the centre.

steps.title: Iqta
steps.body: Revenue assignment, transferable, for maintaining troops and administration; muqtis/walis held them. Became hereditary under Firuz, weakening central control.

steps.title: Central offices
steps.body: Wazir (diwan-i-wizarat, finance), diwan-i-arz (military), diwan-i-insha (correspondence), diwan-i-risalat (religious affairs/appeals), sadr-us-sudur, qazi.

steps.title: Decline
steps.body: Over-extension, noble rivalry, hereditary iqtas, Timur's invasion, rise of regional sultanates (Bengal, Gujarat, Malwa, Jaunpur, Bahmani). Lodis (Bahlul, Sikandar—founded Agra 1504, Ibrahim) fell to Babur at Panipat 1526.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: An iqta was not ownership of land; it was a right to collect revenue.

quiz.why: Sikandar Lodi founded Agra in 1504.
An iqta gave the holder revenue rights in return for service.
Ibrahim Lodi died fighting Babur at Panipat in 1526.

questions.q: First woman ruler of the Delhi Sultanate:
questions.why: Razia ruled 1236–40.
Ziauddin Barani wrote the Tarikh-i-Firuz Shahi.
Minhaj wrote the Tabaqat-i-Nasiri in Nasiruddin Mahmud's reign.
Harihara and Bukka founded Vijayanagara in 1336.

questions.q: A field yields 90 maunds; a one-third demand takes:
questions.why: One-third of 90 is 30 maunds.
Muhammad bin Tughluq created it to extend cultivation.
Alauddin's sarai-i-adl regulated cloth and valuable goods.
He eliminated the Chahalgani to centralise authority.
Making iqtas hereditary weakened the centre.
Devagiri, the Yadava capital, was renamed Daulatabad.

questions.q: Which was NOT a regional sultanate after Tughluq decline?
questions.why: Vijayanagara was a Hindu kingdom rather than a sultanate.

questions.q: Best assessment of Muhammad bin Tughluq:
questions.why: Modern historians see his plans as rational but badly implemented, provoking revolts.

courses.title: Unit 3 · Vijayanagara, Bahmanis, Bhakti and Sufi Traditions
curricula: UGC CBCS / NEP 2020 (History of India IV)
courses.summary: Vijayanagara empire and the nayaka system, the Bahmani kingdom and Deccan sultanates, Bhakti saints from the Alvars to Kabir and Nanak, and Sufi silsilas.
outcomes: Describe Vijayanagara's polity, economy and Hampi
Explain the amara-nayaka system
Outline Bahmani history and successor states
Trace the Bhakti movement's phases and ideas
Explain Sufi silsilas and practices

scenes.text: Portuguese visitor Domingo Paes describes Vijayanagara's bazaars full of jewels.
After the Battle of Talikota (1565) the city is sacked and abandoned.

steps.title: Dynasties
steps.body: Sangama (Harihara, Bukka; 1336), Saluva, Tuluva (Krishnadevaraya 1509–29: Amuktamalyada in Telugu, Ashtadiggajas), Aravidu. Talikota/Rakshasi-Tangadi 1565 against the combined Deccan sultanates.

steps.title: Amara-nayaka system
steps.body: Military chiefs (nayakas) received territories (amaram) to collect revenue and maintain troops and elephants, paying tribute; after 1565 many nayakas became independent (Madurai, Thanjavur).

steps.title: Hampi
steps.body: Royal centre with Mahanavami Dibba, Lotus Mahal, elephant stables; sacred centre with Virupaksha and Vitthala temples; tanks and aqueducts. Rediscovered by Colin Mackenzie (1800).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: The amara-nayaka system was influenced by, but not identical to, the iqta; nayakas had more hereditary local power.

quiz.why: Krishnadevaraya was the greatest ruler of the Tuluva dynasty.
Amaram was land given to a nayaka in return for military service.
The Sangama brothers Harihara and Bukka founded it in 1336.

scenes.text: At Bidar, Mahmud Gawan builds a great madrasa in the 1470s.
His execution in 1481 deepens noble factionalism.

steps.title: Bahmani kingdom (1347)
steps.body: Founded by Alauddin Hasan Bahman Shah (Hasan Gangu) at Gulbarga; capital later Bidar. Rivalry with Vijayanagara over the Raichur doab. Factions: Deccanis vs Afaqis (newcomers).

steps.title: Successor sultanates
steps.body: Bijapur (Adil Shahi), Ahmadnagar (Nizam Shahi), Golconda (Qutb Shahi), Berar (Imad Shahi), Bidar (Barid Shahi). Gol Gumbaz at Bijapur; Charminar at Hyderabad (1591).

steps.title: Culture
steps.body: Dakhni (Deccani Urdu) literature flourished; Ibrahim Adil Shah II wrote Kitab-i-Nauras.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: The Raichur doab lies between the Krishna and Tungabhadra rivers, not between the Godavari and Krishna.

quiz.why: Mahmud Gawan built his madrasa at Bidar.
Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah built it in Hyderabad in 1591.
This fertile doab between Krishna and Tungabhadra was contested for two centuries.

scenes.text: In Banaras, Kabir sings that God is neither in temple nor mosque.
Centuries earlier, Tamil Alvars and Nayanars sang to Vishnu and Shiva.

steps.title: Early bhakti (6th–9th c.)
steps.body: Alvars (Vaishnava; Andal, a woman saint; Nalayira Divya Prabandham) and Nayanars (Shaiva; Appar, Sambandar, Sundarar; Tevaram). Virashaivas/Lingayats of Karnataka under Basavanna (12th c.) rejected caste and ritual.

steps.title: Saguna and nirguna
steps.body: Saguna (God with attributes): Tulsidas (Ramcharitmanas), Surdas, Mirabai, Chaitanya. Nirguna (formless): Kabir, Ravidas, Guru Nanak (1469–1539; founder of Sikhism; langar; Guru Granth Sahib compiled by Guru Arjan, 1604).

steps.title: Maharashtra
steps.body: Varkari tradition of Vitthala at Pandharpur: Jnaneshwar, Namdev, Eknath, Tukaram.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Bhakti was not one unified movement; it had regional, sectarian and social variations.

quiz.why: Andal is the only woman among the twelve Alvars.
Basavanna led the Virashaiva (Lingayat) movement in 12th-century Karnataka.

quiz.q: The Adi Granth was compiled by:
quiz.why: Guru Arjan compiled the Adi Granth in 1604.

scenes.text: At the dargah of Nizamuddin Auliya in Delhi, qawwals sing sama.
His langar (community kitchen) feeds all comers.

steps.title: Ideas
steps.body: Sufis sought mystical union with God through love, devotion to a pir/shaikh, zikr (remembrance) and sama (music). Wahdat-ul-wujud (unity of being, Ibn Arabi) influenced many.

steps.title: Silsilas
steps.body: Chishti: Muinuddin (Ajmer), Qutbuddin Bakhtiyar Kaki, Fariduddin Ganj-i-Shakar (Baba Farid), Nizamuddin Auliya; kept distance from the court. Suhrawardi: Bahauddin Zakariya (Multan), accepted state patronage. Naqshbandi: Shaikh Ahmad Sirhindi stressed orthodoxy (wahdat-ul-shuhud).

steps.title: Sources
steps.body: Malfuzat (conversations), e.g. Fawa'id-ul-Fu'ad of Nizamuddin recorded by Amir Hasan Sijzi; maktubat (letters); tazkiras (biographies). Amir Khusrau was Nizamuddin's disciple.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Not all Sufis avoided rulers—Suhrawardis took state grants; Chishti attitudes also varied.

activity.prompt: Match the Sufi to the silsila or place
pairs: Chishti; verses in the Guru Granth Sahib

quiz.why: Amir Hasan Sijzi compiled Nizamuddin Auliya's conversations in it.
Sama is listening to devotional music to evoke spiritual ecstasy.
Sirhindi proposed 'unity of witness' against Ibn Arabi's 'unity of being'.

questions.why: Talikota was fought in 1565.
It is the tomb of Muhammad Adil Shah in Bijapur.
Hasan Gangu founded it in 1347.
Tevaram collects Shaiva Nayanar hymns.
Tukaram was a Varkari saint devoted to Vitthala.
Guru Nanak was born in 1469 at Talwandi.
They were eight Telugu poets in Krishnadevaraya's court.
Malfuzat preserve teachings in a Sufi's conversations.
Mirabai was a Rajput princess devoted to Krishna.

questions.q: Afaqis in the Bahmani kingdom were:
questions.why: Afaqis were immigrant nobles from Iran and Central Asia.

questions.q: After 1565, nayakas of Madurai and Thanjavur:
questions.why: Weak central power let nayakas set up autonomous states.

questions.q: A historically careful view of Bhakti:
options: One pan-Indian movement with one founder
Diverse regional traditions with shared devotional emphasis
questions.why: Bhakti traditions differed across regions and centuries while sharing personal devotion.

courses.title: Unit 4 · The Mughal Empire: Polity and Administration
curricula: UGC CBCS / NEP 2020 (History of India V)
courses.summary: From Babur to Aurangzeb, the Sur interlude, Akbar's mansabdari, land revenue (zabt), religious policy (sulh-i-kul), and Rajput and Deccan policies.
outcomes: Outline Mughal political history 1526–1707
Explain Sher Shah's reforms
Describe the mansabdari and jagirdari systems
Explain zabt/dahsala revenue with a numerical
Analyse Akbar's religious policy and Aurangzeb's reign

scenes.text: April 1526: Babur's artillery and tulughma tactics defeat Ibrahim Lodi at Panipat.
His son Humayun loses to Sher Khan at Chausa (1539) and Kannauj (1540) and flees to Persia.

steps.title: Babur
steps.body: Panipat 1526 (Ibrahim Lodi), Khanwa 1527 (Rana Sanga), Chanderi 1528 (Medini Rai), Ghaghra 1529 (Afghans). Memoirs: Baburnama (Tuzuk-i-Baburi) in Chaghatai Turkish.

steps.title: Sher Shah Sur (1540–45)
steps.body: Rupiya (silver coin), measurement of land and fixed crop rates (ray), patta and qabuliyat (revenue documents), the Grand Trunk Road (Sonargaon–Peshawar) with sarais, local responsibility for crime.

steps.title: Humayun's return
steps.body: Regained Delhi in 1555 with Persian help; died 1556. Second Battle of Panipat (1556): Bairam Khan for young Akbar defeated Hemu.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Sher Shah did not invent the road from nothing—he rebuilt and extended an older route.

quiz.why: Babur beat Rana Sanga's Rajput coalition at Khanwa in 1527.
The patta recorded the peasant's dues and the qabuliyat was his acceptance of them.
Babur wrote his memoirs in his mother tongue, Chaghatai Turkish.

scenes.text: A noble holds a mansab of 5000 zat / 3000 sawar.
Zat fixes his personal rank and salary; sawar how many horsemen he must keep.

steps.title: Mansab
steps.body: Introduced by Akbar (c. 1570s). Dual rank zat and sawar (sawar added later in Akbar's reign). Mansabdars were appointed, promoted and transferred by the emperor; ranks not hereditary.

steps.title: Jagir
steps.body: Salary paid in cash (naqdi) or by a jagir—revenue assignment equal to the pay claim (jama). Jagirs were transferred every few years to prevent local roots. Khalisa land's revenue went directly to the treasury.

steps.title: Rules
steps.body: Dagh (branding) and chehra (descriptive roll); du-aspa sih-aspa (later, under Jahangir) for extra troopers.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Using a simple 10-horse rule (an illustrative 'dah-bisti' style ratio of one horseman per 10 sawar rank is NOT exact Mughal rule), it is safer to compute only stated figures: a 3000 sawar rank means maintaining 3000 cavalry; a jagir with jama of ₹10 lakh and actual collection (hasil) of ₹7.5 lakh yields 75% of the paper value.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Jagirdari crisis (Satish Chandra) refers to shortage of jagirs (be-jagiri) and gap between jama and hasil in the late 17th century.

activity.prompt: A jagir's assessed revenue (jama) is ₹8,00,000 but actual collection (hasil) is ₹6,00,000. What percentage of jama was realised?

quiz.why: Zat fixed the mansabdar's personal status and pay.

options: Crown land with revenue for the treasury
quiz.why: Khalisa lands paid revenue directly to the imperial treasury.
Regular transfer stopped nobles building local power bases.

scenes.text: Raja Todar Mal's officials measure fields with bamboo jaribs.
Ten years of produce and prices are averaged to fix cash rates (dastur).

steps.title: Zabt
steps.body: Measured land (bigha-i-ilahi); the state demanded about one-third of the average produce, converted to cash using average prices of the previous ten years (dahsala, 1580). Rates in cash per bigha per crop (dastur-ul-amal).

steps.title: Land classes
steps.body: Polaj (cultivated every year), parauti (fallow for a year or two), chachar (fallow 3–4 years), banjar (fallow 5+ years).

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Average wheat yield 18 maunds/bigha; state share 1/3 = 6 maunds. Average price ₹0.5 per maund → cash demand ₹3 per bigha. For 20 bighas, ₹60.

steps.title: Other methods
steps.body: Batai/ghallabakhshi (crop sharing), kankut (estimation), nasaq (assessment based on past records).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Zabt applied in core northern provinces; it was not uniform across the empire.

activity.prompt: Average yield 24 maunds per bigha; state share one-third; average price ₹0.25 per maund. What is the cash demand per bigha in rupees?

quiz.why: Akbar adopted the ten-year (dahsala) system in 1580.
Polaj was continuously cultivated land.
Under batai the harvest was divided between state and peasant.

scenes.text: At Fatehpur Sikri from 1575, Akbar hosts debates among Muslims, then Hindus, Jains, Zoroastrians and Jesuits.
Abul Fazl frames the ideal of sulh-i-kul, 'peace with all'.

steps.title: Akbar (1556–1605)
steps.body: Abolished pilgrim tax (1563) and jizya (1564); Rajput alliances (Amber 1562); Ibadat Khana (1575); mahzar (1579); Din-i-Ilahi/Tauhid-i-Ilahi (1582) as a discipleship circle. Translations of the Mahabharata (Razmnama).

steps.title: Jahangir and Shah Jahan
steps.body: Jahangir: chain of justice, Nur Jahan's influence, Sir Thomas Roe's embassy (1615). Shah Jahan: Taj Mahal, Shahjahanabad, Peacock Throne; war of succession 1657–58.

steps.title: Aurangzeb (1658–1707)
steps.body: Reimposed jizya (1679), Deccan wars and annexation of Bijapur (1686) and Golconda (1687); conflict with Marathas (Shivaji crowned 1674), Jats, Satnamis, Sikhs (Guru Tegh Bahadur executed 1675). Historians debate religion vs. political-economic causes of conflict.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Din-i-Ilahi was not a mass state religion; only a small number of nobles joined.

a.text: An exam asks: 'Was Aurangzeb's reign the cause of Mughal decline?' How do you open?

choices.label: State the debate: religious policy vs. jagirdari crisis and over-extension
Say Aurangzeb alone destroyed the empire
choices.feedback: Too simple; examiners expect multiple causes.

b.text: Which evidence best supports an economic explanation?

choices.label: Be-jagiri and the jama–hasil gap (Satish Chandra)
choices.feedback: Correct—this is the agrarian/jagirdari crisis argument.

c.text: Conclude: decline was multi-causal; Aurangzeb's policies interacted with structural strains.

quiz.why: Akbar abolished jizya in 1564.
Aurangzeb reimposed jizya in 1679.

quiz.q: Sir Thomas Roe visited the court of:
quiz.why: Roe was James I's ambassador to Jahangir from 1615.

questions.q: Grand Trunk Road was rebuilt by:
questions.why: Sher Shah rebuilt and extended it with sarais.
Raja Todar Mal designed the zabt system.
Akbar's forces defeated Hemu at Panipat in 1556.
Sawar set the number of horsemen to be kept.

questions.q: Average yield 15 maunds; one-third share; price ₹0.4/maund. Demand per bigha:

questions.why: Banjar was uncultivated for five years or more.
Akbar set it up at Fatehpur Sikri in 1575.

questions.q: Razmnama is a Persian translation of:
questions.why: Razmnama is the Persian Mahabharata made for Akbar.
Aurangzeb annexed Golconda in 1687.
Paper revenue estimates outran real collections, squeezing nobles.

questions.q: Jagirdari crisis thesis is associated with:
questions.why: Satish Chandra developed the jagirdari crisis argument.
Abul Fazl's sulh-i-kul envisaged harmony among all communities under the emperor.

courses.title: Unit 5 · Mughal Economy, Culture, Marathas and Revision
curricula: UGC CBCS / NEP 2020 (History of India V/VI)
courses.summary: Agrarian society and zamindars, trade and European companies, Mughal art and architecture, the rise of the Marathas, the decline debate, and revision.
outcomes: Describe agrarian hierarchy: zamindars, khud-kashta and pahi-kashta peasants
Explain Mughal trade and the arrival of European companies
Identify features of Mughal architecture and painting
Outline Shivaji's administration
Compare explanations of Mughal decline

scenes.text: In Bayana, peasants grow indigo for Dutch and English buyers.
Silver from the Americas flows into India to pay for textiles.

steps.title: Rural hierarchy
steps.body: Zamindars (hereditary rights over a share of produce; collected revenue), khud-kashta (resident peasants), pahi-kashta (non-resident cultivators), muqaddam/patel (village headman), patwari (accountant). Village panchayats.

steps.title: Trade
steps.body: Exports: cotton textiles, indigo, saltpetre, spices. Ports: Surat, Masulipatnam, Hugli. Bankers: shroffs, hundis (bills of exchange). Merchant princes like Virji Vora of Surat.

steps.title: European companies
steps.body: Portuguese (Vasco da Gama 1498, Goa 1510), English East India Company (charter 1600; Surat factory 1613), Dutch VOC (1602), French (1664).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Zamindars were not landowners in the modern sense; Irfan Habib's Agrarian System of Mughal India (1963) is the standard work.

quiz.q: The English East India Company received its charter in:
quiz.why: Elizabeth I granted the charter on 31 December 1600.
Hundis were bills of exchange moving credit across distances.
Albuquerque captured Goa in 1510.

scenes.text: Humayun's tomb (1560s) sits in a charbagh, a four-part garden.
The Taj Mahal perfects the double dome and pietra dura inlay.

steps.title: Architecture
steps.body: Humayun's tomb (red sandstone, charbagh), Fatehpur Sikri (Buland Darwaza, Panch Mahal), Agra Fort, Akbar's tomb at Sikandra, Itimad-ud-Daulah's tomb (early pietra dura), Taj Mahal, Red Fort and Jama Masjid of Shahjahanabad.

steps.title: Painting
steps.body: Persian masters Mir Sayyid Ali and Abdus Samad; Hamzanama; Akbar's karkhana with Daswanth and Basawan; Jahangir's naturalist studies (Mansur's birds), portraits by Abul Hasan.

steps.title: Literature
steps.body: Abul Fazl's Akbarnama and Ain-i-Akbari; Badauni's critical Muntakhab-ut-Tawarikh; Jahangir's Tuzuk; Dara Shikoh's Majma-ul-Bahrain.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Buland Darwaza commemorates Akbar's Gujarat victory (1573), not the Deccan.

quiz.q: Which tomb is an early major use of pietra dura?
quiz.why: Itimad-ud-Daulah's tomb (1620s), built by Nur Jahan, shows extensive marble inlay.

quiz.q: Badauni's history is notable for being:
quiz.why: Badauni wrote it privately and was hostile to Akbar's religious experiments.
A charbagh divides a garden into four quarters by water channels.

scenes.text: In 1674 Shivaji is crowned Chhatrapati at Raigad.
After 1707 the Mughal centre weakens and regional states rise.

steps.title: Shivaji (1630–80)
steps.body: Ashtapradhan council (Peshwa, Amatya, etc.), chauth (one-fourth) and sardeshmukhi (additional one-tenth) levies, forts, light cavalry and guerrilla tactics; Treaty of Purandar (1665) with Jai Singh; escape from Agra (1666).

steps.title: Decline debate
steps.body: Imperial/ 'Aligarh' view: jagirdari and agrarian crisis (Irfan Habib, Satish Chandra, M. Athar Ali). Religious policy (Jadunath Sarkar). Revisionist view (Muzaffar Alam, C.A. Bayly): 18th century as regional prosperity and new states (Awadh, Bengal, Hyderabad), not universal decline.

steps.title: Worked example: chauth and sardeshmukhi
steps.body: If a district's revenue is ₹1,00,000, chauth = 25% = ₹25,000 and sardeshmukhi = 10% = ₹10,000; total Maratha claim ₹35,000.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Nadir Shah's invasion was 1739; Ahmad Shah Abdali's victory at the Third Battle of Panipat was 1761.

activity.prompt: A region's revenue is ₹2,40,000. What is the total of chauth (25%) plus sardeshmukhi (10%) in rupees?

quiz.q: Treaty of Purandar (1665) was signed with:
quiz.why: Shivaji signed it with the Mughal commander Raja Jai Singh.

quiz.q: The revisionist view of the 18th century stresses:
quiz.why: Alam and Bayly argue decline at the centre coincided with regional vitality.
Nadir Shah sacked Delhi in 1739.

lessons.title: Revision: key points and answer practice

scenes.text: You pin dates from 650 to 1761 on your wall.
Linking dates to themes makes long answers easier.

steps.title: Key dates
steps.body: c. 750–950 tripartite struggle; 985 Rajaraja I; 1025 Somnath raid; 1192 Tarain; 1206 Sultanate; 1336 Vijayanagara; 1347 Bahmani; 1398 Timur; 1526 Panipat; 1540 Sher Shah; 1556 Akbar; 1565 Talikota; 1580 dahsala; 1600 EIC; 1674 Shivaji crowned; 1679 jizya; 1707 Aurangzeb dies; 1739 Nadir Shah; 1761 Third Panipat.

steps.title: Original practice questions
steps.body: 1. 'Examine the iqta and jagir as instruments of control.' 2. 'Compare Alauddin's and Akbar's revenue systems.' 3. 'How did Bhakti and Sufi saints use vernacular languages?' 4. 'Was the Chola state centralised?' 5. 'Discuss historiographical views of the 18th century.'

steps.title: Comparison answers
steps.body: Use a table in your plan: aim, method, share of produce, assessment, outcome. Then write paragraphs comparing point-by-point.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Confusing iqta (Sultanate) with jagir (Mughal) and zat with sawar; writing communal narratives instead of evidence-based analysis.

quiz.why: Talikota (1565) is after 1526, 1398 and 1336.
Alauddin Khalji introduced market regulations; the other pairs are mismatched.

quiz.q: The Third Battle of Panipat was won by:
quiz.why: Abdali defeated the Marathas in 1761.

questions.q: Surat factory of the English was set up in:
questions.why: The English established their Surat factory in 1613.
Chauth was a 25% levy.
It was Shivaji's council of eight ministers.
Akbar built it after conquering Gujarat in 1573.
The VOC was chartered in 1602.

questions.q: Who painted bird studies for Jahangir?
questions.why: Ustad Mansur was Jahangir's natural-history painter.
They cultivated in villages other than their own.

questions.q: Who emphasised religious policy in Mughal decline?
questions.why: Sarkar stressed Aurangzeb's religious policies.
Dara Shikoh explored common ground between Sufism and Vedanta.
He was crowned at Raigad in 1674.

questions.q: Which best captures the revisionist view?
options: The 18th century saw dynamic regional polities
questions.why: Revisionists argue regional states such as Awadh and Bengal thrived economically.

uni-ba-hist-modern-india.title: Modern India (1757–1947)
uni-ba-hist-modern-india.description: Expansion of Company rule, colonial economy, social reform, 1857, rise of nationalism, Gandhian mass movements, communalism and Partition. Study companion; topics commonly taught in Indian BA History programmes.

courses.title: Unit 1 · Expansion of Company Rule (1757–1856)
curricula: UGC CBCS / NEP 2020 (History of India VII)
courses.summary: Plassey and Buxar, diwani and the dual system, Anglo-Mysore and Anglo-Maratha wars, subsidiary alliance, doctrine of lapse, and acts regulating the Company.
outcomes: Explain Plassey and Buxar and their consequences
Describe the dual system in Bengal
Outline wars with Mysore, Marathas and Sikhs
Explain subsidiary alliance and doctrine of lapse
Summarise the Regulating Act and Pitt's India Act

scenes.text: At Plassey, Mir Jafar's troops stand aside while Clive's small force defeats Siraj-ud-Daula.
In 1765 Shah Alam II grants the Company the diwani of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa.

steps.title: Plassey (23 June 1757)
steps.body: Causes: misuse of dastaks (trade permits), fortification of Calcutta, the 'Black Hole' story (numbers disputed). Result: Mir Jafar installed; huge payments to Company officials.

steps.title: Buxar (1764)
steps.body: Mir Qasim, Shuja-ud-Daula of Awadh and Shah Alam II defeated by Hector Munro. Treaty of Allahabad (1765): diwani to the Company.

steps.title: Dual system (1765–72)
steps.body: Company held diwani (revenue) while the nawab nominally held nizamat (law and order) without resources—'power without responsibility'. The Bengal famine of 1770 killed perhaps a third of the population (estimates vary).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Buxar, not Plassey, was the decisive military victory that gave the Company legal revenue rights.

events.text: Dual system ended by Warren Hastings

quiz.q: Diwani of Bengal was granted by:
quiz.why: The Mughal emperor Shah Alam II granted it in 1765.
The Battle of Buxar took place in October 1764.
Company servants used duty-free permits for private trade, hurting the nawab's revenue.

scenes.text: Tipu Sultan sends embassies to France and the Ottomans and plants a 'Tree of Liberty' at Srirangapatna.
He dies defending his capital in 1799.

steps.title: Anglo-Mysore wars
steps.body: First (1767–69, Treaty of Madras), Second (1780–84, Treaty of Mangalore), Third (1790–92, Treaty of Seringapatam—Tipu loses half his territory), Fourth (1799, Tipu killed).

steps.title: Anglo-Maratha wars
steps.body: First (1775–82, Treaty of Salbai), Second (1803–05; Treaty of Bassein 1802 with Peshwa Baji Rao II), Third (1817–18; Peshwaship abolished).

steps.title: Sikhs
steps.body: Ranjit Singh (d. 1839) built a strong Punjab state; Anglo-Sikh wars 1845–46 and 1848–49; Punjab annexed 1849 under Dalhousie.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: The Treaty of Bassein (1802) made the Peshwa accept a subsidiary alliance and triggered the Second Anglo-Maratha War.

lessons.title: Subsidiary alliance and doctrine of lapse

scenes.text: Wellesley offers a ruler protection—if he hosts and pays for a British force.
Dalhousie later annexes states whose rulers die without a natural heir.

steps.title: Subsidiary alliance (Wellesley, 1798–1805)
steps.body: Ruler kept a British force, paid for it (often by ceding territory), accepted a British Resident, could not employ other Europeans or make war without consent. Hyderabad first (1798); Mysore, Awadh (1801), Peshwa (1802).

steps.title: Doctrine of lapse (Dalhousie, 1848–56)
steps.body: Dependent states without natural heirs lapsed to the Company: Satara (1848), Jhansi (1853), Nagpur (1854), Sambalpur, Udaipur (Chhattisgarh). Awadh annexed 1856 on grounds of misgovernment, not lapse.

steps.title: Regulating acts
steps.body: Regulating Act 1773 (Governor-General of Bengal, Supreme Court at Calcutta); Pitt's India Act 1784 (Board of Control); Charter Acts 1813 (ended Company's India trade monopoly), 1833 (Governor-General of India; Company's commercial role ended), 1853.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Awadh was not annexed under the doctrine of lapse.

activity.prompt: Subsidiary alliance or doctrine of lapse/annexation?

quiz.why: The Nizam of Hyderabad signed in 1798.

quiz.q: Awadh was annexed in 1856 on grounds of:
quiz.why: Dalhousie cited misgovernment to annex Awadh.

quiz.q: The Board of Control was set up by:
quiz.why: Pitt's India Act created the Board of Control to supervise the Company.

scenes.text: Was British power imposed by force, or did Indian bankers and merchants help create it?
The Jagat Seths of Murshidabad financed the plot against Siraj.

steps.title: Views
steps.body: Imperialist: 'empire in a fit of absence of mind' (J.R. Seeley's phrase). Nationalist: conspiracy and plunder. Revisionist (C.A. Bayly, P.J. Marshall): Indian intermediaries and regional political economies drew the Company in.

steps.title: Economic factors
steps.body: Revenue of Bengal paid for Company trade (ending need to import bullion), wars and armies (the sepoy army).

steps.title: Answer frame
steps.body: Q: 'Explain the rise of British power.' Military-technical edge and finance; Indian divisions; collaboration of bankers; role of revenue; historiography.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Do not write as though 'India' was a single state that lost a war in 1757.

quiz.why: J.R. Seeley used the phrase in The Expansion of England (1883).

courses.title: Unit 2 · Colonial Economy and Society
curricula: UGC CBCS / NEP 2020 (History of India VII/VIII)
courses.summary: Land revenue settlements, commercialisation of agriculture and famines, deindustrialisation and the drain of wealth, railways, and peasant and tribal resistance.
outcomes: Compare Permanent, Ryotwari and Mahalwari settlements
Explain the drain of wealth theory
Evaluate the deindustrialisation debate
Describe commercialisation and famines
Outline peasant and tribal uprisings

scenes.text: Under the Permanent Settlement, a zamindar who failed to pay by sunset on the due date could have his estate auctioned.
Many old zamindari houses in Bengal lost lands in the 1790s.

steps.title: Permanent Settlement (1793)
steps.body: Cornwallis; Bengal, Bihar, Orissa (later parts of Madras/Benares). Zamindars became proprietors; revenue fixed in perpetuity, about ten-elevenths of rental to the state initially (zamindar kept one-eleventh).

steps.title: Ryotwari
steps.body: Thomas Munro and Alexander Read; Madras (1820) and Bombay; settlement directly with the ryot (cultivator), periodically revised (often 30 years); high assessments.

steps.title: Mahalwari
steps.body: Holt Mackenzie (1822), revised under Bentinck (1833); North-Western Provinces, Punjab; village (mahal) as unit with joint responsibility.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Estate rental ₹11,000. State share 10/11 = ₹10,000; zamindar keeps ₹1,000. If rents later rise to ₹22,000 but revenue is fixed, the zamindar keeps ₹12,000.

activity.prompt: Under the Permanent Settlement ratio, an estate's rental is ₹33,000. How much (₹) does the zamindar keep?

quiz.why: Munro introduced ryotwari in Madras.
The mahal was jointly responsible for the revenue.
Late payment by sunset led to auction of zamindari estates.

scenes.text: Dadabhai Naoroji calculates India's per capita income at ₹20 a year (1867–68 estimate).
He argues a large part of India's wealth flows to Britain without return.

steps.title: Drain theory
steps.body: Naoroji's Poverty and Un-British Rule in India (1901), R.C. Dutt's Economic History of India. Components: home charges (pensions, interest, India Office costs), salaries remitted, profits of foreign capital, export surplus without return imports.

steps.title: Deindustrialisation
steps.body: Decline of handicraft textiles after cheap Manchester imports, one-way free trade, loss of court patronage. Debate: Morris D. Morris argued overall decline is overstated; Amiya Bagchi's Gangetic Bihar data showed fall in industrial employment share.

steps.title: Railways
steps.body: First passenger line Bombay–Thane, 16 April 1853. Built with guaranteed 5% return to British investors; served export of raw materials and troop movement, also created a national market.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Bombay–Thane (1853) is the first passenger train; do not write 'Calcutta–Howrah first'.

activity.prompt: Part of the drain argument or of its critique?

items.text: Home charges paid from Indian revenue
Some outflow paid for services and capital

quiz.q: Poverty and Un-British Rule in India is by:
quiz.why: Naoroji published it in 1901.
It ran on 16 April 1853.

options: Investors got fixed returns paid from Indian revenues if needed
quiz.why: Guaranteed returns shifted the risk to Indian taxpayers.

scenes.text: The American Civil War (1861–65) cuts US cotton supply; Deccan peasants borrow to grow cotton.
When prices fall, debt rises—leading to the Deccan riots of 1875 against moneylenders.

steps.title: Commercial crops
steps.body: Indigo, cotton, jute, opium, tea; forced indigo cultivation sparked the Indigo Revolt (1859–60); Dinabandhu Mitra's play Neel Darpan.

steps.title: Famines
steps.body: Great Famine 1876–78; famines of 1896–97 and 1899–1900; Famine Commissions (1880 Strachey; Famine Code). Bengal Famine 1943. Amartya Sen's entitlement approach: famines arise from collapse of people's ability to command food, not only fall in supply.

steps.title: Debt
steps.body: Deccan Agriculturists' Relief Act (1879) after the riots; Punjab Land Alienation Act (1900).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Sen's argument does not deny supply shocks; it explains why some groups starve while food exists.

quiz.why: Bengal ryots refused indigo cultivation in 1859–60.
Indebted peasants attacked moneylenders and destroyed debt bonds.
Sen showed loss of purchasing power causes starvation even when food is available.

scenes.text: In 1855 the Santhal brothers Sidhu and Kanhu lead a rebellion against moneylenders, zamindars and the Company.
In 1899–1900 Birsa Munda leads the Ulgulan in Chotanagpur.

steps.title: Tribal movements
steps.body: Santhal Hul (1855–56; Santhal Parganas created), Kol uprising (1831–32), Munda Ulgulan (1899–1900; later Chotanagpur Tenancy Act 1908), Rampa (1879, 1922–24 under Alluri Sitarama Raju).

steps.title: Peasant movements
steps.body: Faraizi (Haji Shariatullah, Dudu Miyan), Wahabi/Tariqah-i-Muhammadiya, Pabna (1873, agrarian league), Moplah (Mappila) uprisings in Malabar (19th c. and 1921).

steps.title: Interpretation
steps.body: Ranajit Guha's Elementary Aspects of Peasant Insurgency (1983) read colonial records 'against the grain' to recover peasant consciousness.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Do not reduce tribal revolts to 'law and order' problems; they responded to land alienation, forest laws and debt.

quiz.why: Sidhu and Kanhu Murmu led the 1855 Hul.
The 1908 Act responded to land grievances raised in Birsa's movement.

quiz.q: Elementary Aspects of Peasant Insurgency was written by:
quiz.why: Ranajit Guha published it in 1983.

questions.why: Cornwallis introduced it in 1793.

questions.q: Rental ₹22,000 under the 10/11 rule; state share:
Economic History of India is by:
questions.why: Romesh Chunder Dutt wrote it in two volumes.
They were India's payments in Britain for administration, pensions and debt.
It was passed in 1879.
Pabna's agrarian league formed in 1873.
His 1822 regulation began Mahalwari.
Morris questioned how severe handicraft decline really was.

questions.q: American Civil War affected India by:
questions.why: Cotton prices rose during the war and fell after 1865.
Haji Shariatullah founded the Faraizi movement in Bengal.

questions.q: First Famine Commission (1880) was headed by:
questions.why: Sir Richard Strachey chaired it.

questions.q: Strongest argument for the drain theory:
options: Unrequited export surplus financed payments to Britain
questions.why: Naoroji showed India's export surplus paid for home charges without equivalent return.

courses.title: Unit 3 · Social Reform Movements and the Revolt of 1857
curricula: UGC CBCS / NEP 2020 (History of India VIII)
courses.summary: Orientalism and Anglicism, socio-religious reform (Brahmo, Arya, Aligarh, Satyashodhak), women's reform laws, causes, course and interpretations of 1857, and the Act of 1858.
outcomes: Contrast Orientalists and Anglicists
Describe key reform movements and their leaders
Explain reform legislation on sati, widow remarriage and age of consent
Analyse causes and spread of 1857
Evaluate interpretations of 1857

scenes.text: In 1835 Macaulay claims 'a single shelf of a good European library' is worth all native literature.
Fifty years earlier, William Jones had founded the Asiatic Society (1784) to study Sanskrit and Persian.

steps.title: Orientalists
steps.body: William Jones (Asiatic Society 1784), H.T. Colebrooke; Calcutta Madrasa (1781, Hastings), Sanskrit College at Benares (1791, Jonathan Duncan).

steps.title: Anglicists
steps.body: Macaulay's Minute (1835), English Education Act (Bentinck, 1835), Wood's Despatch (1854) leading to universities of Calcutta, Bombay, Madras (1857). Utilitarians (James Mill's History of British India, 1817) condemned Indian civilisation.

steps.title: Interpretation
steps.body: Edward Said's Orientalism (1978) and Bernard Cohn: knowledge production as part of colonial power.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: James Mill never visited India; his periodisation into Hindu, Muslim and British periods was influential and misleading.

quiz.why: Charles Wood's education despatch came in 1854.
Sir William Jones founded it in Calcutta in 1784.

quiz.q: Universities of Calcutta, Bombay, Madras were founded in:
quiz.why: All three were set up in 1857.

scenes.text: Rammohun Roy writes tracts against sati using the shastras themselves.
In 1829 Bentinck's Regulation XVII bans sati in Bengal Presidency.

steps.title: Bengal
steps.body: Rammohun Roy: Atmiya Sabha (1815), Brahmo Sabha (1828). Debendranath Tagore, Keshab Chandra Sen. Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar: Hindu Widows' Remarriage Act 1856.

steps.title: Western and northern India
steps.body: Prarthana Samaj (1867; M.G. Ranade); Arya Samaj (Dayananda Saraswati, 1875; Satyarth Prakash; 'back to the Vedas', shuddhi); Ramakrishna Mission (Vivekananda, 1897).

steps.title: Anti-caste and Muslim reform
steps.body: Jyotirao Phule: Satyashodhak Samaj (1873), Gulamgiri; Savitribai Phule's girls' school (1848). Narayana Guru in Kerala (SNDP, 1903). Sayyid Ahmad Khan: MAO College Aligarh (1875). Deoband (1867).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Age of Consent Act was 1891 (age 12); the Sarda Act (Child Marriage Restraint) was 1929.

quiz.why: Bentinck's Regulation XVII of 1829 banned it.
Phule wrote Gulamgiri (Slavery) in 1873.
Dayananda founded it in Bombay in 1875.

lessons.title: The Revolt of 1857: causes and course

scenes.text: Sepoys jailed for refusing the new Enfield cartridges are freed by comrades.
They march to Delhi and proclaim Bahadur Shah Zafar their leader.

steps.title: Causes
steps.body: Political: annexations (Awadh 1856), doctrine of lapse. Economic: heavy revenue, ruin of taluqdars. Military: General Service Enlistment Act 1856, low pay, greased cartridges. Social-religious: fears of conversion, reforms.

steps.title: Course and leaders
steps.body: Mangal Pandey at Barrackpore (29 March). Delhi (Bakht Khan), Kanpur (Nana Saheb, Tantia Tope), Lucknow (Begum Hazrat Mahal), Jhansi (Rani Lakshmibai, d. June 1858), Bihar (Kunwar Singh), Bareilly (Khan Bahadur Khan). Delhi recaptured Sept 1857.

steps.title: Aftermath
steps.body: Government of India Act 1858: Crown rule, Secretary of State, Viceroy; Queen's Proclamation (Nov 1858); army reorganised with more Europeans.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: The revolt was strongest in north and central India; Punjab, Bengal and the south were largely quiet.

quiz.q: The revolt began at Meerut on:
quiz.why: Sepoys rose at Meerut on 10 May 1857.

quiz.q: The Queen's Proclamation was issued in:
quiz.why: It was read on 1 November 1858.

quiz.q: Bahadur Shah Zafar was exiled to:
quiz.why: He was exiled to Rangoon, where he died in 1862.

scenes.text: British writers called it the 'Sepoy Mutiny'; Savarkar in 1909 called it 'The First War of Indian Independence'.
Historians since have studied peasants, taluqdars and religion.

steps.title: Interpretations
steps.body: Sepoy mutiny (contemporary British); Muslim conspiracy (Outram); national war (Savarkar 1909); R.C. Majumdar: 'neither first, nor national, nor war of independence'; S.N. Sen (official centenary history, 1957); Eric Stokes (The Peasant Armed): localised peasant and elite grievances; Rudrangshu Mukherjee on Awadh.

steps.title: Answer frame
steps.body: Define the labels; show military origin; spread to civilians in Awadh; limits (geography, leadership); conclude with a nuanced label such as 'popular revolt'.

steps.title: Evidence
steps.body: Azamgarh Proclamation (1857) lists grievances of zamindars, merchants, officials, artisans and priests—useful for showing civilian participation.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Don't present one label as settled truth; examiners want a reasoned view.

pairs: Neither first, nor national, nor war of independence

quiz.why: It was published in 1909.

quiz.q: Azamgarh Proclamation is useful because it:
options: Lists grievances of many civilian groups
quiz.why: It appeals to several social groups, showing broader participation.
Eric Stokes's study (published 1986) examined rural participation.

questions.why: Macaulay wrote it in February 1835.
It was passed in 1856.
Ranade was its leading figure.

questions.q: Mangal Pandey's act took place at:
questions.why: He attacked officers at Barrackpore on 29 March 1857.

questions.q: Government of India Act 1858 created the post of:
questions.why: It transferred control to the Crown under a Secretary of State.
The Child Marriage Restraint Act 1929 was known as the Sarda Act.

questions.q: Savitribai Phule opened a girls' school in Pune in:
questions.why: Savitribai and Jyotirao opened it in 1848.
He served as Nana Saheb's general.
Overseas service threatened caste rules for many high-caste sepoys.

questions.q: James Mill's History of British India:
options: Divided Indian history into Hindu, Muslim, British periods
questions.why: Mill's tripartite communal periodisation became highly influential.
Dar-ul-Ulum Deoband was founded in 1867.

options: A widespread popular revolt with regional limits
questions.why: It began in the army and drew civilians in north India but was regionally limited.

courses.title: Unit 4 · The National Movement (1885–1934)
curricula: UGC CBCS / NEP 2020 (History of India IX)
courses.summary: Founding of the Congress, Moderates and Extremists, Swadeshi, revolutionary nationalism, Gandhi's early campaigns, Non-Cooperation and Civil Disobedience.
outcomes: Explain the foundation of the INC and the safety-valve debate
Compare Moderates and Extremists
Describe the Swadeshi movement
Outline Champaran, Kheda, Ahmedabad and Rowlatt satyagraha
Analyse Non-Cooperation and Civil Disobedience

lessons.title: Early nationalism: the Congress and the Moderates

scenes.text: December 1885: 72 delegates meet at Gokuldas Tejpal Sanskrit College, Bombay; W.C. Bonnerjee presides.
They pass resolutions for civil service reform and expanded councils.

steps.title: Precursors
steps.body: British Indian Association (1851), Indian Association (1876; S.N. Banerjea), Poona Sarvajanik Sabha (1870), Madras Mahajan Sabha (1884). Ilbert Bill controversy (1883).

steps.title: Safety-valve theory
steps.body: Claims A.O. Hume founded the Congress to release discontent (based on W. Wedderburn's biography; Lala Lajpat Rai's use). Bipan Chandra: Indians used Hume as a 'lightning conductor' to avoid suspicion.

steps.title: Moderates (1885–1905)
steps.body: Dadabhai Naoroji, Pherozeshah Mehta, G.K. Gokhale, Surendranath Banerjea. Methods: petitions, prayers, protests; constitutional reform; economic critique (drain). Achievement: Indian Councils Act 1892.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Moderates were not 'pro-British collaborators'; they built the economic critique of colonialism.

statements.s: W.C. Bonnerjee presided over the first Congress session.
statements.why: He presided at Bombay in 1885.

statements.s: The first session had about 72 delegates.
statements.why: That is the standard figure.

statements.s: Moderates used mass strikes as their main method.
statements.why: They relied on petitions and constitutional methods.

statements.s: Bipan Chandra accepted the safety-valve theory.
statements.why: He offered the 'lightning conductor' counter-argument.

quiz.why: Banerjea and Ananda Mohan Bose founded it in 1876.

quiz.q: Indian Councils Act was passed in:
quiz.why: It came in 1892, a modest Moderate gain.
Europeans opposed allowing Indian judges to try them.

scenes.text: 16 October 1905: Bengal is partitioned; people tie rakhis and observe mourning.
British cloth is burnt in bonfires.

steps.title: Extremists
steps.body: Lal-Bal-Pal (Lajpat Rai, Tilak, B.C. Pal) and Aurobindo; 'Swaraj is my birthright'; Shivaji and Ganapati festivals. Surat split 1907.

steps.title: Swadeshi (1905–11)
steps.body: Boycott, national education (Bengal National College), swadeshi enterprises (Bengal Chemicals of P.C. Ray), samitis. Limits: weak peasant and Muslim participation. Partition annulled 1911; capital to Delhi.

steps.title: Revolutionaries and reforms
steps.body: Anushilan Samiti, Jugantar; Khudiram Bose (1908); Ghadar Party (1913, San Francisco). Muslim League founded 1906 (Dhaka); Morley–Minto reforms 1909 introduced separate electorates. Lucknow Pact 1916; Home Rule Leagues 1916 (Tilak, Annie Besant).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Partition of Bengal was in 1905 under Curzon; annulment in 1911 under Hardinge II.

events.text: Lucknow Pact and Home Rule Leagues

quiz.q: Separate electorates for Muslims came with:
quiz.why: The Indian Councils Act 1909 introduced separate electorates.
It was founded in 1913 on the US Pacific coast.
George V's Delhi Durbar announced it in 1911.

scenes.text: Raj Kumar Shukla persuades Gandhi to investigate indigo tinkathia exploitation in Champaran.
Gandhi defies an order to leave; an inquiry follows.

steps.title: Early campaigns
steps.body: Champaran (1917), Ahmedabad mill strike (1918, Gandhi's first hunger strike in India), Kheda (1918, with Vallabhbhai Patel). Rowlatt Act satyagraha (1919); Jallianwala Bagh massacre, 13 April 1919 (General Dyer).

steps.title: Non-Cooperation (1920–22)
steps.body: Merged with the Khilafat movement; Calcutta special session (Sept 1920) and Nagpur (Dec 1920). Boycott of councils, courts, schools, foreign cloth; national schools (Jamia Millia, Kashi Vidyapith). Withdrawn after Chauri Chaura (5 Feb 1922).

steps.title: After
steps.body: Swaraj Party (C.R. Das, Motilal Nehru, 1923); Simon Commission (1927–28, all-white) boycotted; Lajpat Rai dies after lathi charge (1928); Nehru Report (1928).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: The tinkathia system required planting indigo on 3/20 of the land, not one-third.

activity.prompt: Under tinkathia, a peasant had to grow indigo on 3 kathas out of every 20. On 60 kathas of land, how many kathas would be indigo?

quiz.why: Dyer's troops fired on the crowd on 13 April 1919.
Gandhi halted it after police were killed at Chauri Chaura.
Patel emerged as a leader in Kheda (1918).

lessons.title: Civil Disobedience and the Round Tables

scenes.text: On 12 March 1930 Gandhi leaves Sabarmati with 78 followers for Dandi.
On 6 April he picks up salt, breaking the salt law.

steps.title: Background
steps.body: Lahore Congress (Dec 1929, Nehru president): Purna Swaraj; 26 January 1930 celebrated as Independence Day.

steps.title: Movement
steps.body: Salt satyagraha; Dharasana raid (Sarojini Naidu); Khudai Khidmatgars (Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan) in NWFP; Peshawar shooting; no-tax campaigns; women's large participation.

steps.title: Negotiations
steps.body: First Round Table (1930–31, Congress absent); Gandhi–Irwin Pact (March 1931); Second RTC (Gandhi attends); Communal Award (1932); Poona Pact (Sept 1932, Gandhi–Ambedkar: reserved seats for depressed classes within joint electorates); movement withdrawn 1934.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Only the Second Round Table was attended by Gandhi.

quiz.why: It settled Depressed Classes representation through reserved seats.
Lahore Congress under Nehru adopted complete independence.
Ghaffar Khan led these non-violent 'servants of God' in NWFP.

questions.why: It met in Bombay in 1885.

questions.why: Tilak popularised the slogan.
Moderates and Extremists split at Surat in 1907.
It was passed in March 1919.
It is in Gorakhpur district, UP.

questions.why: They formed it in 1923 to contest council elections.
Congress and League agreed on joint demands.
Its all-British membership was an insult to Indians.
British PM MacDonald announced it in 1932.
