courses.title: Unit 5 · Towards Independence and Partition; Revision
curricula: UGC CBCS / NEP 2020 (History of India X)
courses.summary: Act of 1935 and provincial ministries, left and Dalit politics, Quit India, Subhas Bose and the INA, communal politics, the transfer of power and Partition, with revision.
outcomes: Explain the 1935 Act and 1937 elections
Describe left, peasant, workers' and Dalit movements
Analyse Quit India and the INA
Trace the growth of communal politics and the Pakistan demand
Explain the transfer of power and Partition

lessons.title: The 1935 Act, left and Dalit politics

scenes.text: In the 1937 elections, Congress forms ministries in most provinces.
In 1939, they resign over India's entry into the war without consultation.

steps.title: Government of India Act 1935
steps.body: Provincial autonomy, abolished dyarchy in provinces, proposed dyarchy at the centre and an all-India federation (never formed), Federal Court (1937), expanded franchise, Burma separated.

steps.title: Left
steps.body: CPI (in India from 1925), Congress Socialist Party (1934), All India Kisan Sabha (1936; Sahajanand Saraswati), AITUC (1920). Bose's election as Congress president at Tripuri (1939) and resignation; Forward Bloc.

steps.title: Ambedkar
steps.body: Bahishkrit Hitakarini Sabha (1924), Mahad satyagraha (1927), Independent Labour Party (1936), Annihilation of Caste (1936), Scheduled Castes Federation (1942).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: The federation under the 1935 Act never came into being because princely states did not join.

quiz.q: Which provision of the 1935 Act was never implemented?
quiz.why: The federation needed princely accession, which never happened.

quiz.q: Annihilation of Caste was written by:
quiz.why: Ambedkar wrote it in 1936.
They resigned in late 1939 over the war declaration.

scenes.text: At Gowalia Tank, Bombay, 8 August 1942, Gandhi tells the crowd: 'Do or die.'
Leaders are arrested next morning; crowds attack railways and police stations.

steps.title: Background
steps.body: August Offer (1940), individual satyagraha (1940–41; Vinoba Bhave first), Cripps Mission (March 1942: dominion status after war, right of provinces to opt out).

steps.title: Quit India (1942)
steps.body: Leaderless mass upsurge; underground (Jayaprakash Narayan, Aruna Asaf Ali, Usha Mehta's Congress Radio); parallel governments at Ballia, Tamluk (Jatiya Sarkar), Satara (Prati Sarkar).

steps.title: Bose and the INA
steps.body: Mohan Singh first organised the INA (1942); Bose took over in 1943 in Singapore, Provisional Government of Azad Hind (Oct 1943), Imphal–Kohima campaign (1944). INA trials at Red Fort (1945) and RIN mutiny (Feb 1946) shook British confidence.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Bose did not found the INA; Mohan Singh and Rash Behari Bose's league preceded him.

quiz.why: Stafford Cripps arrived in March 1942.
Gandhi chose Vinoba Bhave in October 1940.
Naval ratings rose in Bombay in February 1946.

story.title: A line drawn in five weeks

scenes.text: Cyril Radcliffe, new to India, draws the Punjab and Bengal borders in about five weeks.
Around 15 million people are displaced and perhaps up to a million or more killed (estimates vary widely).

steps.title: Growth of communal politics
steps.body: Separate electorates (1909), Hindu Mahasabha (1915), RSS (1925), Jinnah's Fourteen Points (1929), Iqbal's Allahabad address (1930), 'Pakistan' term (Rahmat Ali, 1933), Lahore Resolution (23 March 1940).

steps.title: Negotiations
steps.body: Simla Conference (1945), elections 1945–46, Cabinet Mission (1946; three-tier grouping plan), Direct Action Day (16 Aug 1946, Calcutta killings), Interim Government (Sept 1946), Attlee's statement (Feb 1947), Mountbatten Plan (3 June 1947), Indian Independence Act (July 1947).

steps.title: Partition historiography
steps.body: High politics (Ayesha Jalal's 'sole spokesman': Jinnah's Pakistan demand as a bargaining counter); people's histories (Urvashi Butalia, The Other Side of Silence) of women and violence.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: The Lahore Resolution spoke of 'independent states' and did not use the word 'Pakistan'.

quiz.why: Ayesha Jalal's 1985 book reinterpreted Jinnah's strategy.
It proposed a weak union with provincial groups.

quiz.q: Direct Action Day saw large-scale violence in:
quiz.why: The Great Calcutta Killings began on 16 August 1946.

scenes.text: Economy, society and politics connect: the drain fed nationalist critique; peasant movements fed Gandhian mass politics.
Use these links to lift answers above narration.

steps.title: Key dates
steps.body: 1757 Plassey; 1764 Buxar; 1793 Permanent Settlement; 1829 sati ban; 1857 revolt; 1858 Crown rule; 1885 INC; 1905 Bengal partition; 1909 Morley–Minto; 1919 Montagu–Chelmsford Act and Jallianwala; 1920–22 NCM; 1930 Dandi; 1932 Poona Pact; 1935 Act; 1942 Quit India; 1946 Cabinet Mission; 1947 Independence.

steps.title: Original practice questions
steps.body: 1. 'How did colonial land settlements reshape rural society?' 2. 'Was 1857 a national revolt?' 3. 'Assess the Moderates' contribution.' 4. 'Gandhi turned nationalism into a mass movement—discuss.' 5. 'Was Partition inevitable?'

steps.title: Historians to cite
steps.body: Bipan Chandra (nationalist), Sumit Sarkar (Modern India 1885–1947), Ranajit Guha (subaltern), Anil Seal (Cambridge school: 'elite competition'), Ayesha Jalal.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Treating Gandhi or any leader as the sole actor; ignoring regional and social variations.

quiz.why: Seal's Emergence of Indian Nationalism (1968) is a Cambridge school classic.
The 1919 Act divided provincial subjects into reserved and transferred.

questions.q: Quit India resolution was passed on:
questions.why: The AICC passed it on 8 August 1942.
The League adopted it on 23 March 1940.

questions.q: Azad Hind provisional government formed in:
questions.why: Bose proclaimed it in October 1943.
Tamluk's government was the Tamralipta Jatiya Sarkar.
It was founded in 1920 with Lala Lajpat Rai as president.
He chaired both the Punjab and Bengal boundary commissions.
Jinnah presented them in 1929.

questions.q: Dyarchy at the provincial level was introduced in:
questions.why: The Montagu–Chelmsford reforms brought it in 1919.

questions.q: The Other Side of Silence focuses on:
questions.why: Butalia uses oral histories of Partition violence.
It was announced on 3 June 1947.
Bose won but resigned after opposition from Gandhi's supporters.

options: Pakistan demand was partly a bargaining strategy
questions.why: She argued Jinnah used the demand to secure parity in a united India.

uni-ba-hist-world-history.title: World History (Renaissance to the Cold War)
uni-ba-hist-world-history.description: Renaissance and Reformation, Atlantic revolutions, Industrial Revolution, nationalism and imperialism, the World Wars, Russian Revolution, and the Cold War. Study companion; topics commonly taught in Indian BA History programmes.

courses.title: Unit 1 · Renaissance, Reformation and Early Modern Europe
curricula: UGC CBCS / NEP 2020 (Rise of the Modern West)
courses.summary: Transition from feudalism, the Italian Renaissance and humanism, voyages of exploration, Protestant and Catholic Reformations, the Scientific Revolution and absolutism.
outcomes: Explain why the Renaissance began in Italy
Define humanism with examples
Describe voyages of discovery and their effects
Compare Luther, Calvin and the Counter-Reformation
Explain the Scientific Revolution and absolutism

scenes.text: Brunelleschi completes the dome of Florence Cathedral in 1436 using ancient Roman ideas and new engineering.
Banking families like the Medici pay for artists and scholars.

steps.title: Why Italy
steps.body: Wealthy city-states (Florence, Venice, Milan), trade with the East, Roman ruins, patronage (Medici, popes), Byzantine scholars arriving especially after the fall of Constantinople (1453).

steps.title: Humanism
steps.body: Study of the studia humanitatis (grammar, rhetoric, poetry, history, moral philosophy) from classical texts. Petrarch ('father of humanism'), Lorenzo Valla (exposed the Donation of Constantine as a forgery), Pico della Mirandola (Oration on the Dignity of Man), Machiavelli (The Prince, 1513).

steps.title: Art
steps.body: Linear perspective, realism, anatomy: Giotto (precursor), Masaccio, Leonardo, Michelangelo, Raphael. Printing press with movable type by Gutenberg (c. 1450) spread ideas.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Burckhardt's 1860 view of a sudden 'rebirth' is now qualified: historians stress continuity with medieval learning.

pairs: Civilisation of the Renaissance in Italy (1860)

quiz.q: Constantinople fell to the Ottomans in:
quiz.why: Mehmed II captured it in 1453.
Machiavelli wrote it in 1513.
They revived classical learning in the humanities.

scenes.text: Vasco da Gama reaches Calicut after rounding the Cape of Good Hope.
Six years earlier Columbus had reached the Caribbean, thinking it was Asia.

steps.title: Motives
steps.body: 'Gold, God, glory': spices, bypassing Ottoman/Venetian middlemen, missionary zeal, royal rivalry. Technology: caravel, astrolabe, magnetic compass, Prince Henry's patronage in Portugal.

steps.title: Voyages
steps.body: Bartolomeu Dias rounds the Cape (1488); Columbus (1492); Vasco da Gama (1498); Treaty of Tordesillas (1494); Magellan–Elcano circumnavigation (1519–22); Cortés conquers the Aztecs (1521); Pizarro the Incas (1532).

steps.title: Consequences
steps.body: Columbian exchange (maize, potato to Europe; smallpox to the Americas), demographic collapse of indigenous peoples, Atlantic slave trade, price revolution from American silver.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Magellan died in the Philippines (1521); Elcano completed the voyage.

quiz.q: Treaty of Tordesillas divided the world between:
quiz.why: It split newly found lands between Spain and Portugal.

quiz.q: The Aztec empire was conquered by:
quiz.why: Hernán Cortés took Tenochtitlan in 1521.

quiz.q: Price revolution was caused largely by:
quiz.why: Massive silver imports fed long-term inflation in Europe.

scenes.text: In 1517 Martin Luther writes 95 theses against the sale of indulgences at Wittenberg.
Printed copies spread across Germany within weeks.

steps.title: Luther
steps.body: Justification by faith alone, scripture alone, priesthood of all believers; excommunicated (1521), Diet of Worms; German Bible translation; Peasants' War (1524–25); Peace of Augsburg (1555): cuius regio, eius religio.

steps.title: Other reformers
steps.body: Zwingli (Zurich), Calvin (Geneva; predestination; Institutes, 1536), Henry VIII's Act of Supremacy (1534).

steps.title: Catholic Reformation
steps.body: Council of Trent (1545–63), Society of Jesus (Ignatius Loyola, 1540), Index of prohibited books, Inquisition. Max Weber later linked Protestant ethic and capitalism (1905)—debated.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Peace of Augsburg recognised Lutheranism, not Calvinism (Calvinism was recognised in 1648 at Westphalia).

quiz.why: He issued them in October 1517.

quiz.q: Cuius regio, eius religio comes from:
quiz.why: Augsburg (1555) let rulers choose their territory's faith.
Loyola founded the Society of Jesus, approved in 1540.

scenes.text: Copernicus's De revolutionibus (1543) places the sun at the centre.
In France, Louis XIV builds Versailles as a stage for absolute monarchy.

steps.title: Science
steps.body: Copernicus (1543), Kepler's laws, Galileo's telescope and trial (1633), Bacon's empiricism, Descartes's rationalism, Newton's Principia (1687). Royal Society (1660).

steps.title: Absolutism
steps.body: Divine right (Bossuet), Louis XIV (1643–1715; 'L'état, c'est moi' attributed), Peter the Great, Hobbes's Leviathan (1651). Thirty Years' War ended with Peace of Westphalia (1648), basis of the state system.

steps.title: Transition debate
steps.body: Dobb–Sweezy debate on feudalism to capitalism: internal class relations (Dobb) vs. trade and towns (Sweezy); the Brenner debate on agrarian class structure.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Galileo was not executed; he was placed under house arrest.

quiz.why: It was published in 1687.
After his 1633 trial he lived under house arrest.
It ended the Thirty Years' War in 1648.

questions.why: Columbus sailed in 1492.
Calvin led the Reformation in Geneva.

questions.q: Valla showed the Donation of Constantine was:
questions.why: His philology proved it a later forgery.
It met in sessions from 1545 to 1563.
Pizarro defeated the Incas from 1532.
It made Henry VIII head of the English Church in 1534.

options: Potato to Europe, smallpox to Americas
questions.why: Crops and diseases crossed the Atlantic both ways.

questions.q: Who wrote Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism?
questions.why: Weber published it in 1904–05.
It was a major uprising in 1524–25.

questions.q: Calvinism was formally recognised in the Empire at:
questions.why: Westphalia extended recognition to Calvinists.

questions.q: Sweezy emphasised which cause of feudal decline?
questions.why: Sweezy stressed external commercial forces against Dobb.

questions.q: Best modern view of the Renaissance:
options: Sudden rupture with the Middle Ages
questions.why: Historians stress medieval roots alongside new developments.

courses.title: Unit 2 · The Age of Revolutions (1640–1815)
curricula: UGC CBCS / NEP 2020 (History of the Modern World)
courses.summary: The English Revolution, the Enlightenment, the American Revolution, the French Revolution and Napoleon.
outcomes: Explain the English Civil War and Glorious Revolution
Summarise key Enlightenment thinkers
Explain causes and results of the American Revolution
Analyse the phases of the French Revolution
Assess Napoleon's legacy

scenes.text: In January 1649 Charles I is tried and executed by Parliament.
In 1689 the Bill of Rights limits royal power.

steps.title: England
steps.body: Civil War (1642–51), Cromwell's Commonwealth and Protectorate, Restoration (1660), Glorious Revolution (1688) with William and Mary, Bill of Rights (1689).

steps.title: Enlightenment
steps.body: Locke (Two Treatises, 1689: natural rights to life, liberty, property), Montesquieu (Spirit of the Laws, 1748: separation of powers), Voltaire, Rousseau (Social Contract, 1762: general will), Diderot's Encyclopédie, Adam Smith (Wealth of Nations, 1776).

steps.title: Historiography
steps.body: Christopher Hill saw the English Revolution as a bourgeois revolution; revisionists (Conrad Russell) stressed short-term political and religious causes.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Hobbes supported strong sovereignty; Locke defended the right to resist tyranny—don't merge them.

quiz.why: He was beheaded in January 1649.

quiz.q: Spirit of the Laws is by:
quiz.why: Montesquieu published it in 1748.
James II was replaced by William and Mary in 1688.

scenes.text: December 1773: colonists dump East India Company tea into Boston Harbour.
On 4 July 1776 the Continental Congress adopts the Declaration of Independence.

steps.title: Causes
steps.body: Debt from the Seven Years' War; Stamp Act (1765), Townshend duties (1767), Tea Act (1773); 'No taxation without representation'; Intolerable Acts (1774).

steps.title: War
steps.body: Lexington and Concord (1775), Saratoga (1777, French alliance follows), Yorktown (1781), Treaty of Paris (1783). Thomas Paine's Common Sense (1776).

steps.title: Results
steps.body: US Constitution (1787), federalism, Bill of Rights (1791); slavery continued; influence on France.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: The Treaty of Paris ending this war is 1783, not 1763 (which ended the Seven Years' War).

quiz.why: Paine's pamphlet appeared in January 1776.

quiz.q: The decisive battle bringing France into the war:
quiz.why: The 1777 victory at Saratoga led to the 1778 French alliance.

quiz.q: US Bill of Rights ratified in:
quiz.why: The first ten amendments were ratified in 1791.

scenes.text: 20 June 1789: locked out, the Third Estate swears not to separate until France has a constitution.
14 July: Parisians storm the Bastille.

steps.title: Causes
steps.body: Fiscal crisis (war debts, incl. American war), privileged First and Second Estates, Third Estate grievances (cahiers), bread prices, Enlightenment ideas. Estates-General (May 1789).

steps.title: Phases
steps.body: National Assembly (1789): Declaration of the Rights of Man; abolition of feudal privileges (4 Aug). Constitutional monarchy (1791). Republic (Sept 1792); Louis XVI executed (Jan 1793). Jacobin Terror under Robespierre and the Committee of Public Safety (1793–94); Thermidor (July 1794); Directory (1795–99).

steps.title: Interpretations
steps.body: Marxist (Lefebvre, Soboul): bourgeois revolution; revisionist (Cobban, Furet): political culture and contingency.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: The Bastille held only seven prisoners when stormed; its significance was symbolic.

quiz.q: Declaration of the Rights of Man was in:
quiz.why: It was adopted in August 1789.
Robespierre dominated the Committee of Public Safety.
Furet challenged the Marxist interpretation.

lessons.title: Napoleon and the Congress of Vienna

scenes.text: In 1804 Napoleon crowns himself Emperor.
In 1815 he is defeated at Waterloo and exiled to St Helena.

steps.title: Reforms
steps.body: Coup of 18 Brumaire (1799), Concordat (1801), Civil Code (1804) codifying legal equality and property, Bank of France, lycées, Continental System (1806).

steps.title: Wars
steps.body: Austerlitz (1805), Trafalgar (1805, British naval victory), Peninsular War, invasion of Russia (1812), Leipzig (1813), Waterloo (1815).

steps.title: Vienna 1814–15
steps.body: Metternich; principles of legitimacy, compensation, balance of power; Concert of Europe.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Trafalgar was a British naval victory over France and Spain, not a land battle won by Napoleon.

statements.s: The Napoleonic Code was issued in 1804.
statements.why: The Civil Code was promulgated in 1804.

statements.s: Napoleon won at Trafalgar.
statements.why: Nelson's fleet defeated the Franco-Spanish fleet.

statements.s: Metternich was a key figure at Vienna.
statements.why: Austria's foreign minister shaped the settlement.

statements.s: The Russian campaign was in 1812.
statements.why: The Grande Armée invaded Russia in June 1812.

quiz.why: Napoleon tried to cripple Britain by barring its trade with Europe.
It was fought on 18 June 1815.
It brought Napoleon to power as First Consul.

questions.why: Rousseau wrote it.
It took place on 14 July 1789.
Cornwallis surrendered at Yorktown in 1781.
Smith published it in 1776.
The Thermidorian reaction toppled Robespierre in July 1794.

questions.q: Christopher Hill interpreted the English Revolution as:
questions.why: Hill, a Marxist, saw it as bourgeois.
It reconciled France with the Catholic Church.
Parliament passed it in 1765.
It ruled until Napoleon's coup.

questions.q: Principle of legitimacy at Vienna meant:
questions.why: It sought to restore 'legitimate' rulers such as the Bourbons.
He emphasised class and peasant revolution.

questions.q: A limitation of the American Revolution's ideals:
questions.why: Liberty was proclaimed while slavery persisted.

courses.title: Unit 3 · Industrialisation, Nationalism and Imperialism (1750–1914)
curricula: UGC CBCS / NEP 2020 (History of the Modern World)
courses.summary: The Industrial Revolution in Britain, its social effects and socialism, 1848 revolutions, unification of Italy and Germany, new imperialism and the scramble for Africa, and Meiji Japan.
outcomes: Explain why industrialisation began in Britain
Describe social consequences and rise of socialism
Compare Italian and German unification
Analyse theories of imperialism
Explain Meiji modernisation

scenes.text: Hargreaves's spinning jenny (c. 1764) lets one worker spin many threads.
By 1830 the Liverpool–Manchester railway carries passengers by steam.

steps.title: Why Britain
steps.body: Agricultural changes (enclosures), coal and iron deposits, colonial markets and raw materials, capital from trade, stable institutions, rivers and canals, patent system.

steps.title: Inventions
steps.body: Flying shuttle (Kay, 1733), spinning jenny (Hargreaves), water frame (Arkwright, 1769), mule (Crompton, 1779), power loom (Cartwright, 1785), Watt's improved steam engine (patent 1769), Stephenson's Rocket (1829).

steps.title: Worked example: productivity
steps.body: If a hand spinner produced 1 spindle of thread and an early jenny had 8 spindles, one worker's output rose about 8 times. Later jennies with 80 spindles gave about an 80-fold rise per worker.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Watt did not invent the steam engine; Newcomen's engine (1712) came earlier—Watt added a separate condenser.

activity.prompt: A factory with 12 workers each operating a 40-spindle jenny replaces hand spinners producing 1 spindle each. How many hand spinners would equal its output?

quiz.why: The separate condenser greatly reduced fuel waste in steam engines.
Richard Arkwright patented the water frame in 1769.
Newcomen's atmospheric engine was built in 1712, decades before Watt.

scenes.text: Engels describes Manchester slums in The Condition of the Working Class in England (1845).
In 1848 Marx and Engels publish the Communist Manifesto.

steps.title: Social change
steps.body: Urbanisation, child labour, Factory Acts (1833), Chartism (People's Charter, 1838), trade unions; E.P. Thompson's The Making of the English Working Class (1963).

steps.title: Socialism
steps.body: Utopian socialists (Owen, Saint-Simon, Fourier); Marx's historical materialism and class struggle; First International (1864).

Revolutions in France (Second Republic), German states (Frankfurt Parliament), Austrian Empire, Italian states; mostly suppressed by 1849—'the turning point at which history failed to turn' (G.M. Trevelyan).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Chartists sought political reforms such as universal male suffrage and secret ballot, not socialism as such.

pairs: Making of the English Working Class

quiz.why: Marx and Engels published it in February 1848, on the eve of the revolutions.
The Charter's six points included manhood suffrage and the secret ballot.
It limited children's working hours and appointed factory inspectors.

scenes.text: Bismarck says great questions are decided 'by iron and blood', not speeches.
In January 1871 the German Empire is proclaimed in the Hall of Mirrors, Versailles.

steps.title: Italy
steps.body: Mazzini (Young Italy, 1831), Cavour (Piedmont; alliance with France, war with Austria 1859), Garibaldi's Thousand (1860, Sicily and Naples), Kingdom of Italy (1861), Venetia (1866), Rome (1870).

steps.title: Germany
steps.body: Zollverein (1834), Bismarck's wars: Denmark (1864), Austria (1866, Königgrätz/Sadowa), France (1870–71, Sedan). Empire proclaimed 18 Jan 1871.

steps.title: Nationalism theory
steps.body: Benedict Anderson: nations as 'imagined communities' (1983); Ernest Gellner links nationalism to industrial society; Hobsbawm on 'invented traditions'.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Garibaldi handed his conquests to Victor Emmanuel II; he did not become king.

quiz.why: Benedict Anderson published Imagined Communities in 1983.
French troops left Rome in 1870, allowing its annexation.
Prussia won the Seven Weeks' War at Königgrätz (Sadowa) in 1866.

story.title: Africa on a map in Berlin

scenes.text: At the Berlin Conference (1884–85), European powers set rules for claiming Africa.
Meanwhile Japan modernises rapidly after the Meiji Restoration (1868).

steps.title: Scramble for Africa
steps.body: Berlin Conference 1884–85 ('effective occupation'); by 1914 only Ethiopia (victory at Adwa, 1896) and Liberia were independent. Congo Free State atrocities under Leopold II.

steps.title: Theories
steps.body: J.A. Hobson (Imperialism, 1902: surplus capital, underconsumption), Lenin (Imperialism, the Highest Stage of Capitalism, 1916: finance capital), Gallagher and Robinson ('imperialism of free trade', 1953).

steps.title: Meiji Japan
steps.body: Commodore Perry (1853), end of the Tokugawa shogunate, Meiji Restoration (1868), abolition of domains (1871), conscription, Meiji Constitution (1889), victory over China (1895) and Russia (1905).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Ethiopia's victory at Adwa was over Italy, not Britain.

quiz.why: Bismarck hosted it from November 1884 to February 1885.
The Russo-Japanese War ended with the Treaty of Portsmouth in 1905.
Hobson published it in 1902, after the Boer War.

questions.why: Samuel Crompton invented it in 1779.
It was proclaimed on 18 January 1871.
It landed in Sicily in 1860.
The Zollverein was a German customs union from 1834.

questions.q: 10 workers with 60-spindle jennies equal how many hand spinners?

questions.why: Commodore Perry arrived in 1853.
Hobsbawm and Ranger edited The Invention of Tradition (1983).
It opened in 1830.
Ethiopia defended its independence at Adwa.
Berlin required real occupation to validate claims.
He argued monopoly finance capital drove colonial expansion.

options: Needs of industrial society for a shared culture
questions.why: Industrial society needs a standardised, literate culture, which nationalism provides.

courses.title: Unit 4 · World Wars, Russian Revolution and the Interwar Years
curricula: UGC CBCS / NEP 2020 (History of the Modern World)
courses.summary: Causes and course of the First World War, the Paris peace settlement, the Russian Revolutions of 1917, the Great Depression, fascism and Nazism, and the Second World War.
outcomes: Analyse long- and short-term causes of WWI
Evaluate the Treaty of Versailles
Explain the February and October Revolutions
Explain the Depression and the rise of fascism
Outline the causes and course of WWII

lessons.title: The First World War and Versailles

scenes.text: Gavrilo Princip shoots Archduke Franz Ferdinand of Austria-Hungary.
Within six weeks, alliances pull Europe's great powers into war.

steps.title: Causes (MAIN)
steps.body: Militarism (Anglo-German naval race), Alliances (Triple Alliance 1882; Triple Entente by 1907), Imperialism (Moroccan crises 1905, 1911), Nationalism (Balkans). Fritz Fischer (1961) stressed German war aims; Christopher Clark's The Sleepwalkers (2012) spreads responsibility.

steps.title: Course
steps.body: Schlieffen Plan fails at the Marne (1914); trench warfare (Verdun and Somme 1916); unrestricted submarine warfare; US entry (April 1917); Armistice 11 November 1918.

steps.title: Versailles (1919)
steps.body: War guilt clause (Article 231), reparations (set at 132 billion gold marks in 1921), loss of Alsace-Lorraine, demilitarised Rhineland, army limited to 100,000; League of Nations. Keynes's critique: The Economic Consequences of the Peace.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: The USA never joined the League of Nations; the Senate rejected the treaty.

quiz.why: Article 231 assigned responsibility for the war to Germany and its allies.
Christopher Clark published it in 2012.

quiz.q: The German army was limited to:
quiz.why: Versailles capped the Reichswehr at 100,000 men.

scenes.text: February 1917 (March by the Western calendar): women's bread protests in Petrograd turn into a general strike; the Tsar abdicates.
In October the Bolsheviks seize the Winter Palace.

steps.title: Background
steps.body: Autocracy under Nicholas II, 1905 revolution and Duma, peasant land hunger, industrial workers, defeats in WWI.
February Revolution: Provisional Government (Lvov, then Kerensky) and Petrograd Soviet (dual power). Lenin's April Theses; July Days; Kornilov affair; October Revolution (25 Oct OS / 7 Nov NS).

steps.title: After
steps.body: Decrees on Peace and Land; Treaty of Brest-Litovsk (March 1918); Civil War (1918–21); War Communism; NEP (1921); USSR formed (1922); Stalin's five-year plans (from 1928) and collectivisation.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Russia used the Julian calendar, 13 days behind the Gregorian; hence 'October' Revolution in November.

activity.prompt: The October Revolution was on 25 October (Julian). Add the 13-day calendar difference: what date in November (Gregorian) is it?

quiz.why: Lenin set out his programme on returning to Petrograd in April 1917.
Lenin introduced the New Economic Policy in 1921.
Soviet Russia made peace with the Central Powers in March 1918.

scenes.text: 29 October 1929: the New York stock market collapses.
In Germany unemployment soars, and the Nazi vote climbs to 37% in July 1932.

steps.title: Depression
steps.body: Over-production, speculative bubble, bank failures, Smoot-Hawley tariff (1930), collapse of world trade; Roosevelt's New Deal (from 1933); Keynes's General Theory (1936).

steps.title: Fascism
steps.body: Mussolini's March on Rome (1922), corporate state, Lateran Treaty (1929), invasion of Ethiopia (1935).

steps.title: Nazism
steps.body: Hyperinflation (1923), Beer Hall Putsch, Hitler appointed Chancellor (30 Jan 1933), Enabling Act (March 1933), Nuremberg Laws (1935), Kristallnacht (1938), the Holocaust.

steps.title: Worked example: unemployment rate
steps.body: If 6 million are unemployed in a labour force of 20 million, the rate is 6 ÷ 20 × 100 = 30%.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Hitler did not win a majority in a free election; he was appointed Chancellor by President Hindenburg.

activity.prompt: A country has 4.5 million unemployed in a labour force of 18 million. What is the unemployment rate in %?

quiz.why: Mussolini's March on Rome took place in October 1922.
Hindenburg appointed him on 30 January 1933.
It was published in 1936.

scenes.text: September 1938: Chamberlain returns from Munich promising peace.
A year later Germany invades Poland.

steps.title: Causes
steps.body: Versailles grievances, Depression, failure of the League (Manchuria 1931, Ethiopia 1935), appeasement (Rhineland 1936, Anschluss 1938, Munich 1938), Nazi–Soviet Pact (Aug 1939). A.J.P. Taylor's controversial Origins of the Second World War (1961).

steps.title: Course
steps.body: Poland (1 Sept 1939), fall of France (1940), Battle of Britain, Operation Barbarossa (June 1941), Pearl Harbor (7 Dec 1941), Stalingrad (1942–43), D-Day (6 June 1944), Germany surrenders (8 May 1945), Hiroshima and Nagasaki (6 and 9 Aug 1945), Japan surrenders (Sept 1945).

steps.title: Outcomes
steps.body: United Nations (24 Oct 1945), Nuremberg trials, decline of European empires, US and USSR as superpowers.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Stalingrad, not D-Day, is often seen as the turning point on the Eastern Front.

quiz.why: Japan attacked Pearl Harbor on 7 December 1941.

quiz.q: Operation Barbarossa was the invasion of:
quiz.why: Germany invaded the Soviet Union in June 1941.
The UN Charter came into force on 24 October 1945.

questions.why: Fighting ended on 11 November 1918.
Fischer argued Germany pursued aggressive war aims.
He led the Provisional Government from July 1917.
The London Schedule fixed 132 billion gold marks.
It began in October 1929.

questions.q: 3 million unemployed out of 12 million labour force =

questions.why: It was passed in March 1933.
Stalin forced collectivisation from 1929.
It let Germany annex the Sudetenland in 1938.

options: An opportunist acting in a traditional German policy
questions.why: Taylor controversially portrayed Hitler as a traditional statesman exploiting chances.
German forces surrendered in February 1943.
Keynes argued excessive reparations would destabilise European recovery.

courses.title: Unit 5 · The Cold War, Decolonisation and Revision
curricula: UGC CBCS / NEP 2020 (History of the Modern World)
courses.summary: Origins of the Cold War, containment and crises, the Chinese Revolution, decolonisation and Non-Alignment, détente and the end of the USSR, with revision.
outcomes: Explain competing interpretations of Cold War origins
Describe key crises: Berlin, Korea, Cuba, Vietnam
Outline the Chinese Revolution of 1949
Explain decolonisation and the Non-Aligned Movement
Explain the end of the Cold War

scenes.text: March 1946: Churchill at Fulton, Missouri, says an 'iron curtain' has descended across Europe.
1948–49: Western planes airlift supplies into blockaded West Berlin.

steps.title: Milestones
steps.body: Yalta and Potsdam (1945), Kennan's Long Telegram (1946), Truman Doctrine (March 1947), Marshall Plan (1947), Berlin Blockade (1948–49), NATO (1949), Soviet atomic test (1949), Warsaw Pact (1955).

steps.title: Interpretations
steps.body: Orthodox: Soviet expansion caused it. Revisionist (W.A. Williams, Gabriel Kolko): US economic expansion. Post-revisionist (John Lewis Gaddis): mutual misperception, later stressing Stalin's role after Soviet archives opened.

steps.title: China
steps.body: Civil war between the Guomindang (Chiang Kai-shek) and Communists (Mao); Long March (1934–35); People's Republic proclaimed 1 Oct 1949; Korean War (1950–53).

steps.title: Common mistakes
