11+, abstract reasoning
Speech production
Grouping items to expand STM capacity
Openness, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness, neuroticism

quiz.q: Conditioned fear in 'Little Albert' was studied by:
quiz.why: The 'Little Albert' experiment on conditioned fear was by Watson and Rayner (1920).
Glutamate is the brain's main excitatory neurotransmitter. GABA is inhibitory.
Retroactive interference is when new learning disrupts memory of older information. Proactive is the reverse.

quiz.q: Industry vs inferiority is Erikson's stage for:
quiz.why: Industry vs inferiority is Erikson's stage for school age, roughly 6–12 years.

scenes.text: Ravi pairs each article number with a one-line meaning and each thinker with a book and year.
Precise references impress examiners.

steps.title: Theory
steps.body:
- Hobbes *Leviathan* 1651; Locke 1689; Rousseau 1762
- Mill harm principle 1859; Berlin liberty 1958; Rawls 1971; Nozick 1974
- Elite: Pareto, Mosca, Michels; pluralism: Dahl; deliberative: Habermas
- Weber: traditional, charismatic, legal-rational authority; Lukes three faces of power

steps.title: Indian Constitution
steps.body:
- CA met 9 Dec 1946; adopted 26 Nov 1949; in force 26 Jan 1950
- Preamble; 42nd Amendment 1976 added socialist, secular, integrity; Fundamental Duties
- Part III (12–35): 14, 17, 19, 21, 21A, 32; writs (5)
- Part IV (36–51) non-justiciable; Part IVA (51A) 11 duties
- Art 52, 54, 74, 75; Art 108 joint sitting; Art 110 money bill; Art 368 amendment
- Seventh Schedule; Art 356 and Bommai 1994; Kesavananda 1973 basic structure
- 73rd/74th Amendments 1992; 106th Amendment 2023 (women's reservation after delimitation)

steps.title: Note
steps.body: This is general education, not legal advice.

activity.prompt: Match the article to its subject.

quiz.why: Article 17 abolishes untouchability.
Isaiah Berlin's two concepts of liberty are negative and positive liberty (1958).
The basic structure doctrine comes from Kesavananda Bharati, decided in 1973.
Legal-rational authority rests on rules and law, as with a civil servant acting under law. A hereditary chief is traditional, and a cult leader is charismatic.
Under Article 80, the Rajya Sabha has up to 12 members nominated by the President, for their special knowledge in areas like art, science, literature and social service.

lessons.title: Mock paper A — solved case questions

scenes.text: 20 minutes: read each case and name the concept before answering.
Compare with the model answers.

steps.title: Solved: psychology case
steps.body:
A student studies late into the night only when the exam is a week away and slacks off after it — like workers paid every Friday who work harder near payday.

- Pattern matches a **fixed-interval schedule** (scalloped response near the reinforcement time)

steps.title: Solved: political theory case
steps.body:
A government argues it must ban junk food 'for people's own good'.

- Mill would object — harm to self is not grounds for coercion; persuasion or information is preferable. A positive-liberty view might support it as enabling healthier choices.

steps.title: Solved: constitution case
steps.body:
A state government is dismissed without a floor test based only on the Governor's report.

- Under *Bommai* (1994), the proper test of majority is the **floor of the House**; the proclamation is subject to judicial review.

steps.title: Note
steps.body: This is general education, not legal or medical advice.

activity.prompt: Can you write a 10-mark answer on:
items: Classical vs operant conditioning with examples

quiz.why: A pay cheque every Friday is a reward after a fixed time period, so it is a fixed-interval schedule.

options: he opposed coercion for one's own good
quiz.why: Mill opposed using coercion for a person's own good. His harm principle limits interference to preventing harm to others.
Bommai's key test is the floor test: a government's majority must be decided in the legislature, not by the Governor's view alone.
The idea of a 'power elite' controlling key decisions is C. Wright Mills's. Dahl's pluralism says power is dispersed.

quiz.q: A child insisting the moon follows her is showing:
quiz.why: A child who insists the moon follows her cannot see things from another's view and mixes her own view with reality. That is egocentrism, in the preoperational stage.

questions.q: Psychology is the scientific study of:
questions.why: Psychology is the scientific study of behaviour and mental processes. It isn't limited to animals, the brain or dreams.
The Lok Sabha's normal term is 5 years from its first sitting (Article 83), unless dissolved earlier.
Ivan Pavlov discovered classical conditioning, in his experiments with dogs.
The 'general will' is Rousseau's idea, from The Social Contract (1762).

questions.q: Writ commanding a public official to perform a duty:
questions.why: Mandamus ('we command') is the writ that orders a public official to perform a public duty.
Object permanence, knowing that objects continue to exist when out of sight, develops in the sensorimotor stage, in infancy.
Negative liberty means freedom from interference by others. Positive liberty is the capacity for self-mastery.
The amygdala is most linked to emotion, especially fear.

questions.q: Assertion: The Rajya Sabha cannot remove the Council of Ministers. Reason: Ministers are collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha.
questions.why: Ministers are collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha (Article 75(3)). So the Rajya Sabha can't remove the Council of Ministers. Both true, and the reason explains the assertion.
By Weber's law, JND = fraction × base = 0.05 × 800 g = 40 g.
The Fundamental Duties were added by the 42nd Amendment (1976).

questions.q: Deviation IQ 85 is how many SD from the mean?
questions.why: z = (85 − 100)/15 = −1, so a deviation IQ of 85 is one standard deviation below the mean.

questions.q: Case: A teacher gives stickers at random intervals for good behaviour. Schedule:
questions.why: Stickers at random time intervals follow a variable-interval schedule: the timing is unpredictable and depends on time, not the number of responses.

questions.q: Case: A citizen's PIL asks the Supreme Court to direct a state to stop illegal mining. Likely writ:
questions.why: A PIL asking the court to direct a state to carry out its duty (stop illegal mining) fits the writ of mandamus, which enforces a public or statutory duty.

questions.q: Rawls's difference principle would favour a tax policy that:
options: maximises the position of the worst-off
questions.why: Rawls's difference principle says inequalities are fair only if they benefit the least advantaged. So it favours a tax policy that maximises the position of the worst-off (maximin).

questions.q: Michels' iron law states organisations tend toward:
questions.why: Michels' iron law of oligarchy says that organisations, even democratic ones, tend towards rule by a few leaders.

questions.q: A patient can't form new explicit memories but learns a new motor skill. This suggests:
options: separate systems for explicit and procedural memory
questions.why: A patient who can't form new explicit memories but still learns a motor skill shows that the two use separate memory systems. This dissociation was seen in patient H.M.

questions.q: Which statement about Article 368 is correct?
options: Amendments can be passed at a joint sitting
Some amendments also need ratification by half the state legislatures
questions.why: Under Article 368, some amendments, such as those on federal provisions, also need ratification by at least half of the state legislatures. A joint sitting cannot pass an amendment, and the basic structure can't be destroyed.

questions.q: Lukes's third face of power refers to:
questions.why: Lukes's third face of power is the shaping of people's preferences and perceptions, so they accept the existing order without open conflict.

questions.q: A study shows ice-cream sales and drownings both rise in summer. The best explanation:
questions.why: Ice-cream sales and drownings both rise in summer because of a third variable, hot weather. This shows that correlation doesn't prove causation.

uni-ba-humanities-b.title: BA Humanities II — History & Sociology, unit by unit
uni-ba-humanities-b.description: Core BA papers in History (ancient, medieval and modern India) and Sociology (classical thinkers and Indian society), with source-based reasoning, timelines, case questions and unit exams.

courses.title: History I · ancient and medieval India
courses.note: topic order may differ by university
courses.summary: The Harappan civilisation, the Vedic age, Mahajanapadas with Buddhism and Jainism, the Mauryan and Gupta empires, and the Delhi Sultanate, Vijayanagara, the Mughals and Bhakti–Sufi traditions.
outcomes: Learners can describe Harappan town planning, economy and sources
Learners can explain the rise of Magadha and the teachings of Buddha and Mahavira
Learners can analyse Ashoka's dhamma and Gupta achievements using sources
Learners can explain key institutions of the Sultanate and Mughal states

scenes.text: In the 1920s, archaeologists dug at Harappa and Mohenjo-daro and found grid-like streets, baked-brick houses and covered drains.
With no deciphered script, historians read this civilisation through its bricks, seals, beads and weights.

steps.title: Key features
steps.body:
- Excavations: Harappa (Daya Ram Sahni, 1921), Mohenjo-daro (R. D. Banerji, 1922)
- Mature phase about **2600–1900 BCE**
- Planned cities: citadel and lower town, grid streets, **standardised bricks (ratio about 1 : 2 : 4)**, covered drains; the **Great Bath** at Mohenjo-daro
- Sites: **Lothal** (Gujarat; dockyard and bead-making), **Kalibangan** (Rajasthan; ploughed field), **Dholavira** (Gujarat; water reservoirs; UNESCO World Heritage Site, 2021), Rakhigarhi (Haryana)
- Economy: agriculture (wheat, barley), crafts (beads, shell, metal), long-distance trade (including with Mesopotamia), standardised weights
- Seals (mostly steatite) with an **undeciphered script**
- Decline (c. 1900 BCE onwards): likely multiple causes — climate change, shifting rivers, decline of trade; the 'Aryan invasion' explanation is no longer accepted as the cause

steps.title: Solved: reading evidence
steps.body:
Finding: identical weights at sites hundreds of kilometres apart.

- Inference: a shared system of **standardised measurement**, suggesting coordinated trade and possibly some central authority
- Caution: we cannot name rulers — there are no deciphered texts

steps.title: Solved: match site to feature
steps.body:
- Dockyard → **Lothal**
- Great Bath → **Mohenjo-daro**
- Ploughed field → **Kalibangan**
- Elaborate water management → **Dholavira**

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Claiming the script has been deciphered.
- Presenting a single cause for the decline as certain.
- Mixing Harappan and Vedic features (e.g. horses and iron are not typical Harappan finds).
- Treating all sites as identical — regional variation existed.

activity.prompt: Match the Harappan site to its notable find.

quiz.why: The Harappan script is still undeciphered. Brahmi and Kharosthi are later scripts.
Lothal, in Gujarat, has a famous dockyard, evidence of Harappan maritime trade.
The mature Harappan phase dates to about 2600–1900 BCE, in the Bronze Age.
Harappan bricks have a standard ratio of about 1 : 2 : 4 for thickness, width and length.

quiz.q: Dholavira was inscribed as a World Heritage Site in:
quiz.why: Dholavira was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2021.

lessons.title: Vedic age, Mahajanapadas, Buddhism and Jainism

story.title: The prince who left the palace

scenes.text: A prince of the Shakya clan left home in search of an answer to suffering.
Enlightened at Bodh Gaya, he gave his first sermon at Sarnath. Buddhism spread across Asia.

steps.title: From Vedas to kingdoms
steps.body:
- **Rig Veda** (earliest text; composed roughly 1500–1000 BCE): pastoral life, tribal assemblies (sabha, samiti)
- **Later Vedic** period (c. 1000–600 BCE): iron, agriculture expands into the Ganga valley, varna hierarchy sharpens
- **Sixteen Mahajanapadas** (listed in Buddhist texts such as the Anguttara Nikaya) by the 6th century BCE; **Magadha** rose (fertile land, iron ores, rivers, able rulers; capitals Rajagriha then Pataliputra)

steps.title: Buddhism and Jainism
steps.body:
- **Gautama Buddha** (6th–5th century BCE): born Lumbini; enlightenment Bodh Gaya; first sermon Sarnath; passed away at Kushinagar. **Four Noble Truths**, **Eightfold Path**, Middle Way
- **Vardhamana Mahavira**: 24th tirthankara; five vows — ahimsa, satya, asteya, aparigraha, brahmacharya; three jewels (right faith, knowledge, conduct)
- Both rejected animal sacrifice and the exclusivity of Brahmanical ritual and preached in Prakrit/Pali

steps.title: Solved: why Magadha?
steps.body:
- Fertile middle Ganga plains → surplus
- Iron deposits nearby → tools and weapons
- Rivers for transport and defence
- Ambitious rulers (Bimbisara, Ajatashatru; later Nandas, then Mauryas)

steps.title: Solved: compare the faiths
steps.body: Both: non-violence, karma, monastic orders. Differences: Buddhism's Middle Way vs Jainism's stricter asceticism; Buddhism spread widely outside India while Jainism remained concentrated in India (especially Gujarat, Rajasthan, Karnataka).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Placing the first sermon at Bodh Gaya (it was Sarnath).
- Calling Mahavira the founder of Jainism (he was the 24th tirthankara).
- Giving exact dates for the Buddha's life as settled facts.
- Assuming Vedic and Harappan cultures were the same.

activity.prompt: Match the place to the event in the Buddha's life.

quiz.why: In Jain tradition, Mahavira was the 24th and last tirthankara.
The Rig Veda is the earliest and oldest Vedic text.

quiz.q: Number of Mahajanapadas in Buddhist texts:
quiz.why: Buddhist texts such as the Anguttara Nikaya list 16 Mahajanapadas.

quiz.q: Not one of Mahavira's five vows:
quiz.why: Mahavira's five vows include ahimsa, satya, asteya, brahmacharya and aparigraha. 'Satyagraha' is a Gandhian term.

quiz.q: A key reason for Magadha's rise:
quiz.why: Magadha rose because of iron ore deposits and fertile land, which helped agriculture, tools and weapons.

scenes.text: After the bloody Kalinga war, Ashoka inscribed his remorse on a rock edict.
His edicts, read again in 1837 when James Prinsep deciphered Brahmi, are among India's earliest royal messages.

steps.title: Mauryas (c. 321–185 BCE)
steps.body:
- **Chandragupta Maurya** with **Kautilya** (Arthashastra on statecraft); Greek envoy **Megasthenes** (Indica, surviving in fragments)
- **Ashoka**: Kalinga war (c. 261 BCE) described in **Rock Edict XIII**; **dhamma** — tolerance, non-violence, respect for elders, welfare; dhamma-mahamattas
- Edicts mostly in **Prakrit** using **Brahmi** script (Kharosthi in the north-west; Greek and Aramaic in Afghanistan)
- Third Buddhist council at Pataliputra (tradition)

steps.title: Guptas (c. 320–550 CE)
steps.body:
- **Chandragupta I** begins the Gupta era (c. 319–320 CE)
- **Samudragupta**: conquests recorded in the **Prayag (Allahabad) pillar inscription** composed by **Harishena**
- **Chandragupta II**: patron of arts; Chinese pilgrim **Faxian (Fa-Hien)** visited
- Achievements: **Aryabhata** (*Aryabhatiya*, 499 CE), Kalidasa's works, Nalanda's beginnings, temple architecture
- 'Golden Age' label is debated — prosperity for elites, but also land grants, feudal tendencies and caste rigidity

steps.title: Solved: source criticism
steps.body:
The Prayag inscription praises Samudragupta as unconquerable.

- It is a **prashasti** (court eulogy) — valuable for names and campaigns, but one-sided
- Cross-check with coins, other inscriptions and foreign accounts

steps.title: Solved: interpreting dhamma
steps.body: Ashoka's dhamma was not a call to convert everyone to Buddhism; it promoted ethical conduct and tolerance across sects — arguably also a tool for holding together a vast, diverse empire.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying Ashoka's edicts are in Sanskrit.
- Treating Megasthenes' Indica as complete (only fragments survive in later writers).
- Calling the Gupta period 'golden' for everyone without qualification.
- Confusing Chandragupta Maurya with Chandragupta I or II.

events.text: Chandragupta Maurya founds the Mauryan empire
Gupta era begins under Chandragupta I

quiz.why: The Arthashastra, a text on statecraft, is attributed to Kautilya (Chanakya).
Ashoka's Rock Edict XIII describes the Kalinga war and his remorse.
The Prayag pillar inscription, written by Harishena, praises Samudragupta.
James Prinsep deciphered the Brahmi script in 1837.
The Chinese pilgrim Faxian visited India during the reign of Chandragupta II, in the early 5th century.

lessons.title: Delhi Sultanate, Vijayanagara and the Mughals

scenes.text: Sultan Muhammad bin Tughlaq issued bronze/copper token coins to stand in for silver.
Forgers flooded the market, and the experiment had to be withdrawn — an early lesson in monetary trust.

steps.title: Delhi Sultanate (1206–1526)
steps.body:
- **Qutbuddin Aibak** (1206); **Iltutmish** consolidated rule, issued the silver **tanka** and copper **jital**; **iqta** system of revenue assignments
- **Alauddin Khalji** (1296–1316): market regulation and price control, defence against Mongols
- **Muhammad bin Tughlaq** (1325–51): shift of capital to Daulatabad, token currency
- Lodis ended at the **First Battle of Panipat (1526)**

steps.title: Vijayanagara and the Mughals
steps.body:
- **Vijayanagara** founded 1336 by Harihara and Bukka; peak under **Krishnadeva Raya**; defeated at **Talikota (1565)**; ruins at Hampi
- **Babur** defeats Ibrahim Lodi at Panipat (1526)
- **Akbar** (r. 1556–1605): Second Battle of Panipat (1556); **mansabdari** (rank-based nobility), **zabt** land revenue system associated with Raja Todar Mal, **sulh-i-kul** (universal peace), discussions at the Ibadat Khana (Fatehpur Sikri)
- **Bhakti**: Kabir, Guru Nanak, Mirabai, Tulsidas — devotion beyond ritual and caste; **Sufi**: Chishti order — Khwaja Moinuddin Chishti (Ajmer), Nizamuddin Auliya (Delhi)

steps.title: Solved: institution and purpose
steps.body:
- **Iqta**: assigning revenue of territories to officers in return for military service → central control over nobles
- **Mansabdari**: ranks (zat and sawar) fixing pay and cavalry obligations → a graded, transferable nobility
- **Zabt**: measurement-based revenue assessment → predictable state income

steps.title: Solved: why did Tughlaq's token currency fail?
steps.body:
- Coins were easy to forge and the state could not control issue
- People hoarded silver and paid taxes in tokens
- Lesson: fiat money needs trust and anti-counterfeiting capacity

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Mixing up the First (1526) and Second (1556) Battles of Panipat.
- Calling sulh-i-kul a new religion.
- Placing Vijayanagara's founding under the Mughals.
- Treating Bhakti and Sufi movements as opposed (they shared ideas of devotion and equality).

events.text: Qutbuddin Aibak's rule begins in Delhi
First Battle of Panipat — Babur wins
Akbar's reign begins; Second Battle of Panipat

quiz.why: Alauddin Khalji is associated with market control and price regulation.
Akbar organised the mansabdari system, which ranked Mughal nobles and officials.
The Vijayanagara empire was founded in 1336 by Harihara and Bukka.
Moinuddin Chishti is the Chishti saint whose dargah is at Ajmer.
Muhammad bin Tughlaq introduced token currency in the 14th century.

questions.why: The Great Bath is at Mohenjo-daro, in Sindh.
The Buddha gave his first sermon at Sarnath, in the Deer Park.

questions.q: Founder of the Mughal empire in India:
questions.why: Babur founded the Mughal empire in India, after winning the First Battle of Panipat in 1526.
Ashoka's edicts were mostly in Prakrit, a popular language, written in the Brahmi script.
Aryabhata's Aryabhatiya was composed in 499 CE, in the Gupta period.
The iqta system, assigning revenue of land to officers, belongs to the Delhi Sultanate.

questions.q: Assertion: The Prayag inscription must be used cautiously. Reason: As a prashasti, it was written to glorify the ruler.
questions.why: A prashasti is written to praise the ruler, so it may be biased and needs care. Both statements are true and the reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: Which Harappan site has evidence of a ploughed field?
questions.why: Kalibangan, in Rajasthan, has evidence of a ploughed field.

questions.q: The Second Battle of Panipat (1556) was fought between:
questions.why: The Second Battle of Panipat (1556) was fought between Akbar's forces, led by Bairam Khan, and Hemu. It secured Akbar's accession.

questions.q: Case: Mesopotamian texts mention trade with a land called 'Meluhha'. Best inference about the Harappans:
questions.why: Mesopotamian texts mention trade with Meluhha, which is widely identified with the Indus region. So the Harappans likely traded with Mesopotamia.

questions.q: Which best explains why Ashoka's dhamma is not simply Buddhism?
options: It stressed general ethics and tolerance across sects
It was written in Greek only
questions.why: Ashoka's dhamma was an ethical code, stressing tolerance and moral conduct across sects. It was not simply Buddhism and didn't order conversions.

options: measurement of land and fixed cash rates
questions.why: The zabt system, associated with Todar Mal, measured land and fixed cash revenue rates.

questions.q: Why is the 'Golden Age' label for the Guptas debated?
options: achievements coexisted with growing land grants, inequality and caste rigidity
questions.why: The 'Golden Age' label is debated because Gupta achievements coexisted with growing land grants, inequality and caste rigidity.
Talikota was fought in 1565, not 1526. Panipat I was 1526, the Sultanate began in 1206 and Vijayanagara was founded in 1336.

questions.q: A common theme of Bhakti saints like Kabir:
options: devotion over ritual and critique of caste distinctions
questions.why: Bhakti saints like Kabir stressed devotion over ritual and criticised caste distinctions. They used vernacular languages.

courses.title: History II · modern India and the freedom struggle
courses.note: topic order may differ by university
courses.summary: The East India Company's expansion and land settlements, the revolt of 1857, the national movement from 1885 through the Gandhian mass movements, and independence, partition and integration of princely states. Violence is discussed factually and without graphic detail.
outcomes: Learners can explain Company expansion and compare land-revenue systems
Learners can analyse causes and consequences of 1857
Learners can trace the national movement's phases and methods
Learners can explain the road to independence, partition and integration

story.title: A battle in a mango grove

scenes.text: At Plassey in 1757, Robert Clive's small force won largely because the Nawab's commander Mir Jafar defected.
Within eight years the Company held the diwani — the right to collect revenue — of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa.

steps.title: Expansion
steps.body:
- **Plassey (1757)**: Clive defeats Siraj-ud-Daulah
- **Buxar (1764)**: Company defeats the combined forces of Mir Qasim, Shuja-ud-Daulah and Shah Alam II
- **Diwani (1765)** by the Treaty of Allahabad
- **Regulating Act (1773)**; Pitt's India Act (1784)
- **Subsidiary alliance** (Wellesley, from 1798); **doctrine of lapse** (Dalhousie; e.g. Satara 1848, Jhansi and Nagpur 1854)
- Social reform: **sati abolished (1829)** under Bentinck, with Raja Ram Mohan Roy's campaign; **Hindu Widows' Remarriage Act (1856)** with Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar

steps.title: Land revenue systems
steps.body:
- **Permanent Settlement (1793)**, Cornwallis, mainly Bengal: zamindars pay a fixed revenue in perpetuity
- **Ryotwari**, associated with Thomas Munro, Madras and Bombay: direct settlement with cultivators (ryots), periodically revised
- **Mahalwari** (from 1822, Holt Mackenzie; North-Western Provinces, Punjab): settlement with village communities (mahals)
- Common effects: high demands, rigid collection, rise of moneylenders, land alienation

steps.title: Solved: compare the settlements
steps.body:
- Who paid the state? Zamindar (Permanent) / ryot (Ryotwari) / village body (Mahalwari)
- Was revenue fixed forever? Only under the Permanent Settlement
- Main winner: zamindars under the Permanent Settlement; the state under periodically revised systems

steps.title: Solved: doctrine of lapse
steps.body: A ruler of a dependent state died without a natural heir. Under Dalhousie's policy the state 'lapsed' to the Company — adopted sons were not recognised as heirs for succession. Jhansi's annexation became a grievance behind 1857.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Dating diwani to 1757.
- Associating Ryotwari with Bengal.
- Mixing up Wellesley (subsidiary alliance) and Dalhousie (lapse).
- Treating Company rule as purely 'trade' — it became a territorial power.

activity.prompt: Match the policy to the person.

quiz.why: The Battle of Plassey was fought in 1757, when Robert Clive defeated the Nawab of Bengal.
The Permanent Settlement was introduced in 1793 by Lord Cornwallis.
Mahalwari settled land revenue with village communities. 'Mahal' means estate or village.
The Hindu Widows' Remarriage Act was passed in 1856, after Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar's campaign.

quiz.q: Diwani was granted by the Treaty of:
quiz.why: The Treaty of Allahabad (1765) gave the Company the diwani of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa, from Shah Alam II.

scenes.text: Sepoys at Meerut, punished for refusing new cartridges, broke out and marched to Delhi.
They proclaimed the aged Bahadur Shah Zafar their leader. Revolt spread across north and central India.

steps.title: Causes and course
steps.body:
- **Political**: annexations (doctrine of lapse, Awadh 1856)
- **Economic**: heavy land revenue, ruin of artisans
- **Socio-religious**: fear of interference with customs
- **Military**: grievances of sepoys; the immediate trigger was the **Enfield rifle cartridges** rumoured to be greased with animal fat
- Centres and leaders: Delhi (Bahadur Shah Zafar, Bakht Khan), Kanpur (Nana Saheb, Tantia Tope), Lucknow (Begum Hazrat Mahal), Jhansi (Rani Lakshmibai), Bihar (Kunwar Singh)
- Suppressed by 1858–59 with great loss of life on all sides

steps.title: Consequences and interpretations
steps.body:
- **Government of India Act, 1858**: Crown takes over from the Company; Secretary of State for India; Governor-General also Viceroy
- Queen's Proclamation (1858): non-interference in religion, end of annexation policy
- Army reorganised; 'divide and rule' strategies grew
- Interpretations: 'sepoy mutiny' (colonial view), 'first war of independence' (V. D. Savarkar, 1909), a broad popular uprising with varied local causes (many modern historians)

steps.title: Solved: why did it fail?
steps.body:
- Limited geographical spread (south and east largely unaffected)
- Lack of a unified leadership and programme
- Many princes and elites sided with the British
- Superior British resources, telegraph and railways

steps.title: Solved: source question
steps.body: Two accounts: a British officer's diary calls the rebels 'mutineers'; a proclamation from Delhi calls on Hindus and Muslims to unite against foreign rule. Use both: each reveals its author's position — compare, don't simply believe either.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling it a purely military mutiny.
- Saying 1857 led to immediate independence.
- Ignoring the role of peasants and artisans.
- Dating the Government of India Act to 1857.

activity.prompt: Match the leader to the centre of the revolt.

quiz.q: The revolt began at Meerut on:
quiz.why: The revolt of 1857 began at Meerut on 10 May 1857.

lessons.title: The national movement: 1885 to Quit India

scenes.text: On 12 March 1930, Gandhi set out from Sabarmati with 78 followers; on 6 April he picked up salt at Dandi.
A simple act against an unjust tax drew millions into civil disobedience.

steps.title: Phases
steps.body:
- **Indian National Congress** founded 1885 in Bombay (first president W. C. Bonnerjee; A. O. Hume a founder member); **moderates** (Naoroji's drain theory, petitions)
- **Partition of Bengal (1905)** by Curzon → **Swadeshi and boycott**; Surat split (1907); Morley–Minto reforms (1909) with separate electorates; partition annulled 1911
- **Lucknow Pact (1916)** between Congress and the Muslim League; Home Rule Leagues (Tilak, Annie Besant)
- Gandhi's early campaigns: **Champaran (1917)**, Kheda and Ahmedabad (1918)
- **Rowlatt Act** protests; **Jallianwala Bagh massacre, 13 April 1919**
- **Non-Cooperation (1920–22)**, withdrawn after **Chauri Chaura (February 1922)**
- Simon Commission boycott (1928); **Lahore session (1929)**: Purna Swaraj; **Civil Disobedience** with the **Dandi March (1930)**; Gandhi–Irwin Pact (1931); Poona Pact (1932); Government of India Act 1935
- **Quit India**, launched **8 August 1942** ('Do or Die'); INA under Subhas Chandra Bose

steps.title: Solved: methods compared
steps.body:
- Moderates: petitions, memoranda, economic critique (drain of wealth)
- Extremists/Swadeshi: boycott of foreign goods, national education
- Gandhian: mass non-violent satyagraha — non-cooperation, civil disobedience, constructive programme (khadi, Hindu–Muslim unity, removal of untouchability)

steps.title: Solved: why salt?
steps.body: Salt was used by everyone, rich or poor, and the tax was visibly unjust; breaking the law was easy and non-violent; it connected an everyday grievance to the demand for swaraj.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Dating Jallianwala Bagh to 1920.
- Mixing up Non-Cooperation (1920) and Civil Disobedience (1930).
- Saying the Congress demanded full independence in 1885 (that came in 1929).
- Ignoring revolutionaries, peasants, workers and women's roles.

activity.prompt: Order these events of the national movement.

quiz.why: W. C. Bonnerjee was the first president of the Indian National Congress, at Bombay in 1885.
Gandhi withdrew the Non-Cooperation Movement after the violence at Chauri Chaura in February 1922.

quiz.q: Purna Swaraj resolution was passed at:
quiz.why: The Purna Swaraj (complete independence) resolution was passed at the Lahore session of 1929, under Nehru's presidency.
The Quit India Movement was launched on 8 August 1942 at the Bombay session.
The Champaran satyagraha (Bihar, 1917) was about indigo cultivators forced to grow indigo.

scenes.text: At midnight Nehru spoke of a 'tryst with destiny' as India became independent.
The same months saw partition — mass migration and terrible communal violence that displaced millions. Remembering both is part of honest history.

steps.title: The road to 1947
steps.body:
- **Cripps Mission (1942)** — offer of post-war dominion status, rejected
- **Cabinet Mission (1946)** — proposed a loose federation; elections to a Constituent Assembly
- Direct Action Day (16 August 1946) and communal violence
- **Mountbatten Plan (3 June 1947)** → **Indian Independence Act (July 1947)** → independence on **15 August 1947**; boundaries drawn by the Radcliffe commission
- Partition caused one of the largest migrations in history; estimates of deaths vary widely (often cited from several hundred thousand to about a million or more)

steps.title: Integrating princely states
steps.body:
About 560 princely states were integrated, led by **Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel** with **V. P. Menon**, mainly through the **Instrument of Accession** and later merger agreements.

- **Junagadh**: plebiscite (1948) favoured India
- **Hyderabad**: police action, **Operation Polo (September 1948)**
- **Jammu and Kashmir**: Instrument of Accession signed in October 1947

steps.title: Solved: why partition?
steps.body: Historians stress several interacting factors: growth of communal politics and separate electorates; the Muslim League's demand for Pakistan (Lahore Resolution, 1940); failure of Congress–League negotiations; British haste to withdraw after the war; and escalating violence in 1946–47. Avoid single-cause answers.

steps.title: Solved: method of integration
steps.body: Instrument of Accession: rulers ceded defence, external affairs and communications to India. Later, merger agreements and constitutional changes brought states fully into the Union.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying all princely states joined voluntarily on 15 August 1947.
- Giving a single precise death toll for partition as certain.
- Confusing the Cripps (1942) and Cabinet (1946) Missions.
- Treating partition as only a political event and ignoring its human cost.

activity.prompt: Many families in India carry memories of 1947 — of migration, loss or resettlement. If you know such a story, or have read one, write a few lines about what it teaches about living together.

scenes.text: Manju draws one long timeline from Harappa to 1947 on her wall.
Every new fact gets pinned near a known peg — so nothing floats.

steps.title: Ancient and medieval pegs
steps.body:
- c. 2600–1900 BCE mature Harappan
- c. 1500–1000 BCE early Vedic; c. 1000–600 BCE later Vedic
- 6th–5th c. BCE Buddha, Mahavira; Mahajanapadas

- c. 320 CE Guptas; 499 CE Aryabhatiya

steps.title: Modern pegs

- 1757 Plassey; 1764 Buxar; 1765 diwani; 1793 Permanent Settlement
- 1829 sati abolished; 1856 widow remarriage; 1857 revolt; 1858 Crown rule
- 1885 INC; 1905 Bengal partition; 1916 Lucknow Pact; 1917 Champaran; 1919 Jallianwala
- 1920 Non-Cooperation; 1929 Purna Swaraj; 1930 Dandi; 1932 Poona Pact; 1935 GoI Act

steps.title: Answer frame
steps.body: Context → causes → course → consequences → historians' interpretations, with at least one source named.

scenes.text: Every source has an author, an audience and a purpose.
Ask those three questions before using any document.

steps.title: The method
steps.body:
- **Provenance**: who, when, where?
- **Purpose and audience**: why was it written, for whom?
- **Content**: what does it say? What does it leave out?
- **Corroboration**: what other sources agree or disagree?
- **Use**: what can it reliably tell us?

steps.title: Solved: an edict
steps.body:
Ashoka's Rock Edict XIII speaks of remorse after Kalinga.

- Provenance: royal inscription; purpose: public message of the emperor's dhamma
- Reliable for: the emperor's stated values and his account of the war
- Limits: official viewpoint; casualty figures may be rhetorical

steps.title: Solved: a colonial report
steps.body:
A British district officer's 1858 report blames 'agitators' for rebellion.

- Purpose: justify policy to superiors
- Use with peasants' petitions, rebel proclamations and later historians' work to build a fuller picture

quiz.why: A prashasti is a eulogy, so it is likely to be biased in favour of the ruler. Use it carefully.

courses.title: Sociology I · concepts and classical thinkers
courses.note: topic order may differ by university
courses.summary: Basic sociological concepts, socialisation and research methods, and the classical thinkers Durkheim, Marx and Weber with their key works and ideas.
outcomes: Learners can define culture, norms, status, role and socialisation and choose research methods
Learners can explain Durkheim's social facts, solidarity and suicide types
Learners can explain Marx's materialism, class and alienation
Learners can explain Weber's social action, ideal types, authority and the Protestant ethic

story.title: One job loss, a million job losses

scenes.text: When one person loses a job, it's a personal trouble. When millions do in a recession, it's a public issue.
C. Wright Mills called the ability to link the two 'the sociological imagination' (1959).

steps.title: Core concepts
steps.body:
- **Auguste Comte** coined 'sociology'; positivism; law of three stages (theological, metaphysical, positive)
- **Society**, **culture** (material and non-material), **norms** (folkways, mores, laws), **values**
- **Status** (ascribed vs achieved) and **role** (role conflict, role strain)
- **Socialisation**: primary (family) and secondary (school, peers, media, workplace); resocialisation
- **Groups**: primary (Cooley) vs secondary; reference groups

steps.title: Research methods
steps.body:
- Quantitative: surveys, questionnaires, statistical analysis
- Qualitative: participant observation, interviews, case studies, ethnography
- Sampling: random, stratified, purposive, snowball
- Ethics: informed consent, anonymity, avoiding harm
- Reflexivity: the researcher's position shapes findings

steps.title: Solved: classify
steps.body:
- Being born into a family → **ascribed** status; becoming a doctor → **achieved** status
- A working mother torn between office and child's school event → **role conflict**
- Learning table manners at home → **primary socialisation**

steps.title: Solved: choose a method
steps.body:
Topic: everyday life of street vendors.

- Best: **participant observation and interviews** (rich, contextual data)
- If the question is 'what % of vendors use UPI?', a **survey** with a representative sample is better

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating personal troubles and public issues as unrelated.
- Confusing norms (rules) with values (ideals).
- Assuming qualitative research is 'unscientific'.
- Forgetting ethics in studies of vulnerable groups.

quiz.why: Auguste Comte coined the word 'sociology', and he founded positivism.
The Sociological Imagination (1959) is by C. Wright Mills. It links personal troubles to public issues.

quiz.q: Family is the main agent of:
quiz.why: The family is the main agent of primary socialisation, in a person's early years.
Mores are norms with strong moral weight, whose violation is seriously condemned. Folkways are casual customs.

quiz.q: Best method for studying lived experience in depth:
quiz.why: Participant observation gives in-depth, qualitative understanding of lived experience.

scenes.text: Durkheim noticed that suicide rates differed steadily between groups and countries year after year.
He argued social integration and regulation — not just individual psychology — shape such rates.

steps.title: Key ideas
steps.body:
- **Social facts**: ways of acting, thinking and feeling external to individuals and exercising constraint (*The Rules of Sociological Method*, 1895)
- **The Division of Labour in Society** (1893): **mechanical solidarity** (similarity; repressive law; simple societies) vs **organic solidarity** (interdependence through specialisation; restitutive law)
- **Suicide** (1897): **egoistic** (low integration), **altruistic** (excessive integration), **anomic** (low regulation, e.g. sudden economic change), **fatalistic** (excessive regulation)
- **The Elementary Forms of Religious Life** (1912): sacred vs profane; religion as collective representation
- **Anomie**: normlessness during rapid change

steps.title: Solved: classify the suicide type
steps.body:
- An isolated elderly person with no social ties → **egoistic**
- A sudden market crash leaves people without stable norms → **anomic**
- A soldier sacrificing life for the group → **altruistic**
- A person under oppressively strict control → **fatalistic**

(Sociological categories only; any real person at risk needs help — Tele-MANAS 14416.)

steps.title: Solved: solidarity
steps.body: A village where everyone farms and shares rituals → **mechanical**. A metro city where people depend on doctors, drivers, coders and farmers they never meet → **organic**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Swapping mechanical and organic solidarity.
- Thinking Durkheim explained suicide by individual psychology.
- Confusing anomie (normlessness) with alienation (Marx).
- Using his typology to label real individuals rather than social patterns.

activity.prompt: Match Durkheim's concept to its meaning.
pairs: External, constraining way of acting or thinking

quiz.q: The Division of Labour in Society:
quiz.why: Durkheim's The Division of Labour in Society was published in 1893.
Organic solidarity is based on interdependence, as people specialise and depend on each other. Mechanical solidarity is based on similarity.

quiz.q: Suicide linked to sudden economic disruption:
quiz.why: Anomic suicide is linked to sudden disruption, like an economic crash, which weakens social regulation.
Durkheim's Elementary Forms of Religious Life (1912) discusses the distinction between the sacred and the profane.
Durkheim's social facts are external to the individual and constraining on them.

scenes.text: An assembly-line worker fits one part into thousands of phones a day but could never afford one.
Marx would call this alienation — and ask who owns the factory and gets the surplus.

steps.title: Key ideas
steps.body:
- **Historical materialism**: the economic **base** (forces and relations of production) shapes the **superstructure** (law, politics, religion, ideology)
- **Class struggle**: 'The history of all hitherto existing society is the history of class struggles' (*The Communist Manifesto*, 1848, with Engels)
- **Bourgeoisie** (owners of means of production) vs **proletariat** (sell labour power)
- **Surplus value**: value produced by workers beyond their wages (*Capital*, Vol. I, 1867)
- **Alienation** from the product, the process, one's species-being and other people
- **Class in itself** vs **class for itself** (class consciousness); false consciousness

steps.title: Solved: surplus value
steps.body:
A worker paid ₹600 a day produces goods worth ₹1,500 (after materials).

- Surplus value = ₹1,500 − ₹600 = **₹900** appropriated by the owner (Marx's framework)

steps.title: Solved: base and superstructure
steps.body: Laws protecting private property and contracts are part of the superstructure that, in Marx's view, stabilise capitalist relations of production in the base.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Equating Marx's sociology with any particular later government.
- Confusing alienation with anomie.
- Thinking base–superstructure is a one-way, mechanical relation in all readings (many Marxists stress interaction).
- Calling all wage earners 'bourgeoisie'.

items.back: Workers don't own or control what they make
Work is repetitive and directed by others
Work no longer expresses human creativity

quiz.q: The Communist Manifesto was published in:
quiz.why: The Communist Manifesto was published in 1848, by Marx and Engels.

quiz.q: Owners of the means of production:
quiz.why: In Marx, the bourgeoisie are the owners of the means of production. The proletariat sell their labour.
Surplus value is the value workers create beyond their wages, which the owners keep. Marx saw it as the source of exploitation.

quiz.q: Law and religion belong to the:
quiz.why: Law and religion belong to the superstructure, shaped by the economic base, in Marx's theory.

quiz.q: Class becoming aware of its interests:
quiz.why: A class that is aware of its common interests and acts on them is a 'class for itself'.

story.title: Why the office runs on files

scenes.text: A government office runs by written rules, fixed hierarchy and files — regardless of who sits in which chair.
Weber saw bureaucracy as the most efficient form of legal-rational organisation — and feared its 'iron cage'.

steps.title: Key ideas
steps.body:
- **Verstehen**: interpretive understanding of the meanings actors give to action
- **Types of social action**: instrumentally rational, value-rational, affectual, traditional
- **Ideal type**: an analytical model built by accentuating features (not a moral ideal)
- ***The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism*** (1904–05): Calvinist ideas of calling and worldly asceticism had an elective affinity with the capitalist spirit
- **Authority**: traditional, charismatic, legal-rational
- **Bureaucracy**: hierarchy, written rules, specialisation, impersonality, merit-based appointment; the **iron cage** of rationalisation
- Stratification: **class, status and party**

steps.title: Solved: classify the action
steps.body:
- Choosing the cheapest flight to reach a meeting → **instrumentally rational**
- Refusing a bribe because it is wrong, whatever the cost → **value-rational**
- Hugging a friend who passed an exam → **affectual**
- Touching elders' feet because it has always been done → **traditional**

steps.title: Solved: Weber vs Marx
steps.body: Marx: economic base drives ideas. Weber: ideas (e.g. religious ethics) can also shape economic life, and stratification has several dimensions (class, status, party), not class alone.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating an 'ideal type' as the best or perfect form.
- Saying Weber argued Protestantism alone caused capitalism (he argued an affinity among several factors).
- Mixing his three types of authority with his four types of action.

items.text: Comparing prices online to buy a laptop
Donating anonymously out of religious duty
Celebrating a festival as the family always has
Choosing a course for its job prospects

quiz.why: Verstehen is Weber's term for interpretive understanding: grasping the meanings people attach to their actions.

quiz.q: The Protestant Ethic was published in:
quiz.why: Weber's The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism appeared as two essays in 1904–05.
Weber's 'iron cage' refers to rationalised, bureaucratic life that traps people in rules and efficiency.
Weber's three dimensions of stratification are class, status and party.
An ideal type is an analytical model that stresses key features for comparison. It is not a moral ideal or an average.

questions.why: Sociology studies society and social relationships.
Suicide (1897) was written by Émile Durkheim.
Capital, Volume I (1867), is by Karl Marx.
An achieved status is earned by effort, like being a doctor. Sex, age and caste at birth are ascribed.
Unity through specialisation and interdependence is organic solidarity, in Durkheim.
Bureaucracy is associated with Weber's legal-rational authority.

questions.q: Assertion: Durkheim treated suicide rates as social facts. Reason: Rates varied systematically with integration and regulation across groups.
questions.why: Durkheim treated suicide rates as social facts because they varied systematically with social integration and regulation. Both true, and the reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: Worker paid ₹500 produces value ₹1,200 (net of materials). Surplus value:
questions.why: Surplus value = value produced − wages = 1,200 − 500 = ₹700.

options: telling the truth despite personal loss
questions.why: Value-rational action is done for a belief in a value, whatever the cost. Telling the truth despite personal loss is an example.

questions.q: Case: After sudden demonetisation-type shocks, a study finds a spike in confusion and normlessness among small traders. Durkheim's concept:
questions.why: A spike in confusion and normlessness after a sudden shock is anomie, in Durkheim's sense: a breakdown of social regulation.

questions.q: Weber's argument in the Protestant Ethic is best described as:
options: Protestantism was the sole cause of capitalism
religious ideas had an elective affinity with the capitalist spirit
questions.why: Weber argued that Protestant religious ideas had an elective affinity with the capitalist spirit. He did not say it was the sole cause.

options: workers adopting ideas that serve the ruling class
questions.why: False consciousness, in Marx, means workers adopting ideas that serve the ruling class's interests, against their own.
Mechanical solidarity belongs to Durkheim, not Weber. The other pairings are correct.

questions.q: A researcher joins a village festival committee for a year to study rituals. Method and a key risk:
questions.why: Joining a village festival committee for a year is participant observation. A key risk is researcher bias, or 'going native'.

questions.q: Altruistic suicide in Durkheim's scheme is linked to:
questions.why: In Durkheim's typology, altruistic suicide is linked to excessive social integration, where the individual is subordinated to the group.

scenes.text: In a village, a family from a historically marginalised caste opens the first computer centre; youth of all castes now train there.
Caste persists in many ways, yet education, law and markets are changing its shape. Sociologists study both continuity and change.

steps.title: Concepts
steps.body:
- **Varna** (fourfold scriptural scheme) vs **jati** (thousands of local endogamous groups that operate in practice)
- **G. S. Ghurye's features**: segmental division, hierarchy, restrictions on commensality and social intercourse, civil and religious disabilities, restricted choice of occupation, **endogamy**
- **Louis Dumont** (*Homo Hierarchicus*, 1966): purity and pollution as the organising principle
- **M. N. Srinivas**: **sanskritisation** (lower castes adopting customs of higher castes to claim status), **westernisation**, and **dominant caste** (numerical strength, land, political power) — from his Coorg and Rampura studies
- Constitution: Art 15 (no discrimination), **Art 17 (untouchability abolished)**, reservations for SCs/STs/OBCs; laws such as the SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989

steps.title: Solved: name the process
steps.body:
- A caste group gives up meat-eating and adopts Sanskritic rituals to claim higher status → **sanskritisation**
- A family adopts English education, Western dress and lifestyles → **westernisation**
- A landowning, numerous caste dominates village politics → **dominant caste**

steps.title: Solved: continuity and change
steps.body:
Change: urban jobs, education, inter-caste marriages (still a minority), political mobilisation of marginalised groups.
Continuity: endogamy remains common; discrimination persists in places — documented by studies and court cases. Balanced answers cite both.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating varna and jati as the same thing.
- Claiming caste has disappeared in cities.
- Using caste slurs or stereotypes in answers — use respectful, constitutional terms.
- Confusing sanskritisation with westernisation.

activity.prompt: Match the concept to the scholar.

quiz.why: Article 17 of the Constitution abolishes untouchability.
M. N. Srinivas coined 'Sanskritisation', in his study of the Coorgs.
Endogamy means marrying within one's own group, such as caste.
In Srinivas's concept, a dominant caste has large numbers, land ownership and political power in a village.
Homo Hierarchicus (1966) is by Louis Dumont.

scenes.text: Nani grew up in a joint family of 25 people under one roof and one kitchen.
Her grandchildren live in nuclear families in different cities — yet still gather for every festival. Families change form, but kinship ties remain.

steps.title: Key ideas
steps.body:
- **Joint family**: several generations sharing residence, property and kitchen; **nuclear family**: couple and unmarried children
- Many urban families are 'functionally joint' — separate homes but shared obligations
- **Descent**: patrilineal (most of India), **matrilineal** (Khasi and Garo of Meghalaya; historically the Nairs of Kerala), bilateral
- **Residence**: patrilocal, matrilocal, neolocal
- **Marriage rules**: endogamy (within caste/community), exogamy (outside clan/gotra); cross-cousin marriage more common in South Indian kinship patterns
- **Iravati Karve** (*Kinship Organisation in India*, 1953) mapped regional kinship zones
- Legal changes: Hindu Marriage Act 1955; Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act 2005 gave daughters equal coparcenary rights; Prohibition of Child Marriage Act 2006

steps.title: Solved: classify
steps.body:
- Property and family name pass through the mother's line → **matrilineal** (e.g. Khasi)
- A newly married couple sets up home in a new city → **neolocal**
- Marriage forbidden within the same gotra → **gotra exogamy**

steps.title: Solved: is the joint family disappearing?
steps.body: Evidence of change: urbanisation and migration increase nuclear households. Evidence of continuity: strong support networks, elder care, shared financial decisions. Sociologists like A. M. Shah argued household form changes cyclically and the joint family ideal persists.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Equating matrilineal with matriarchal (descent through women does not mean women hold all power).
- Assuming all rural families are joint and all urban ones nuclear.
- Confusing endogamy with exogamy.

items.text: Village exogamy in parts of North India

quiz.why: The Khasi of Meghalaya are matrilineal: descent is traced through the mother.
Kinship Organisation in India (1953) is by Iravati Karve, who described regional kinship zones.

quiz.q: Couple living in a new independent home:
quiz.why: A couple living in a new, independent home is neolocal residence.

quiz.q: Daughters got equal coparcenary rights by:
quiz.why: The Hindu Succession (Amendment) Act, 2005, gave daughters equal coparcenary rights.
Matrilineal means descent is traced through the mother's line. It doesn't mean women rule.

scenes.text: A forest-dwelling community has gathered mahua and tendu leaves for generations, but has no paper title to the land.
The Forest Rights Act, 2006 recognised such rights — showing how law and community life intersect.

steps.title: Key facts
steps.body:
- **Scheduled Tribes** notified under Article 342; about 8.6% of India's population (Census 2011)
- **Fifth Schedule**: Scheduled Areas and Tribes Advisory Councils in several states
- **Sixth Schedule**: Autonomous District Councils in Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram
- **PESA Act, 1996**: extends panchayati raj to Fifth Schedule areas, empowering gram sabhas
- **Forest Rights Act, 2006**: recognises individual and community forest rights
- Debates: isolation vs assimilation vs integration (Verrier Elwin, G. S. Ghurye, Nehru's 'Panchsheel' for tribal policy); displacement by dams and mines; identity and indigeneity

steps.title: Solved: which provision?
steps.body:
- A gram sabha in a Scheduled Area must be consulted before land acquisition → **PESA 1996**
- A Khasi district council makes rules on land and customs → **Sixth Schedule**
- A community claims rights to collect forest produce → **Forest Rights Act 2006**

steps.title: Solved: debates
steps.body: Elwin initially favoured protecting tribal ways of life; Ghurye saw tribes as 'backward Hindus' to be assimilated; Nehru's policy sought integration while respecting tribal culture and rights. Modern views emphasise self-determination and consent.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating all tribal communities as identical.
- Confusing Fifth and Sixth Schedules.
- Using outdated or derogatory terms ('primitive') — use 'Scheduled Tribes' or the community's own name; 'Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Groups' is the official term for the most vulnerable.

activity.prompt: Match the provision to its purpose.
pairs: Autonomous District Councils in the North-East
Gram sabha powers in Scheduled Areas

quiz.q: Autonomous District Councils are under the:
quiz.why: Autonomous District Councils in the North-East come under the Sixth Schedule.
The PESA Act (Panchayats Extension to Scheduled Areas) was passed in 1996.
Scheduled Tribes were about 8.6% of India's population in the 2011 Census.
The Forest Rights Act, 2006, recognises individual and community rights of forest dwellers.
Scheduled Tribes are notified under Article 342. Article 341 is for Scheduled Castes.

scenes.text: In 1973 in Chamoli, women and villagers embraced trees to stop commercial felling.
The Chipko movement became a symbol of ecological and women's activism worldwide.

steps.title: Processes
steps.body:
- **Modernisation**: industrialisation, secularisation, rational-legal institutions (Yogendra Singh's *Modernization of Indian Tradition*, 1973)
- **Westernisation** and **sanskritisation** (Srinivas)
- **Urbanisation**: urban share about 31% in Census 2011; migration, slums, new middle classes
- **Globalisation**: IT and service jobs, consumer culture, cultural hybridity, new inequalities
- **Gender**: education and work participation changes; laws on dowry, domestic violence (2005), workplace harassment (POSH Act 2013)

steps.title: Social movements
steps.body:
- Characteristics: collective action, shared identity, sustained over time, aims at change
- Types: reformist, revolutionary, redemptive, alternative; 'old' (class-based) vs 'new' social movements (environment, gender, identity)
- Examples: **Chipko (1973)** — Gaura Devi, Chandi Prasad Bhatt, Sunderlal Bahuguna; **Narmada Bachao Andolan** (from the mid-1980s; Medha Patkar); Dalit movements inspired by Ambedkar; women's movements; farmers' movements

steps.title: Solved: classify the movement
steps.body:
- Chipko → **new social movement** (ecology, livelihood, women's participation); reformist in aims
- A movement seeking complete overthrow of an economic system → **revolutionary**

steps.title: Solved: urbanisation effects
steps.body: Push factors (rural distress) and pull factors (jobs) drive migration; outcomes include informal work, slums, and weaker caste controls in public spaces — but also new forms of exclusion (e.g. housing discrimination).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Treating modernisation as identical to westernisation.
- Assuming social movements always succeed or always fail.
- Giving precise statistics you are not sure of — state the source and year if you quote numbers.

quiz.why: The Narmada Bachao Andolan is linked with Medha Patkar, against big dams on the Narmada.

quiz.why: New social movements focus on identity, environment and gender, rather than only class and wages.

questions.why: A group adopting vegetarianism and Sanskritic rituals to claim higher status is sanskritisation.

options: caste endogamy is weakening slowly but persists
questions.why: Rising but still small inter-caste marriages in cities suggest caste endogamy is weakening slowly but persists.

questions.why: Dumont saw caste as organised by the ideology of purity and pollution, in Homo Hierarchicus.

questions.q: Which is a reason the joint-family ideal persists in cities?
options: functional ties of support and shared obligations
questions.why: The joint-family ideal persists in cities through functional ties of mutual support and shared obligations, even when households are separate.

the Sixth Schedule covers all states

steps.title: Indian sociology
steps.body:

- Karve: kinship zones (1953); Yogendra Singh: modernisation (1973)
- STs ≈ 8.6% (2011); Fifth/Sixth Schedules; PESA 1996; FRA 2006

steps.body: Define → explain with a thinker → apply to an Indian example → note a criticism → conclude.

steps.title: Durkheim's lens

steps.title: Weber's lens

quiz.why: The ideal type is a methodological tool of Max Weber.

questions.why: A couple living with the husband's parents is patrilocal residence.

options: Weber adds status and party to class

questions.why: Household forms change, but obligations of the joint family often continue. So it hasn't fully disappeared, and it isn't legally mandatory.

uni-ba-pol-comparative-politics.title: Comparative Politics
uni-ba-pol-comparative-politics.description: Approaches to comparative politics, constitutionalism, parliamentary and presidential systems (UK, USA and others), federalism, electoral and party systems, pressure groups, development, dependency and democratisation. Study companion; topics commonly taught in Indian B.A. Political Science programmes.

courses.title: Unit 1 · Nature and Approaches of Comparative Politics
curricula: UGC CBCS / NEP 2020 (Comparative Government and Politics core)
courses.summary: Meaning, scope and method of comparison; the shift from comparative government to comparative politics; institutional, systems, structural-functional, political-culture and political-economy approaches; Eurocentrism critique.
outcomes: Distinguish comparative government from comparative politics
Explain the comparative method, including most-similar and most-different designs
Apply Easton's systems model and Almond's structural-functionalism
Explain political culture (Almond and Verba) and political economy approaches

lessons.title: Meaning, scope and the comparative method

scenes.text: India and Pakistan became independent in 1947 with shared colonial institutions.
One sustained elected government; the other saw repeated military rule.
Comparing them helps isolate what explains democratic survival.

steps.title: From comparative government to comparative politics
steps.body: Traditional comparative government (Bryce, Finer, Carl Friedrich) compared formal constitutions and institutions of mainly Western states using legal-historical description. After 1945 'comparative politics' widened to informal processes (parties, groups, culture), non-Western 'new states', and aimed at theory-building with scientific methods. Roy Macridis's 1955 critique called traditional study parochial, descriptive, formal and static.

steps.title: The comparative method
steps.body: Comparison is the social scientist's substitute for the experiment (Lijphart, 1971). J.S. Mill's method of agreement (cases differ in many ways but share the outcome and one factor) and method of difference (cases similar in most ways but differ in outcome and one factor). Przeworski and Teune: most-similar systems design vs most-different systems design. Problems: 'many variables, small N', selection bias, conceptual stretching (Sartori).

steps.title: Worked example: method of difference
steps.body: India and Pakistan: similar colonial legacy, partition and initial institutions (controls). Outcome differs: democracy vs repeated coups. Candidate variable: a strong mass party (Congress) that had subordinated the military and built nationwide organisation, vs the Muslim League's weaker roots in West Pakistan. This is a most-similar design.

steps.title: Eurocentrism critique
steps.body: Early modernisation and development theories took Western Europe and the USA as the model. Critics (Edward Said's Orientalism, post-colonial scholars, Howard Wiarda) urged non-Western concepts and multiple paths.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Comparison is not just listing features of two countries; it must explain variation. 'Conceptual stretching' is Sartori's warning against applying concepts so broadly they lose meaning.

activity.prompt: Traditional comparative government or modern comparative politics?

items.text: Study of parties, groups and culture
Includes Asian, African and Latin American states

quiz.q: 'Comparison is a substitute for experiment' is associated with
quiz.why: Lijphart's 1971 article framed the comparative method as a quasi-experimental tool.

quiz.q: Choosing similar cases that differ in outcome is
quiz.why: Most-similar designs hold many factors constant to isolate the cause of different outcomes.

quiz.q: Macridis criticised traditional comparative government as
quiz.why: He said it was limited to Western states and formal legal institutions.

scenes.text: Farmers demand loan waivers; taxpayers resist; media debates.
Inside the 'political system' demands are converted into decisions.
A policy emerges — and its effects feed back into new demands.

steps.title: Old and new institutionalism
steps.body: Old institutionalism studied formal-legal structures (constitutions, legislatures). New institutionalism (March and Olsen, 1984) holds that institutions — formal rules and informal norms — shape behaviour. Variants: rational-choice (rules as incentives), historical (path dependence and critical junctures), sociological (norms and 'logic of appropriateness').

steps.title: Easton's systems analysis
steps.body: David Easton (A Systems Analysis of Political Life, 1965): the political system receives inputs from the environment — demands and supports — converts them via 'conversion' processes (the black box) into outputs (decisions and policies), and feedback links outputs back to inputs. Gatekeepers (parties, groups) regulate demand flow; stress arises from demand overload or support decline; the system seeks persistence.

steps.title: Worked example: mapping a policy
steps.body: Input-demand: farmers' unions demand MSP guarantee. Input-support: voting, tax-paying, loyalty. Gatekeepers: farmer organisations, parties. Conversion: Cabinet, Parliament, bureaucracy. Output: committee on MSP or a new scheme. Feedback: unions judge the response and renew or escalate demands.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Easton's model is abstract and status-quo-oriented (focus on persistence); critics say it neglects power and conflict inside the black box.

activity.prompt: Order the flow in Easton's model
items: Feedback to the environment and new inputs

quiz.q: In Easton's model, voting and paying taxes are
quiz.why: They express backing for the system and its authorities.
Historical institutionalists argue early choices lock in later trajectories.
March and Olsen's sociological view says actors follow norms of appropriate conduct.

scenes.text: In one country, parties aggregate interests; in another, the army does.
Almond asks: which structures perform which functions?
And how do citizens' attitudes shape the system?

steps.title: Almond's structural-functionalism
steps.body: Gabriel Almond (with Coleman, The Politics of the Developing Areas, 1960; with Powell, 1966): every political system performs the same functions, through different structures. Input functions: political socialisation and recruitment, interest articulation, interest aggregation, political communication. Output functions: rule-making, rule-application, rule-adjudication. Later system, process and policy functions. Concept of multifunctionality: one structure may perform several functions.

steps.title: Political culture: Almond and Verba
steps.body: The Civic Culture (1963), a survey of five nations (USA, UK, West Germany, Italy, Mexico). Types: parochial (little awareness of the political system), subject (aware of outputs, passive), participant (active orientation to inputs and outputs). The 'civic culture' — a mix with participant orientations balanced by subject and parochial ones — was found strongest in the UK and USA. Lucian Pye and Sidney Verba extended it to development.

steps.title: Worked example: classify orientations
steps.body: A tribal villager unaware of national elections — parochial. A city resident who obeys laws and pays taxes but never votes or petitions — subject. A student who campaigns, writes to MPs and joins protests — participant.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Critics (e.g. Pateman, Lijphart in 'The Civic Culture Revisited', 1980) say the civic-culture model was Anglo-American-centred and treated passivity as a virtue for stability.

activity.prompt: Match the function to an example structure
pairs: Political party combining demands into a manifesto

quiz.q: The Civic Culture surveyed how many countries?
quiz.why: Almond and Verba studied the USA, UK, West Germany, Italy and Mexico.

quiz.q: A citizen aware of government outputs but passive is
quiz.why: Subject orientation focuses on outputs without active input.

lessons.title: Political economy and the state-centred approach

scenes.text: South Korea's state picked industries and disciplined business in the 1970s.
Growth followed — not just markets at work.
Scholars argued the state is an actor, not just an arena.

steps.title: Political economy approach
steps.body: Studies the interplay of state and market, classes and production. Marxist variants: class analysis, mode of production; Barrington Moore's Social Origins of Dictatorship and Democracy (1966) — 'no bourgeoisie, no democracy', showing how agrarian class relations shaped routes to democracy, fascism or communism.

steps.title: State-centred approach
steps.body: Theda Skocpol (States and Social Revolutions, 1979; 'Bringing the State Back In', 1985) treated the state as an autonomous actor with its own interests. Peter Evans's 'embedded autonomy' (1995) explained developmental states (South Korea, Taiwan) — bureaucracies insulated from capture yet linked to business.

steps.title: Rational choice
steps.body: Actors are utility-maximisers; politics explained by strategic interaction (Anthony Downs's An Economic Theory of Democracy, 1957 — median voter; Mancur Olson's The Logic of Collective Action, 1965 — free-rider problem).

steps.title: Worked example: median voter
steps.body: Five voters on a left–right scale at positions 1, 3, 5, 7, 9. The median is 5. A party at 5 beats a party at 3: voters at 1 and 3 prefer the party at 3 (2 votes), voters at 5, 7, 9 prefer the party at 5 (3 votes). Downs predicts two parties converge on the median.

steps.title: Common mistakes

courses.title: Unit 2 · Constitutionalism and Forms of Government
curricula: UGC CBCS / NEP 2020 (Comparative Government and Politics core)
courses.summary: Constitutionalism; the British parliamentary system; the US presidential system; semi-presidentialism (France); federal and unitary systems (USA, Switzerland, China comparisons).
outcomes: Define constitutionalism and distinguish written/unwritten, rigid/flexible constitutions
Explain the UK's parliamentary system and conventions
Explain the US separation of powers and checks and balances
Compare parliamentary, presidential and semi-presidential systems and federal arrangements

scenes.text: Britain has no single document called 'the Constitution'.
Yet Magna Carta, statutes, conventions and court rulings limit power.
Constitutionalism is about limited government, not just a written text.

steps.title: Constitutionalism
steps.body: Constitutionalism is the idea that government must be limited by law — power is restrained by rules, rights and institutions (C.H. McIlwain, Carl Friedrich). Elements: rule of law, separation of powers, independent judiciary, fundamental rights, accountability, and a procedure for amendment. A state may have a constitution without constitutionalism (e.g. documents in authoritarian states that do not actually limit rulers).

steps.title: Classifications (K.C. Wheare, Bryce)
steps.body: Written (codified, e.g. USA 1787) vs unwritten (uncodified, e.g. UK). Rigid (special amendment procedure — USA needs two-thirds of both Houses + three-fourths of states) vs flexible (ordinary law-making — UK). Federal vs unitary. Presidential vs parliamentary. India is written and partly rigid, partly flexible.

steps.title: Dicey's rule of law
steps.body: A.V. Dicey (1885): (1) supremacy of regular law over arbitrary power; (2) equality before the law — officials and citizens under the same ordinary courts; (3) constitution is the result of ordinary law — rights flow from judicial decisions. Dicey also defined conventions as rules not enforced by courts but observed in practice.

steps.title: Worked example: US amendment arithmetic
steps.body: With 50 states, ratification needs three-fourths = 37.5 → 38 states. Congress proposal needs two-thirds of both Houses: Senate 100 → 67; House 435 (if all present) → 290. Only 27 amendments have been ratified since 1789, showing extreme rigidity.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: 'Unwritten' does not mean nothing is written — much of the UK constitution is in statutes (e.g. Parliament Acts 1911 and 1949, Human Rights Act 1998).

items.text: Judicial review of federal law (Marbury v Madison)

quiz.q: US constitutional amendments ratified so far
quiz.why: Twenty-seven amendments have been ratified, the last in 1992.

story.title: The Queen's speech written by the PM

scenes.text: Each session the monarch reads the 'King's Speech' — written by the government.
It shows the British formula: the Crown reigns, the Cabinet rules.
Bagehot called these the 'dignified' and 'efficient' parts.

steps.title: Crown and conventions
steps.body: Constitutional monarchy: formal powers (royal prerogative) are exercised on ministerial advice. Bagehot (The English Constitution, 1867): the monarch's rights — to be consulted, to encourage, to warn. Conventions: monarch assents to bills (last refusal 1708, Queen Anne), appoints as PM the leader who commands the Commons, PM sits in the Commons.

steps.title: Parliament
steps.body: House of Commons: 650 MPs elected by FPTP; supremacy over Lords via Parliament Acts 1911 (Lords' veto on money bills removed; delay for other bills 2 years) and 1949 (delay reduced to 1 year). House of Lords: life peers, 92 hereditary peers (after the House of Lords Act 1999) and 26 Lords Spiritual. The Supreme Court of the UK (since 2009) replaced the Appellate Committee of the Lords.

steps.title: Cabinet and PM
steps.body: Cabinet government with collective responsibility; Crossman and Mackintosh argued it had become 'prime ministerial government'. Fusion of executive and legislature — ministers drawn from Parliament. Opposition: 'His Majesty's Loyal Opposition' with a Shadow Cabinet. Rule of law and parliamentary sovereignty (Dicey) — no court can strike down an Act of Parliament, though the Human Rights Act 1998 allows 'declarations of incompatibility'.

steps.title: Worked example: majority in the Commons
steps.body: 650 seats; Speaker and deputies don't vote and Sinn Féin MPs (usually 7) don't take seats. Effective working majority threshold ≈ (650 − 7 − 4) / 2 ≈ 320 rather than 326. 2024 election: Labour won 411 seats — a majority of 172 over all others (411 − 239).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: The Lords cannot veto money bills at all since 1911. Parliamentary sovereignty means Parliament can make or unmake any law — not that the Lords are equal to the Commons.

scenes.text: The President wants a budget; Congress, controlled by the other party, refuses.
Federal offices close for weeks.
Separation of powers can mean gridlock — by design, to prevent tyranny.

steps.title: Separation of powers and checks
steps.body: Madison (Federalist No. 51): 'ambition must be made to counteract ambition'. Article I Congress, Article II President, Article III judiciary. Checks: presidential veto (overridden by two-thirds of both Houses), Senate confirmation of appointments and two-thirds for treaty ratification, impeachment (House impeaches by simple majority; Senate convicts by two-thirds), judicial review (Marbury v Madison, 1803).

steps.title: The presidency
steps.body: Fixed four-year term; maximum two elected terms (22nd Amendment, 1951). Elected through the Electoral College: 538 electors (435 House + 100 Senate + 3 for DC); 270 needed to win. Winner-take-all in 48 states; Maine and Nebraska split by district. Presidents can win the Electoral College while losing the popular vote (e.g. 2000, 2016).

steps.title: Congress
steps.body: House: 435 members, 2-year terms, seats apportioned by population; originates revenue bills. Senate: 100 (2 per state), 6-year staggered terms, one-third elected every 2 years; filibuster (cloture needs 60 votes). Strong committee system.

steps.title: Worked example: veto override
steps.body: President vetoes a bill. All 435 House members vote: override needs 2/3 × 435 = 290. In the Senate with 100 voting: 67. If the House votes 300–135 and the Senate 64–36, the House overrides but the Senate fails (64 < 67), so the veto stands.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: The President is not responsible to Congress and cannot dissolve it. Impeachment ≠ removal; removal requires Senate conviction by two-thirds.

lessons.title: Parliamentary vs presidential vs semi-presidential; federalism

scenes.text: In 1986 French President Mitterrand (Socialist) had to appoint a right-wing PM, Chirac.
Two leaders, two parties, one executive.
Semi-presidentialism mixes both models.

steps.title: Comparing systems
steps.body: Parliamentary: fused executive and legislature, executive responsible to legislature, nominal vs real executive, flexible term (dissolution). Presidential: separation, fixed terms, single executive. Juan Linz ('The Perils of Presidentialism', 1990): dual legitimacy, rigidity and winner-take-all make presidential democracies more fragile. Defenders (Mainwaring and Shugart) note it depends on party systems and powers.

steps.title: Semi-presidentialism (Duverger)
steps.body: Maurice Duverger (1980): popularly elected President with considerable powers plus a PM and cabinet responsible to parliament. France (Fifth Republic, 1958): President elected for 5 years (quinquennat since 2002); appoints PM; can dissolve the National Assembly; Article 16 emergency powers. Cohabitation: 1986–88, 1993–95, 1997–2002.

steps.title: Federal and unitary
steps.body: Federal: constitutional division of powers, written rigid constitution, independent judiciary, bicameralism (USA — 'coming together', residual powers with states, 10th Amendment). Switzerland: 26 cantons, collegial 7-member Federal Council, direct democracy (referendum, initiative with 100,000 signatures). Unitary: power concentrated at centre, local units are creations (UK with devolution to Scotland, Wales, Northern Ireland since 1998; China — unitary party-state with National People's Congress formally supreme, CPC leading role).

steps.title: Worked example: which system?
steps.body: Country Z: directly elected President (fixed 5 years), PM chosen by President but can be removed by a no-confidence vote of the assembly. Answer: semi-presidential (like France), because executive is dual and the PM is responsible to parliament.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Devolution in the UK does not make it federal — Westminster can legally revoke devolved powers. Switzerland's Federal Council has no single head of government; the presidency rotates annually.
