courses.title: Unit 3 · Electoral Systems, Party Systems and Pressure Groups
curricula: UGC CBCS / NEP 2020 (Comparative Government and Politics core)
courses.summary: Majoritarian, proportional and mixed electoral systems with seat-allocation methods; classifications of party systems (Duverger, Sartori); and pressure groups and their methods.
outcomes: Compare FPTP, two-round, AV, list-PR, STV and MMP systems
Allocate seats using D'Hondt and Sainte-Laguë
Classify party systems using Duverger and Sartori
Distinguish pressure groups from parties and explain their methods

scenes.text: Imagine the same national vote counted under UK rules and under Dutch rules.
Under FPTP one party gets a majority; under PR five parties share seats.
Electoral rules shape party systems and governments.

steps.title: Majoritarian/plurality systems
steps.body: FPTP (UK, India, USA, Canada): single-member districts, plurality wins. Two-round system (France): a majority is needed in round one, otherwise a run-off (French legislative candidates with at least 12.5% of registered voters qualify). Alternative Vote (Australian House): voters rank candidates; lowest eliminated and votes transferred until someone has over 50%.

steps.title: Proportional systems
steps.body: List PR (Netherlands, Israel, South Africa): parties get seats in proportion to votes, often with a legal threshold (Germany 5%, Israel 3.25%, Netherlands effectively about 0.67% = 1/150). STV (Ireland, Malta; India's Rajya Sabha): multi-member districts with ranked preferences and a quota — Droop quota = floor(votes/(seats + 1)) + 1.

steps.title: Mixed systems
steps.body: Mixed-member proportional (Germany, New Zealand): voters have two votes — constituency and party list; list seats compensate to make the overall result proportional. Mixed parallel (Japan): the two tiers are counted separately.

steps.title: Worked example: Droop quota
steps.body: An STV constituency elects 4 members; 50,000 valid votes. Droop quota = floor(50,000/5) + 1 = 10,000 + 1 = 10,001. A candidate with 13,001 first preferences is elected with a surplus of 3,000, which is transferred according to next preferences.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: AV is not proportional — it is a majoritarian system in single-member seats. STV is proportional only in multi-member districts.

lessons.title: Lab: Allocating seats with D'Hondt and Sainte-Laguë

scenes.text: Officials must divide 7 seats among four parties.
They divide each party's votes by a series of divisors.
The seven highest quotients win seats.

steps.title: Highest-averages methods
steps.body: D'Hondt divisors: 1, 2, 3, 4 … (favours larger parties). Sainte-Laguë divisors: 1, 3, 5, 7 … (more proportional, kinder to mid-sized parties). Allocate seats one by one to the highest remaining quotient.

steps.title: Interpretation
steps.body: Exact proportional entitlement: A 7 × 100/230 = 3.04; B 2.43; C 0.91; D 0.61. Sainte-Laguë (3, 2, 1, 1) tracks this more closely than D'Hondt (3, 3, 1, 0), which over-rewards B.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Do not stop after giving each party one seat; always rank all quotients. Ties at the last seat must be resolved by a stated rule (often lot).

items: Divide each total by 1, 2, 3, … up to the number of seats
List all quotients in descending order
Award seats to the highest quotients until all seats are filled

quiz.why: D'Hondt's small step between divisors makes extra seats cheaper for big parties relative to small ones.

scenes.text: India has over 2,000 registered parties.
But only some shape who governs.

steps.title: Parties and their functions
steps.body: Edmund Burke: a party is 'a body of men united for promoting by their joint endeavours the national interest upon some particular principle in which they are all agreed'. Functions: interest aggregation, recruitment of leaders, forming governments, opposition, political socialisation. Types: cadre vs mass parties (Duverger), catch-all parties (Otto Kirchheimer), cartel parties (Katz and Mair).

steps.title: Duverger's law
steps.body: Duverger (Political Parties, 1951): plurality single-ballot elections favour two-party systems (mechanical effect — under-representation of third parties; psychological effect — voters avoid wasting votes). PR and run-off systems favour multipartism (Duverger's hypothesis).

steps.title: Sartori's typology
steps.body: Giovanni Sartori (Parties and Party Systems, 1976) counted 'relevant' parties (coalition or blackmail potential) and ideological distance: one-party, hegemonic party, predominant party, two-party, moderate pluralism (3–5 parties, small distance), polarised pluralism (6+, anti-system parties, centrifugal competition — e.g. Weimar, post-war Italy), atomised.

steps.title: Worked example: effective number of parties
steps.body: Laakso–Taagepera: N = 1 / Σ(pᵢ²), using seat shares. Seat shares 0.5, 0.3, 0.2 → Σp² = 0.25 + 0.09 + 0.04 = 0.38 → N = 1/0.38 ≈ 2.63. Two equal parties (0.5, 0.5) → N = 1/0.5 = 2.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Sartori's 'predominant party' system (e.g. India's Congress era) is competitive; a 'hegemonic' system does not allow real competition.

scenes.text: An industry federation meets ministry officials before the budget.
A farmers' union blocks highways.
Both seek influence, not office — they are pressure groups.

steps.title: Meaning
steps.body: Pressure (interest) groups are organised associations that seek to influence public policy without seeking to form government. Unlike parties, they do not contest elections as a group and usually focus on narrow issues.

steps.title: Classifications
steps.body: Almond's types: anomic (spontaneous riots), non-associational (kinship, caste, religion), institutional (army, bureaucracy, churches), associational (unions, business federations). Sectional/interest groups (FICCI, CII, trade unions like AITUC, farmers' groups) vs promotional/cause groups (Greenpeace, Amnesty). Insider vs outsider groups (Wyn Grant).

steps.title: Methods and effects
steps.body: Lobbying ministers and officials, advising committees, election campaigning and funding, litigation (PILs), media campaigns, protest and direct action. Pluralists see groups as healthy competition; critics warn of 'iron triangles' (US — agency, congressional committee, interest group), corporatism (Schmitter — peak associations bargaining with the state, e.g. Austria, Sweden), and unequal resources.

steps.title: Worked example: classify
steps.body: FICCI meeting the Finance Ministry — associational, sectional, insider. Greenpeace India campaigning on coal — promotional, often outsider. A spontaneous riot after a price rise — anomic.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: A party's student wing is not an independent pressure group. Corporatism here means state–group bargaining, not 'corporate' companies.

courses.title: Unit 4 · Development, Dependency and Democratisation
curricula: UGC CBCS / NEP 2020 (Comparative Government and Politics core)
courses.summary: Modernisation and political development theories, dependency and world-systems critiques, colonialism and nationalism in the developing world, and theories of democratic transition and backsliding.
outcomes: Explain modernisation theory (Rostow, Lipset) and Huntington's political order
Explain dependency and world-systems theory
Analyse colonialism, decolonisation and post-colonial states
Describe waves of democratisation, transition paths and democratic backsliding

scenes.text: In 1960 an economist compared development to an aircraft taking off.
Traditional societies would modernise, industrialise and democratise — like the West had.
But would every country follow the same runway?

steps.title: Modernisation theory
steps.body: W.W. Rostow (The Stages of Economic Growth: A Non-Communist Manifesto, 1960): traditional society → preconditions for take-off → take-off → drive to maturity → age of high mass consumption. Seymour Martin Lipset (1959): 'the more well-to-do a nation, the greater the chances that it will sustain democracy' — economic development correlates with democracy. Daniel Lerner: urbanisation, literacy and media participation.

steps.title: Political development
steps.body: Lucian Pye's development syndrome: equality, capacity, differentiation. Crises of development (Binder, LaPalombara, Pye et al.): identity, legitimacy, penetration, participation, distribution, integration. Almond and Powell: system capabilities.

steps.title: Huntington's political order
steps.body: Samuel Huntington (Political Order in Changing Societies, 1968): rapid modernisation raises participation faster than institutions can absorb it, causing 'political decay'. Stability = institutionalisation ÷ participation (conceptually). Institutionalisation is measured by adaptability, complexity, autonomy and coherence. He favoured strong parties and order before democracy.

steps.title: Worked example: applying Huntington
steps.body: A country's literacy jumps from 30% to 70% in 20 years, urbanisation doubles, but parties are personalised and weak. Huntington predicts rising demands outrun institutions → instability, coups or mass unrest. Strong institutionalised parties (e.g. Congress in early India, per many scholars) can channel participation.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Lipset showed correlation, not inevitability; India is a famous outlier — democratic at low income.

quiz.q: 'Political Order in Changing Societies' is by
quiz.why: Huntington's 1968 book argued institutions must keep pace with participation.
His 1959 article showed richer countries were likelier to sustain democracy.

quiz.q: India is often cited as an outlier to modernisation theory because it
quiz.why: It defied the expectation that poor countries cannot sustain democracy.

scenes.text: A Latin American country exports coffee and imports cars.
Over decades the coffee buys fewer cars.
Dependency theorists said the periphery is underdeveloped because of its link to the core.

steps.title: Dependency theory
steps.body: Raúl Prebisch and Hans Singer (1950): declining terms of trade for primary-commodity exporters. Andre Gunder Frank: 'development of underdevelopment' — the periphery's underdevelopment results from its incorporation into world capitalism; satellites serve metropoles. Remedy proposals: import-substitution industrialisation (ECLA), de-linking (Samir Amin).

steps.title: World-systems theory
steps.body: Immanuel Wallerstein (The Modern World-System, 1974): a capitalist world-economy since the 16th century with core, semi-periphery and periphery; unequal exchange transfers surplus to the core; the semi-periphery stabilises the system. Cardoso and Faletto: 'associated dependent development' — growth can occur within dependency.

steps.title: Worked example: terms of trade
steps.body: Year 1: 1 tonne coffee = ₹2,00,000; a tractor = ₹10,00,000 → 5 tonnes buy a tractor. Year 20: coffee ₹2,50,000; tractor ₹20,00,000 → 8 tonnes needed. Terms of trade index = (Px/Pm) now ÷ (Px/Pm) then = (2.5/20) ÷ (2/10) = 0.125 ÷ 0.2 = 0.625 — a 37.5% deterioration.

steps.title: Critiques
steps.body: East Asian success (South Korea, Taiwan) via export-led growth challenged dependency's pessimism; critics say it underplays domestic factors (governance, class structures).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Wallerstein's three tiers include the semi-periphery — don't reduce it to core vs periphery.

lessons.title: Colonialism, nationalism and the post-colonial state

scenes.text: At the Berlin Conference (1884–85), European powers drew African borders.
Decades later, new nations inherited these borders and colonial bureaucracies.
Post-colonial states faced building nations inside imposed frames.

steps.title: Colonialism and imperialism
steps.body: Colonialism: direct political control and economic exploitation of territories. Lenin (Imperialism, the Highest Stage of Capitalism, 1916): monopoly capital exports capital and divides the world. Hobson (1902): underconsumption at home drives imperial expansion. Indirect rule (Lugard) vs direct rule.

steps.title: Anti-colonial nationalism
steps.body: Partha Chatterjee (The Nation and Its Fragments, 1993): anti-colonial nationalism divided the world into material (where the West was copied) and spiritual (inner domain kept sovereign). Frantz Fanon (The Wretched of the Earth, 1961) on decolonisation and violence. Bandung Conference (1955) and the Non-Aligned Movement (Belgrade, 1961).

steps.title: Post-colonial state
steps.body: Hamza Alavi: the 'overdeveloped' post-colonial state (Pakistan, Bangladesh) — a powerful bureaucratic-military apparatus inherited from colonialism, mediating between several propertied classes. Guillermo O'Donnell's 'bureaucratic authoritarianism' (Latin America, 1960s–70s). Joel Migdal: 'strong societies and weak states'.

steps.title: Worked example: why coups?
steps.body: Pakistan 1958: weak party institutionalisation (Huntington), overdeveloped bureaucratic-military apparatus (Alavi), regional tensions (East vs West). Contrast India: Congress's organisation, civilian supremacy, linguistic reorganisation addressing identity crises.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Bandung (1955) preceded the formal Non-Aligned Movement (1961). Alavi's 'overdeveloped state' refers to the apparatus, not the economy.

scenes.text: On 25 April 1974 Portuguese soldiers put carnations in their rifles and ended a dictatorship.
Huntington saw it as the start of a 'third wave' of democratisation.
Decades later scholars worry about a reverse wave.

steps.title: Huntington's three waves
steps.body: The Third Wave (1991): first long wave 1828–1926 (reverse 1922–42); second short wave 1943–62 (reverse 1958–75); third wave from 1974 (Portugal) through Southern Europe, Latin America, East Asia and post-1989 Eastern Europe.

steps.title: Transition and consolidation
steps.body: O'Donnell and Schmitter (1986): transitions driven by splits between hardliners and softliners within regimes and pacts with moderate opposition. Huntington's modes: transformation (from above), replacement (regime collapses), transplacement (negotiated). Linz and Stepan: democracy is consolidated when it becomes 'the only game in town' behaviourally, attitudinally and constitutionally. Przeworski's 'two-turnover test' (Huntington): power changes hands peacefully twice.

steps.title: Hybrid regimes and backsliding
steps.body: Levitsky and Way: competitive authoritarianism — elections exist but are skewed. Fareed Zakaria: 'illiberal democracy' (1997). Nancy Bermeo (2016): backsliding today happens mostly through executive aggrandisement and strategic election manipulation rather than open coups. Indices: V-Dem, Freedom House, EIU Democracy Index.

steps.title: Worked example: two-turnover test
steps.body: Country K: founding election 1992 won by Party A; A loses to B in 1997 and hands over (turnover 1); B loses to A in 2002 and hands over (turnover 2). K passes the two-turnover test by 2002.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: The third wave starts in 1974 (Portugal), not 1989. 'Only game in town' is Linz and Stepan, not Huntington.

outcomes: Recall the key thinkers and concepts of comparative politics

scenes.text: Comparative politics has many names; group them by approach.
Link each name to one concept and one country.
That triple anchors every answer.

steps.title: Approaches
steps.body: Macridis (critique of tradition, 1955) · Easton (systems, 1965) · Almond (structural-functional; Civic Culture 1963 with Verba) · March & Olsen (new institutionalism, 1984) · Skocpol (state-centred) · Moore (Social Origins, 1966) · Downs (1957) · Olson (1965).

steps.body: Dicey (rule of law, 1885) · Bagehot (1867) · Madison (Federalist 51) · Linz (perils of presidentialism, 1990) · Duverger (semi-presidential, 1980; party law, 1951) · Sartori (1976) · Lijphart (consensus vs majoritarian democracy, Patterns of Democracy 1999).

steps.body: Rostow (1960) · Lipset (1959) · Pye · Huntington (1968; Third Wave 1991) · Frank · Wallerstein (1974) · Cardoso & Faletto · Alavi · O'Donnell & Schmitter (1986) · Linz & Stepan · Levitsky & Way · Zakaria · Bermeo (2016).

steps.title: Lijphart in one line
steps.body: Majoritarian (Westminster) democracy concentrates power (UK, NZ before 1996); consensus democracy disperses it (Switzerland, Belgium) through coalitions, PR, federalism and bicameralism.

scenes.text: Poor, diverse, post-colonial — theory predicted fragility.
Yet India has held regular elections since 1951–52.
Use each theory to explain — or fail to explain — the case.

steps.title: Modernisation
steps.body: Lipset predicts low democratic survival at low income; India is the classic outlier. Explanations offered: elite consensus from the national movement, Congress's institutionalisation (Huntington-style), federal accommodation of linguistic identities.

steps.title: Lijphart's consociationalism
steps.body: Lijphart (1996, 'The Puzzle of Indian Democracy') argued India under Congress had consociational features: grand coalition within Congress, cultural autonomy (linguistic states, personal laws), proportionality (reservations), minority veto in practice. Critics (e.g. Steven Wilkinson) dispute how consociational India really was.

steps.title: Party systems and elections
steps.body: Kothari's 'Congress system' fits Sartori's predominant-party type; post-1989 multipartism shows how FPTP plus regionally concentrated parties can produce many parties nationally while contests are bipolar locally (Duverger at constituency level, Chhibber and Kollman's aggregation argument).

steps.title: Worked example: answer skeleton
steps.body: Q: 'India disproves modernisation theory.' Discuss. Intro: Lipset's thesis. Body: India's survival at low income; explanations (institutions, elite choice, federalism); counter-points (Emergency 1975–77, backsliding debates in V-Dem ratings); Conclusion: India qualifies rather than wholly disproves the thesis — correlation is probabilistic.

uni-ba-pol-indian-govt-politics.title: Indian Government & Politics
uni-ba-pol-indian-govt-politics.description: Making and philosophy of the Indian Constitution, rights and directive principles, Union government, judiciary, federalism, local self-government, parties, elections and social dynamics. Study companion; topics commonly taught in Indian B.A. Political Science programmes.

courses.title: Unit 1 · Making and Philosophy of the Constitution
curricula: UGC CBCS / NEP 2020 (Indian Government and Politics core)
courses.summary: The Constituent Assembly, sources and salient features of the Constitution, the Preamble, Fundamental Rights, Directive Principles, Fundamental Duties and the amendment process with the basic structure doctrine.
outcomes: Describe the composition and working of the Constituent Assembly
Explain the Preamble's values and the salient features of the Constitution
Classify Fundamental Rights and compare them with DPSPs
Explain Article 368 and the basic structure doctrine through landmark cases

scenes.text: On 9 December 1946 the Constituent Assembly met in the Constitution Hall, New Delhi.
Through 11 sessions and about 2 years 11 months it debated every clause.
On 26 November 1949 the Constitution was adopted; it came fully into force on 26 January 1950.

steps.title: Composition
steps.body: Formed under the Cabinet Mission Plan (1946). Members were indirectly elected by the provincial legislative assemblies (single transferable vote) plus nominees of princely states. Planned strength 389 (296 for British India, 93 for princely states); after Partition it was about 299. Dr Sachchidananda Sinha was temporary chairman; Dr Rajendra Prasad was elected President; H.C. Mukherjee and later V.T. Krishnamachari vice-presidents; B.N. Rau was constitutional adviser.

steps.title: Key committees and resolutions
steps.body: Objectives Resolution moved by Nehru on 13 December 1946, adopted 22 January 1947 — later the basis of the Preamble. Drafting Committee (chair Dr B.R. Ambedkar, set up 29 August 1947). Union Powers and Union Constitution Committees (Nehru); Provincial Constitution and Advisory Committee on Fundamental Rights and Minorities (Sardar Patel).

steps.title: Sources
steps.body: Government of India Act 1935 (federal scheme, emergency provisions, much administrative detail); UK (parliamentary government, rule of law, cabinet system); USA (fundamental rights, judicial review, independent judiciary); Ireland (Directive Principles); Canada (strong Centre federation, residuary powers with Centre); Australia (concurrent list); Weimar Germany (suspension of rights in emergency); USSR (fundamental duties, added later); South Africa (amendment procedure); France (republic, liberty-equality-fraternity).

steps.title: Criticism and defence
steps.body: Critics: not directly elected; dominated by Congress; 'a lawyers' paradise'; Ivor Jennings called it too long and rigid; 'borrowed'. Granville Austin called the Assembly's method 'consensus and accommodation' and described the Constitution as 'first and foremost a social document'.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Adoption date is 26 November 1949 (Constitution Day); commencement 26 January 1950 (Republic Day). Ambedkar chaired the Drafting Committee, not the Assembly.

activity.prompt: Match the person to the role

quiz.why: It was adopted on 26 November 1949, observed as Constitution Day.
They were modelled on the Directive Principles of Social Policy of the Irish Constitution.

quiz.q: Members of the Assembly were chosen by
quiz.why: Under the Cabinet Mission Plan, provincial legislatures elected them.

quiz.q: 'Social document' description of the Constitution is from
quiz.why: Austin's The Indian Constitution: Cornerstone of a Nation calls it first and foremost a social document.

story.title: The identity card of the Constitution

scenes.text: N.A. Palkhivala called the Preamble the 'identity card of the Constitution'.
It tells us where authority comes from, what kind of state India is, and what it aims for.
Courts use it to interpret ambiguous provisions.

steps.title: Text and elements
steps.body: Source of authority: 'We, the people of India'. Nature of state: Sovereign, Socialist, Secular, Democratic, Republic. Objectives: Justice (social, economic, political); Liberty (of thought, expression, belief, faith and worship); Equality (of status and opportunity); Fraternity (assuring the dignity of the individual and the unity and integrity of the Nation). Date of adoption: 26 November 1949.

steps.title: Is the Preamble part of the Constitution?
steps.body: Berubari Union (1960): not a part. Kesavananda Bharati (1973): it is a part and can be amended, but not its basic features. It was amended once — the 42nd Amendment (1976) added 'Socialist', 'Secular' and 'Integrity'. LIC of India (1995) reaffirmed it as an integral part. It is not enforceable in court on its own.

steps.title: Salient features
steps.body: Lengthiest written constitution; blend of rigidity and flexibility; federal system with unitary bias ('Union of States', Art. 1); parliamentary government; synthesis of parliamentary sovereignty and judicial supremacy; integrated and independent judiciary; Fundamental Rights, DPSPs, Fundamental Duties; secular state; universal adult franchise; single citizenship; independent bodies (ECI, CAG, UPSC); emergency provisions; three-tier government after the 73rd/74th Amendments.

steps.title: Federal with unitary bias
steps.body: K.C. Wheare called India 'quasi-federal'. Unitary features: strong Centre, single constitution, single citizenship, integrated judiciary, All-India Services, governor appointed by the Centre, Parliament can alter state boundaries (Art. 3), emergency provisions.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: The Preamble was amended once (1976), not never. 'Integrity' was also added, not only 'socialist' and 'secular'.

items.text: Division of powers in Seventh Schedule
Bicameral Parliament with Rajya Sabha representing states

quiz.q: Which words were added by the 42nd Amendment?
quiz.why: The 1976 amendment inserted socialist, secular and integrity.

quiz.q: In which case was the Preamble held to be part of the Constitution?
quiz.why: The 1973 judgment reversed the Berubari view.
He noted strong unitary features within a federal form.

scenes.text: Fundamental Rights are a shield citizens can raise in court.
Directive Principles are a compass for governments.
The courts have tried to make shield and compass work together.

steps.title: Six Fundamental Rights (Part III)
steps.body: Right to Equality (Arts 14–18); Right to Freedom (19–22); Right against Exploitation (23–24); Right to Freedom of Religion (25–28); Cultural and Educational Rights (29–30); Right to Constitutional Remedies (32). The right to property (Art. 31) was removed by the 44th Amendment (1978) and is now a constitutional legal right under Article 300A.

steps.title: Writs under Article 32
steps.body: Habeas corpus (produce the detained person), Mandamus (command a public authority to perform duty), Prohibition (stop a lower court acting beyond jurisdiction), Certiorari (quash an order of a lower court/tribunal), Quo warranto (by what authority one holds a public office). High Courts issue writs under Article 226 (wider — also for 'any other purpose').

steps.title: Directive Principles (Part IV, Arts 36–51)
steps.body: Non-justiciable (Art. 37) but 'fundamental in the governance of the country'. Socialist (Arts 38, 39, 41, 42, 43), Gandhian (40 village panchayats, 43 cottage industries, 46 weaker sections, 47 prohibition, 48 cow protection), Liberal-intellectual (44 uniform civil code, 45 early childhood care, 48A environment, 50 separation of judiciary, 51 international peace).

steps.title: FR vs DPSP — the case trail
steps.body: Champakam Dorairajan (1951): DPSPs subordinate. Golaknath (1967): Parliament cannot amend FRs. Kesavananda (1973): can amend but not the basic structure. Minerva Mills (1980): harmony and balance between FRs and DPSPs is itself part of the basic structure. Fundamental Duties: Article 51A, ten added by the 42nd Amendment (1976) on Swaran Singh Committee advice; the eleventh (education of children 6–14) by the 86th Amendment (2002).

steps.title: Worked example: choosing a writ
steps.body: A student is detained by police for 3 days without being produced before a magistrate. Article 22(2) requires production within 24 hours (excluding travel time). The correct remedy is a writ of habeas corpus under Article 32 (Supreme Court) or 226 (High Court).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Article 32 itself is a fundamental right; Article 226 is not in Part III. There are 11 Fundamental Duties today, not 10.

quiz.why: The 44th Amendment (1978) moved it to Article 300A as a constitutional legal right.

quiz.why: Minerva Mills (1980) struck down parts of the 42nd Amendment on this reasoning.

quiz.why: The 86th Amendment (2002) added the duty of parents to provide education to children aged 6–14.

lessons.title: Amendment and the basic structure doctrine

scenes.text: In 1972–73, 13 judges sat for 68 days — the largest bench in Indian history.
By 7:6 they held Parliament can amend any part — but not destroy the basic structure.
That doctrine still guards the Constitution's core.

steps.title: Article 368 — three methods
steps.body: (1) Simple majority of Parliament for provisions outside Art. 368 (e.g. creating new states under Art. 2/3, citizenship, quorum) — technically not 'amendments' under 368. (2) Special majority: a majority of the total membership of each House AND two-thirds of members present and voting. (3) Special majority plus ratification by legislatures of at least half the states — for federal provisions (election of President, Supreme Court/High Courts, distribution of powers, representation of states in Parliament, Art. 368 itself). The President must assent (24th Amendment, 1971); there is no joint sitting for amendment bills.

steps.title: Worked example: checking special majority
steps.body: Lok Sabha total membership 543; on the vote 450 are present and voting, and 310 vote yes. Condition 1: 310 > 543/2 = 271.5 ✓. Condition 2: two-thirds of 450 = 300; 310 ≥ 300 ✓. The bill passes in Lok Sabha. If only 290 had voted yes, condition 1 holds (290 > 271.5) but condition 2 fails (290 < 300), so it would fail.

steps.title: Case trail
steps.body: Shankari Prasad (1951) and Sajjan Singh (1965): Parliament can amend FRs. Golaknath (1967, 11 judges): cannot. 24th Amendment (1971) reasserted power. Kesavananda Bharati (24 April 1973, 13 judges, 7:6): basic structure doctrine. Indira Gandhi v Raj Narain (1975): free and fair elections part of basic structure. Minerva Mills (1980): limited amending power is itself basic. Waman Rao (1981): Ninth Schedule laws after 24 April 1973 open to review; I.R. Coelho (2007) reaffirmed.

steps.title: Elements of basic structure (judicially identified)
steps.body: Supremacy of the Constitution, republican and democratic form, secularism, separation of powers, federalism, judicial review, rule of law, free and fair elections, parliamentary system, harmony between FRs and DPSPs, independence of judiciary (Fourth Judges / NJAC case 2015).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Special majority is NOT simply two-thirds of total membership. Basic structure is a judicial doctrine; it is not listed in the text.

quiz.q: Rajya Sabha has 245 members; 200 present and voting; 125 vote yes. Does it meet special majority?
options: No — fails majority of total membership
No — fails two-thirds of present and voting
quiz.why: 125 exceeds half of 245 (122.5), but two-thirds of 200 is about 133.3, so the second test fails.

quiz.why: The 13-judge bench split 7:6.

quiz.q: Amendments affecting federal provisions need ratification by
quiz.why: Article 368(2) proviso requires ratification by legislatures of not less than half the states.

courses.title: Unit 2 · Union Executive and Parliament
curricula: UGC CBCS / NEP 2020 (Indian Government and Politics core)
courses.summary: The President, Vice-President, Prime Minister and Council of Ministers; composition and powers of Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha; legislative and financial procedure; parliamentary committees and the anti-defection law.
outcomes: Explain the election, powers and position of the President
Analyse the Prime Minister's role and collective responsibility
Compare Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha and trace how a bill becomes law
Explain money bills, budget procedure, committees and the Tenth Schedule

scenes.text: Rashtrapati Bhavan houses the head of the world's largest democracy.
Most decisions are signed on ministerial advice — yet some moments call for discretion.
Understanding when the President can act alone is key.

steps.title: Election (Arts 54–55)
steps.body: Elected indirectly by an electoral college of elected members of both Houses of Parliament and elected members of state Legislative Assemblies (including Delhi and Puducherry, added by the 70th Amendment), by proportional representation by single transferable vote with secret ballot. Value of an MLA's vote = (state population as per 1971 census ÷ elected MLAs) ÷ 1000. Value of an MP's vote = total value of all MLA votes ÷ total elected MPs.

steps.title: Worked example: value of an MLA vote
steps.body: Uttar Pradesh: 1971 population 8,38,49,905; 403 elected MLAs. 83,849,905 ÷ 403 = 208,064.28; ÷ 1000 = 208.06 → 208 (fraction under 0.5 ignored). Total UP value = 208 × 403 = 83,824. Sikkim: 1971 population 2,09,843; 32 MLAs. 209,843 ÷ 32 = 6,557.6; ÷ 1000 = 6.56 → 7. So a UP MLA's vote counts about 30 times a Sikkim MLA's.

steps.title: Powers
steps.body: Executive (appoints PM, ministers, Governors, judges, CAG, CEC); legislative (summons/prorogues, dissolves Lok Sabha, addresses Parliament, assent/withholding/return of bills, ordinances under Art. 123); financial (money bills only on recommendation); judicial (pardons under Art. 72); emergency (Arts 352, 356, 360); military (Supreme Commander).

steps.title: Position
steps.body: Art. 74(1): Council of Ministers with PM at head to aid and advise; the 42nd Amendment made advice binding, and the 44th allowed the President to return advice once for reconsideration. Discretion arises in: appointing PM in a hung House, suspensive veto, pocket veto (no time limit for ordinary bills — Zail Singh and the Indian Post Office (Amendment) Bill, 1986). Impeachment under Art. 61 for 'violation of the Constitution' needs two-thirds of total membership in each House.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Nominated members and MLCs do NOT vote in presidential elections. Pocket veto is not available for constitutional amendment bills (24th Amendment requires assent).

activity.prompt: Match the Article to the power

quiz.q: A state with 1971 population 5,00,00,000 and 250 MLAs: value of each MLA's vote is
Who does NOT vote in the presidential election?
quiz.why: Only elected members form the electoral college under Article 54.

quiz.q: The pocket veto was famously used by
quiz.why: Zail Singh kept the 1986 Post Office (Amendment) Bill pending indefinitely.

lessons.title: Prime Minister and Council of Ministers

scenes.text: The Prime Minister announces a major policy on national television.
In Cabinet, ministers debate; once decided, all must defend it in Parliament.
The PM is the keystone of the cabinet arch.

steps.title: Appointment and size
steps.body: Art. 75: the President appoints the PM and, on the PM's advice, other ministers. A non-member may be minister for 6 months. The 91st Amendment (2003) caps the Council of Ministers at 15% of Lok Sabha strength (so at most 81 for 543 members) and debars defectors from ministerial office.

steps.title: Collective and individual responsibility
steps.body: Art. 75(3): the Council is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha — it stands or falls together; a no-confidence motion (Lok Sabha Rule 198, needs support of 50 members to be admitted) brings it down. Ministers hold office during the pleasure of the President (individual responsibility, effectively to the PM). Ranks: Cabinet ministers, Ministers of State (independent charge or attached), Deputy Ministers.

steps.title: Role of the PM
steps.body: Leader of the majority, chair of Cabinet, link between President and Cabinet (Art. 78 duty to communicate decisions), chief spokesperson, chair of NITI Aayog, leader of foreign policy. Debate: from 'primus inter pares' (first among equals) to 'prime-ministerial government', especially under dominant leaders; coalition eras (1989–2014) diluted PM power.

steps.title: Worked example: maximum ministry size
steps.body: Lok Sabha strength 543 × 15% = 81.45 → maximum 81 ministers including the PM. For a state assembly of 60 members, 15% is 9, but the 91st Amendment sets a minimum of 12, so up to 12 ministers are allowed.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: The Council is responsible to Lok Sabha only, not Rajya Sabha. 'Cabinet' was mentioned in the text only in Art. 352 (inserted by the 44th Amendment).

statements.s: The Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the Rajya Sabha.
statements.why: Article 75(3) makes it responsible to the House of the People.

statements.s: The 91st Amendment limits the ministry to 15% of the Lok Sabha.
statements.why: It inserted Article 75(1A) in 2003.

statements.s: A non-MP can be appointed minister for up to six months.
statements.why: Article 75(5) allows six months to become a member.

statements.s: The PM chairs NITI Aayog.
statements.why: The Prime Minister is the ex officio Chairperson of NITI Aayog.

quiz.why: Collective responsibility is owed to the Lok Sabha.

quiz.q: For a 40-member state assembly, the maximum ministry size is
quiz.why: 15% of 40 is 6, but the minimum of 12 applies.

options: Duty of PM to inform the President
quiz.why: Article 78 obliges the PM to communicate Cabinet decisions and furnish information.

scenes.text: A Digital Personal Data Protection Bill is introduced in the Lok Sabha.
It goes through readings, committee scrutiny and Rajya Sabha debate.
Only after presidential assent does it become an Act.

steps.title: Composition
steps.body: Lok Sabha (Art. 81): maximum 550 elected (530 states + 20 UTs; currently 543) — the provision for 2 nominated Anglo-Indians ended by the 104th Amendment (2019). Term 5 years. Rajya Sabha (Art. 80): maximum 250 (238 elected by state/UT MLAs via STV + 12 nominated for art, science, literature, social service); currently 245 seats. Permanent body; one-third members retire every second year; term 6 years. Vice-President is ex officio Chairman.

steps.title: Ordinary bill procedure
steps.body: First reading (introduction), second reading (general discussion → may go to select/joint committee or departmental standing committee → clause-by-clause consideration), third reading (passage). Then the other House repeats. In deadlock, the President may call a joint sitting (Art. 108), presided by the Speaker — used for Dowry Prohibition (1961), Banking Service Commission Repeal (1978), Prevention of Terrorism Act (2002).

steps.title: Money bills (Art. 110)
steps.body: Introduced only in Lok Sabha on the President's recommendation; Speaker certifies a money bill (final). Rajya Sabha can only recommend amendments within 14 days; Lok Sabha may reject them. No joint sitting. Budget = Annual Financial Statement (Art. 112); stages: presentation, general discussion, scrutiny by departmental committees, voting on demands for grants (Lok Sabha only), Appropriation Bill (Art. 114), Finance Bill. Cut motions: disapproval of policy (to ₹1), economy cut, token cut (₹100).

steps.title: Worked example: Rajya Sabha retirement
steps.body: With 233 elected Rajya Sabha members from states/UTs, roughly one-third — about 77–78 seats — fall vacant every two years, so the House never dissolves and its composition changes gradually.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Joint sitting is presided over by the Speaker, not the Vice-President. Money bills and constitutional amendment bills never go to joint sittings.

items: Same stages in the other House

quiz.q: Rajya Sabha must return a money bill within
quiz.why: Article 109 gives the Rajya Sabha 14 days, after which the bill is deemed passed.

quiz.q: Who presides over a joint sitting?
quiz.why: Article 118(4) makes the Speaker preside.

quiz.q: Who decides whether a bill is a money bill?
quiz.why: Article 110(3) makes the Speaker's decision final.
Article 80 provides 12 nominated members with special knowledge.

scenes.text: The CAG reports wasteful spending in a defence deal.
The Public Accounts Committee, chaired by an opposition MP, questions officials.
Committees let Parliament scrutinise detail the floor never could.

steps.title: Financial committees
steps.body: Public Accounts Committee: 22 members (15 LS + 7 RS); examines CAG audit reports; by convention chaired by an opposition member since 1967. Estimates Committee: 30 members, all from Lok Sabha; suggests economies. Committee on Public Undertakings: 22 (15 + 7).

steps.title: Departmentally Related Standing Committees
steps.body: Set up in 1993; now 24 DRSCs, each 31 members (21 LS + 10 RS). They examine demands for grants, bills referred to them and annual reports. Other tools of accountability: Question Hour, Zero Hour (Indian innovation, not in rules originally), calling attention, adjournment motion, short-duration discussion.

steps.title: Anti-defection law (Tenth Schedule)
steps.body: Added by the 52nd Amendment (1985). A member is disqualified if they voluntarily give up party membership or vote/abstain against the party whip without permission (not condoned within 15 days). An independent joining a party, or a nominated member joining after 6 months, is disqualified. Merger exception: two-thirds of the legislature party agreeing to merge. The 1/3 'split' exception was deleted by the 91st Amendment (2003). Kihoto Hollohan (1992): Presiding Officer's decision subject to judicial review.

steps.title: Worked example: merger threshold
steps.body: A party has 37 MLAs. For a valid merger, two-thirds must agree: 2/3 × 37 = 24.67, so at least 25 MLAs are needed. If 24 leave, they are not protected and face disqualification.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Estimates Committee has no Rajya Sabha members. Since 2003 a 'split' by one-third is no longer a defence.

quiz.why: Two-thirds of 52 is 34.67, so 35 members are needed.

courses.title: Unit 3 · Judiciary, Federalism and Local Government
curricula: UGC CBCS / NEP 2020 (Indian Government and Politics core)
courses.summary: Supreme Court and High Courts, judicial review, activism and PIL, appointment of judges; Centre–state legislative, administrative and financial relations; Governor; emergency provisions; Panchayati Raj and urban local bodies.
outcomes: Describe the jurisdiction of the Supreme Court and the collegium debate
Explain judicial review, activism and PIL with cases
Analyse Centre–state relations, the Governor's role and Article 356
Explain the 73rd and 74th Amendments and evaluate local democracy

lessons.title: Supreme Court, judicial review and appointments

scenes.text: In the early 1980s, letters from prisoners and activists reached Supreme Court judges.
Justice P.N. Bhagwati and others treated them as writ petitions.
Public Interest Litigation opened the court's doors to the voiceless.

steps.title: Structure and jurisdiction
steps.body: Supreme Court (Art. 124): Chief Justice and up to 33 other judges (sanctioned strength 34 after the 2019 Act). Jurisdiction: original (Art. 131 — Centre–state and inter-state disputes), writ (Art. 32), appellate (Arts 132–134 and special leave under Art. 136), advisory (Art. 143 — e.g. Ayodhya reference 1993, Special Reference 1998 on appointments), court of record (Art. 129, contempt power), review of its own judgments (Art. 137). Judges retire at 65 (High Court: 62); removal by Parliament on 'proved misbehaviour or incapacity' (Art. 124(4)) by special majority.

steps.title: Judicial review
steps.body: Power to declare laws and executive actions void if they violate the Constitution (Arts 13, 32, 226). Indian review is narrower than the US 'due process' model originally — 'procedure established by law' (Art. 21) — but Maneka Gandhi (1978) required the procedure to be 'just, fair and reasonable', bringing in substantive due process in effect.

steps.title: Activism and PIL
steps.body: PIL relaxed locus standi: S.P. Gupta (1981), Hussainara Khatoon (1979, undertrial prisoners), Bandhua Mukti Morcha (1984, bonded labour), M.C. Mehta cases (environment), Vishaka (1997, sexual harassment guidelines), Olga Tellis (1985). Critics warn of 'judicial overreach' into executive domain and separation-of-powers concerns.

steps.title: Appointments: the collegium
steps.body: First Judges (1981): executive primacy. Second Judges (1993): primacy to CJI with collegium. Third Judges (1998): collegium of CJI + four senior-most judges for the SC. The 99th Amendment and NJAC Act (2014) were struck down in the Fourth Judges case (2015) as violating judicial independence, restoring the collegium.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Article 131 original jurisdiction excludes private citizens. Advisory opinions under Art. 143 are not binding on the President.

activity.prompt: Match the case to its contribution
pairs: Procedure must be just, fair and reasonable

quiz.q: Disputes between the Centre and a state go to the SC under its
quiz.why: Article 131 gives exclusive original jurisdiction over federal disputes.
Article 124(2) sets the retirement age at 65.
Any public-spirited person could approach the court on behalf of those unable to.

quiz.q: Which Article lets the President seek the SC's advice?
quiz.why: Article 143 provides advisory jurisdiction.

scenes.text: At midnight on 1 July 2017, Parliament's Central Hall launched GST.
Centre and states had pooled taxing powers in a new GST Council.
Cooperative federalism — but states still argue over compensation and votes.

steps.title: Legislative relations
steps.body: Seventh Schedule: Union List (originally 97 entries, now about 98–100 after amendments), State List (originally 66, now 61), Concurrent List (originally 47, now 52). Residuary powers with Parliament (Art. 248). Parliament can legislate on State List: in national interest on a Rajya Sabha resolution by two-thirds present and voting (Art. 249), during emergency (Art. 250), on request of two or more states (Art. 252), to implement treaties (Art. 253). Repugnancy: Union law prevails on Concurrent List (Art. 254). The 42nd Amendment moved education, forests, weights and measures, wildlife and administration of justice to Concurrent.

steps.title: Administrative and financial relations
steps.body: Arts 256–257: states must comply with Union laws; Centre may give directions. All-India Services (Art. 312). Finance: Finance Commission every five years (Art. 280) recommends sharing of central taxes (15th FC: 41% to states for 2021–26). GST (101st Amendment, 2016) created the GST Council (Art. 279A) — Union has one-third of votes, states two-thirds; decisions need three-fourths of weighted votes.

steps.title: Worked example: GST Council vote
steps.body: Union weight = 1/3 = 33.33%; states together 2/3 = 66.67%, shared equally among states present. Passing needs ≥ 75%. If the Union supports, states supplying at least 75 − 33.33 = 41.67 percentage points must agree, i.e. 41.67 / 66.67 = 62.5% of states present. Without the Union, states maximum = 66.67% < 75%, so nothing passes — the Union effectively has a veto, and so does any bloc of states holding more than 25% weight (i.e. more than 37.5% of states present).

steps.title: Commissions
steps.body: Administrative Reforms Commission (1966), Rajamannar Committee (Tamil Nadu, 1969), Anandpur Sahib Resolution (1973), Sarkaria Commission (1983–88: Governor should be eminent outsider, Art. 356 as last resort, Inter-State Council — set up 1990 under Art. 263), Punchhi Commission (2007–10).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Residuary powers in India lie with the Union (like Canada), not the states (like the USA). Art. 249 needs a Rajya Sabha resolution, not Lok Sabha.

quiz.why: Article 248 gives Parliament exclusive power over residuary matters.

quiz.q: The Inter-State Council was set up in 1990 on recommendation of
quiz.why: Sarkaria recommended a permanent body under Article 263.
Article 279A(9) requires at least three-fourths of weighted votes.

quiz.q: Education moved to the Concurrent List via the
quiz.why: The 42nd Amendment (1976) transferred it from the State List.

scenes.text: A state government is dismissed by a Governor's report before it can test its majority.
Years later, the Supreme Court rules the floor of the House is the proper test.
S.R. Bommai reshaped the use of Article 356.

steps.title: The Governor
steps.body: Appointed by the President (Art. 155), holds office during pleasure (Art. 156), normally 5 years. Acts on advice of the state Council of Ministers (Art. 163) except discretionary functions: appointing CM in a hung assembly, reporting under Art. 356, reserving bills for the President (Art. 200), special responsibilities (e.g. Art. 371 for some states). B.P. Singhal (2010): Governors cannot be removed arbitrarily. Nabam Rebia (2016): Governor cannot summon assembly at own discretion against advice when the government has majority.

steps.title: Three emergencies
steps.body: National emergency (Art. 352): war, external aggression or armed rebellion ('internal disturbance' replaced by 44th Amendment); written advice of Cabinet; approval by both Houses within one month by special majority; renewable every 6 months. Imposed 1962, 1971, 1975. President's rule (Art. 356): failure of constitutional machinery; approval within 2 months by simple majority; max 3 years (beyond one year only with national emergency + ECI certificate). Financial emergency (Art. 360): never imposed.

steps.title: S.R. Bommai (1994)
steps.body: Nine-judge bench: Art. 356 proclamation is subject to judicial review; majority must be tested on the floor; the assembly should be kept in suspended animation until Parliament approves; secularism is basic structure and a state acting against it may face Art. 356. Use of Art. 356 has declined sharply since.

steps.title: Worked example: timelines
steps.body: President's rule proclaimed on 1 March. Must be approved by both Houses by about 1 May (2 months). If approved, valid for 6 months from 1 March → 1 September; renewable in 6-month steps up to 3 years.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: National emergency approval needs special majority; Art. 356 approval needs only simple majority. Article 19 is suspended automatically only in an emergency for war/external aggression (Art. 358), not armed rebellion.

pairs: War, external aggression or armed rebellion
Failure of constitutional machinery in a state
Floor test and judicial review of Art. 356

quiz.q: A national emergency must be approved by Parliament within
quiz.why: After the 44th Amendment, approval is required within one month.
Article 360 has never been invoked.

quiz.q: The Governor reserves bills for the President under Article
quiz.why: Article 200 lists assent, withholding, return or reservation.

lessons.title: Panchayati Raj and urban local bodies

scenes.text: A woman is elected sarpanch on a reserved seat.
At first her husband attends meetings as 'sarpanch-pati'.
By her second term she runs the gram sabha herself — reservation slowly changes power.

steps.title: Committees before 1992
steps.body: Balwant Rai Mehta Committee (1957): three-tier system (village, block, district) — first launched at Nagaur, Rajasthan, on 2 October 1959. Ashok Mehta Committee (1977–78): two-tier, party participation. G.V.K. Rao (1985) and L.M. Singhvi (1986): constitutional status.

steps.title: 73rd Amendment (1992) — Part IX
steps.body: Gram sabha (Art. 243A); three tiers (intermediate tier optional for states with population under 20 lakh); direct elections; reservation for SC/ST in proportion to population and not less than one-third for women (many states now 50%); five-year term with election within 6 months of dissolution; State Election Commission (243K); State Finance Commission every 5 years (243I); Eleventh Schedule — 29 subjects. PESA Act 1996 extends to Fifth Schedule areas.

steps.title: 74th Amendment (1992) — Part IXA
steps.body: Nagar panchayat (transitional area), municipal council (smaller urban), municipal corporation (larger urban); ward committees for populations of 3 lakh or more; District Planning Committee (243ZD); Metropolitan Planning Committee (243ZE) for areas of 10 lakh+; Twelfth Schedule — 18 subjects.

steps.title: Worked example: seats
steps.body: A panchayat samiti has 30 seats; SC population 20%, ST 10%. SC seats ≈ 0.20 × 30 = 6, ST = 0.10 × 30 = 3. Women: not less than one-third of total = 10 (including women's seats within SC/ST). Under a 50% law, women get 15.

steps.title: Evaluation
steps.body: Gains: about 31 lakh elected representatives, over 14 lakh women (Ministry of Panchayati Raj figures). Problems: '3Fs' deficit — functions, funds, functionaries not fully devolved; proxy representation; dependence on state grants.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Eleventh Schedule = 29 subjects (panchayats); Twelfth = 18 (municipalities). Not the other way round.

quiz.why: One-third of 45 is 15.

quiz.why: The Eleventh Schedule lists 29 subjects for panchayats.

quiz.q: Metropolitan Planning Committees are for areas with population of at least
quiz.why: Article 243P defines a metropolitan area as 10 lakh or more.

questions.why: Article 136 gives the Supreme Court discretionary appellate power.
Article 217 fixes the age at 62.

questions.why: It expanded the collegium to five for Supreme Court appointments.

options: Rajya Sabha by two-thirds present and voting
questions.why: Article 249 requires a Rajya Sabha resolution with two-thirds support.

questions.why: It recommended 41% for 2021–26, adjusting for the creation of two UTs from J&K.

questions.why: Article 279A gives the Centre one-third of total votes.

questions.why: Article 356(3) requires approval by both Houses within two months.
The nine-judge judgment came in March 1994.

questions.why: The 44th Amendment replaced internal disturbance with armed rebellion.

questions.why: Nehru inaugurated it at Nagaur, Rajasthan, on 2 October 1959.
It extends Part IX with modifications to Fifth Schedule tribal areas.

questions.why: Article 243S requires them where population is three lakh or more.

courses.title: Unit 4 · Parties, Elections and Social Dynamics
curricula: UGC CBCS / NEP 2020 (Indian Government and Politics core)
courses.summary: Evolution of the party system, the Election Commission and electoral reforms, and the role of caste, religion, region, class and social movements in Indian politics.
outcomes: Trace the party system from the 'Congress system' to coalition and dominant-party phases
Explain the Election Commission's powers and the FPTP system with its effects
Analyse caste, religion and regionalism as forces in politics
Evaluate new social movements in India

scenes.text: In the 1950s one big umbrella — Congress — sheltered many groups.
From 1967 storms came: states elected non-Congress governments.
By 1989 coalitions became normal; since 2014 a new dominant party has emerged.

steps.title: Phase 1: The 'Congress system' (1952–67)
steps.body: Rajni Kothari called it the 'Congress system' — a one-party dominant system where factions within Congress performed the competitive function, and opposition parties acted as 'parties of pressure' on the margin. W.H. Morris-Jones also stressed Congress's consensus role.

steps.title: Phase 2: Challenge and restoration (1967–89)
steps.body: 1967: Congress lost power in several states (Samyukta Vidhayak Dal governments); 'Aaya Ram Gaya Ram' defections. 1969 Congress split. 1971 'Garibi Hatao' victory. Emergency (1975–77) → Janata Party government (1977), the first non-Congress Union government. Congress returned in 1980 and 1984.

steps.title: Phase 3: Coalition era (1989–2014)
steps.body: No single party majority in Lok Sabha from 1989 to 2014; National Front, United Front, NDA (1998–2004), UPA (2004–14). Rise of regional and caste-based parties (BSP, SP, RJD, TDP, DMK/AIADMK); Yogendra Yadav called it a 'third electoral system' with federalisation of the party system.

steps.title: Phase 4: Since 2014
steps.body: BJP won a single-party majority in 2014 (282 seats) and 2019 (303); scholars (e.g. Suhas Palshikar) discussed a new 'BJP system'. In 2024 the BJP won 240 seats and governs with NDA allies — coalition dynamics returned.

steps.title: Recognition of parties
steps.body: The Election Commission recognises national and state parties under the Election Symbols (Reservation and Allotment) Order, 1968, based on vote share and seats (e.g. a national party: recognised as a state party in at least four states, or 2% of Lok Sabha seats from at least three states, or 6% votes in four states plus 4 Lok Sabha seats).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: 'Congress system' is Kothari's term, not Morris-Jones's. Coalition era begins 1989 at the Centre, though states had coalitions from 1967.

quiz.why: Kothari's 1964 essay described Congress dominance with internal competition.

quiz.q: The first non-Congress government at the Centre was formed in
quiz.why: The Janata Party formed it after the 1977 election.
It came from a Haryana MLA who changed parties three times in a fortnight in 1967.

story.title: The polling booth in Gir forest

scenes.text: Every election, officials set up a booth in Gir forest for a single voter.
The rule: no voter should travel more than 2 km to vote.
It symbolises the Election Commission's commitment to universal franchise.

steps.title: Election Commission (Art. 324)
steps.body: Superintendence, direction and control of elections to Parliament, state legislatures, President and Vice-President. Multi-member since 1993 (CEC + 2 ECs). CEC removable like a Supreme Court judge. Anoop Baranwal (2023) proposed a selection committee; Parliament then passed the CEC and Other ECs (Appointment, Conditions of Service and Term of Office) Act, 2023. Tools: Model Code of Conduct (no statutory basis, enforced through moral and administrative authority), EVMs (used nationwide since 2004), VVPAT, NOTA (introduced 2013 after PUCL v Union of India).

steps.title: First-past-the-post (FPTP)
steps.body: Single-member constituencies; the candidate with the most votes wins, even without a majority. Effects: seat–vote disproportionality, strategic voting, 'Duverger's law' tendency toward two-party competition at constituency level. Rajya Sabha, President and Vice-President use STV.

steps.title: Worked example: seat–vote gap
steps.body: Constituency votes: A 38%, B 35%, C 27%. A wins with 38% — 62% voted against. Nationally, 2019: BJP won about 37.4% of votes but 303/543 = 55.8% of seats. Disproportionality = 55.8 − 37.4 ≈ 18.4 percentage points.

steps.title: Reforms
steps.body: Dinesh Goswami Committee (1990), Indrajit Gupta Committee (1998, state funding), Law Commission reports (170th, 1999; 255th, 2015). Disclosure of criminal records and assets (ADR case, 2002). Electoral bonds (2018) struck down by the Supreme Court in Association for Democratic Reforms v Union of India (Feb 2024). Debate on 'One Nation, One Election' (Kovind Committee report, 2024).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: The Model Code is not a law. NOTA votes do not cause re-election even if they are the largest — the top candidate still wins.

statements.s: The Election Commission became multi-member in 1993 and has remained so.
statements.why: Two Election Commissioners have served with the CEC since 1993.

statements.s: The Model Code of Conduct is a statute passed by Parliament.
statements.why: It is a consensus code enforced by the Commission, not a law.

statements.s: NOTA was introduced after a Supreme Court judgment in 2013.
statements.why: PUCL v Union of India (2013) directed a NOTA option.

statements.s: Lok Sabha elections use proportional representation.
statements.why: They use first-past-the-post in single-member constituencies.

quiz.q: A party gets 31% votes and 52% seats. Disproportionality is
quiz.why: 52 − 31 = 21 percentage points.

quiz.q: Electoral bonds were struck down in
quiz.why: The Constitution Bench ruled them unconstitutional in February 2024.
State MLAs elect Rajya Sabha members by single transferable vote.

story.title: Caste in politics or politics in caste?

scenes.text: A caste association in Gujarat becomes a vote bank.
Leaders must bargain beyond their caste to win.
Rajni Kothari: it is not just caste shaping politics — politics reshapes caste.

steps.title: Caste and politics
steps.body: Kothari (Caste in Indian Politics, 1970): politicisation of caste — caste becomes an interest group, transforming itself. Rudolph and Rudolph: 'The Modernity of Tradition' — caste associations as vehicles of democracy. M.N. Srinivas: 'dominant caste' and Sanskritisation. Mandal Commission (1980; implemented 1990) — 27% OBC reservation, 'Mandal politics'. Christophe Jaffrelot: 'silent revolution' of lower castes in North India.

steps.title: Religion and communalism
steps.body: Communalism: political mobilisation of religious identity against others (Bipan Chandra's stages: religious community has common interests → interests differ from others → interests are antagonistic). Key moments: Shah Bano (1985) and the Muslim Women Act (1986); Ram Janmabhoomi movement and Babri Masjid demolition (1992); Ayodhya verdict (2019). Debate between Nehruvian secularism and Hindutva nationalism.

steps.title: Regionalism
steps.body: Linguistic reorganisation: Potti Sriramulu's fast and Andhra State (1953); States Reorganisation Commission (Fazl Ali, 1955) → States Reorganisation Act 1956. New states: Maharashtra and Gujarat (1960), Nagaland (1963), Haryana (1966), Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, Uttarakhand (2000), Telangana (2014). Regional parties (DMK, Akali Dal, TDP, AGP) express sub-national identity; demands range from autonomy to secession (Khalistan, NE insurgencies).

steps.title: Worked example: analysing an election
steps.body: A party wins by consolidating Yadav + Muslim votes (M-Y). Analyse: caste/religious coalition; rival builds a non-Yadav OBC + Dalit + upper caste coalition. Kothari's point applies: identities are bundled through political strategy, not fixed.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Mandal Commission report was submitted in 1980 but implemented in 1990 (V.P. Singh). SRC was chaired by Fazl Ali, with K.M. Panikkar and H.N. Kunzru as members.

activity.prompt: Match the concept to the scholar or event

quiz.q: Andhra State was created in 1953 after the fast of
quiz.why: Sriramulu's death after a 58-day fast forced creation of Andhra State.
It was formed on 2 June 2014.
Lloyd and Susanne Rudolph argued tradition can adapt to modern politics.

scenes.text: In 1973 villagers in Chamoli hugged trees to stop contractors felling them.
Women like Gaura Devi led the resistance.
Chipko became a symbol of India's environmental movement.

steps.title: Old and new social movements
steps.body: Old movements: class-based (peasant, trade-union). New social movements (NSMs): identity, environment, gender, human rights; often non-party, decentralised. Ghanshyam Shah's classification of Indian movements: peasant, tribal, Dalit, backward caste, women's, student, middle-class, human rights, environmental.

steps.title: Major Indian movements
steps.body: Chipko (1973, Uttarakhand — Sunderlal Bahuguna, Chandi Prasad Bhatt, Gaura Devi); Narmada Bachao Andolan (from 1985, Medha Patkar, Baba Amte); Dalit Panthers (1972, Maharashtra); women's movement (anti-dowry, Mathura rape case 1979 → 1983 law amendment); MKSS's right-to-information campaign in Rajasthan (1990s) → RTI Act 2005; India Against Corruption (2011, Anna Hazare) → Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act 2013; farmers' protests (2020–21) → repeal of three farm laws (November 2021).

steps.title: Worked example: movement → policy
steps.body: MKSS held jan sunwais (public hearings) reading out panchayat accounts; this showed the power of information. National Campaign for People's Right to Information built pressure; Rajasthan passed an RTI law (2000), then Parliament passed the RTI Act 2005 — a clear chain from movement to law.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Narmada Bachao Andolan opposed the Sardar Sarovar dam displacement; it was not part of Chipko. MKSS was founded by Aruna Roy, Nikhil Dey and Shanker Singh.

quiz.why: It began in Chamoli district in 1973.

quiz.why: They were founded in Mumbai in 1972, inspired by the Black Panthers.

quiz.q: New social movements typically focus on
quiz.why: NSMs centre on identity, quality of life and rights rather than class alone.

questions.why: No single party won a Lok Sabha majority in that period.

questions.why: Yadav used it for the post-1989 federalised, plural party system.

questions.why: It won 240 seats and formed the government with NDA allies.
Article 324(5) protects the CEC with SC-judge-like removal.

questions.why: FPTP elects the candidate with the most votes, even without a majority.

M.N. Srinivas described lower castes adopting upper-caste practices to rise.

questions.why: It reorganised states on linguistic lines in 1956.

questions.why: Parliament passed it in 1986 after the 1985 Shah Bano judgment.

questions.why: Telangana was formed in 2014.

questions.why: The extreme stage treats other communities' interests as hostile.
Plurality single-member districts encourage competition between two main parties.

scenes.text: Counting trends flash across TV screens.
A student learns to compute vote share, seat share and swing.
Numbers become political arguments.

steps.title: Data (hypothetical state, 80 seats)
steps.body: Party P: 42% votes, 48 seats. Party Q: 36% votes, 26 seats. Party R: 15% votes, 5 seats. Others: 7% votes, 1 seat.

steps.title: Step 2: seat–vote gaps
steps.body: P: 60 − 42 = +18; Q: 32.5 − 36 = −3.5; R: 6.25 − 15 = −8.75; Others: 1.25 − 7 = −5.75. FPTP rewards the leader and punishes spread-out smaller parties.

steps.title: Step 3: swing
steps.body: If last time P had 38% and Q 40%, P gained 4 points and Q lost 4 points. Butler swing = (4 + 4)/2 = 4 points from Q to P.

steps.title: Step 4: majority mark
steps.body: Majority = more than half of 80 = 41 seats. P (48) has a majority on its own.

steps.title: Interpretation
steps.body: In an answer, connect numbers to theory: Duverger's law, regional party consolidation, or anti-incumbency.

scenes.text: Three questions, 90 minutes.
Outline first, write second.
Check every answer against the self-check list.

steps.title: Q1 (15 marks)
steps.body: 'The Indian Constitution is federal in form but unitary in spirit.' Discuss. Outline: Wheare/Austin ('cooperative federalism'); federal features; unitary features; Bommai; GST Council; Finance Commission; conclusion — 'federation with a centralising tendency' moderated by courts and coalition politics.

steps.title: Q2 (15 marks)
steps.body: Evaluate the role of the Supreme Court as guardian of the Constitution. Outline: jurisdictions; judicial review; basic structure; PIL; ADM Jabalpur as a failure; collegium debate; overreach critique; conclusion.

steps.title: Q3 (10 marks)
steps.body: Explain the changing nature of the party system in India. Outline: four phases with years and seat numbers; Kothari, Yadav, Palshikar; regionalisation.

steps.title: Q4 (5 marks)
steps.body: Short note on the Tenth Schedule. Outline: 52nd Amendment; grounds; merger two-thirds; 91st Amendment; Kihoto Hollohan.
